articles.title: Zelensky in Oslo for talks with US envoys as Ukraine claims missile holdup
articles.body:
Ukraine ‘losing people and time’, Zelensky says after Oslo talks
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has wrapped up talks with US envoys in Norway Tuesday where he was determined to put diplomacy back on a "more constructive path”, Oslo officials said. Zelensky told a post-meeting press briefing that Ukraine was not losing the war but was “losing people and time”, adding that he was hopeful moving forward because “we have some clear ideas of how to get peace”.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky held talks in Oslo on Tuesday with top US envoys in a bid to get strained relations with Washington "on a more constructive path", Oslo said.
Following the talks, the Ukrainian leader told a press briefing that although Ukraine was not losing the war, it was “losing people and time”.

He said several European countries were ready to transfer Patriot interceptor missiles from their own stockpiles but were still awaiting US approval.

"To be honest, I think it's time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine."

articles.title: Ukraine must join potential Trump-Putin-Xi talks: Zelenskyy
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Tuesday that Kyiv must be included in any talks on the war in Ukraine involving U.S. President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping, following reports of a possible meeting among the three leaders.
"I don't know what the trilateral meeting will be about between America and China, and Russia, it's up to them. But of course, if there are issues about Ukraine, our future, it can be acceptable only when we are at the table of negotiations. It's absolutely clear," Zelenskyy told reporters in Oslo.
Zelenskyy also said Tuesday that Kyiv is once again receiving early warnings from its partners following recent Russian missile attacks that he said occurred without enough notice.
For at least a week, the Ukrainian leader has said that his country's military has not received early warnings about ballistic missiles aimed at the capital. He said such intelligence saves lives by allowing alerts to the public and giving military units time to try to intercept the missiles.
Zelenskyy said the change happened after talks with his American counterparts, including a phone call with Secretary of State Marco Rubio earlier in the day.
"We are thankful that intelligence works now, and I'm speaking about early warning, which is very important for our people, for children, adults, civilians, because we can hear when ballistic is coming," Zelenskyy said on a visit to Norway. "So we are thankful to American side now that it works."
In other developments, Russia unleashed another missile and drone blitz of civilian areas in Ukraine, killing at least nine people, officials said, as Zelenskyy sought more American and European help during meetings in Norway.
Zelenskyy was joined in Norway by U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff, who has tried without success to steer Russia and Ukraine toward a settlement to end the war. Jared Kushner, another envoy who is U.S. President Donald Trump's son-in-law, was due to attend a meeting with Zelenskyy by videoconference.
Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb also met with Zelenskyy in Norway's capital.
"We are maintaining all contacts that can help bring peace," Zelenskyy said in a post on X after he arrived in Oslo. He said officials gathered in Norway would discuss strengthening Ukraine's air defenses and joint production of weapons.
Meanwhile, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told reporters that Moscow hopes a meeting in Russia between the envoys and Russian President Vladimir Putin can be organized soon, perhaps as early as Wednesday.
"We highly appreciate the mediation efforts of the American negotiators," Peskov said.
With further U.S. support for Ukraine in doubt as relations between Zelenskyy and Trump sour again, the Ukrainian leader said he spoke with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is on a trip to Asia.
That conversation came after Zelenskyy told a bipartisan group of U.S. lawmakers Monday that he believes "some political decision has been made to slow down... support for us."
Ukraine has nearly run out of American-made Patriot air-defense interceptors that it needs to stop Russia's ballistic missiles, according to Zelenskyy, who has pleaded for Washington to send more. But he said the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles that other countries have purchased for Ukraine.
Zelenskyy also said he sought Rubio's help to ensure that the United States continues to share vital intelligence with Ukraine after Kyiv received no or belated warnings about Russian missile attacks in recent days.
The Ukrainian leader also said speed restrictions were still in place on his country's use of Starshield, the military-grade version of U.S. company SpaceX's satellite internet service Starlink, hampering battlefield operations.
Trump also has waived sanctions on Russia, a move that Zelenskyy slammed as helping Putin push on with Moscow's full-scale invasion, which will hit the five-year mark in February.
Zelenskyy said he had "a substantive conversation" with Rubio.
"I am grateful for his readiness to help and his clear position," Zelenskyy said on social media.
Rubio, who arrived Tuesday in India on an official trip, denied that the U.S. is withholding assistance from Ukraine.
"Nothing has changed," he told reporters.
The Patriot ammunition Ukraine needs is in short supply and is also required elsewhere in the world, Rubio said.
"There has not been some deliberate political directive to go out and harm Ukraine," he said.
With the Russian army held up on the front line, Putin is trying to bomb Ukraine into submission while robbing it of vital U.S. support, Western leaders and analysts say.
European countries, worried about Russia's plans on the continent and viewing Ukraine as a bulwark against Moscow's ambitions, are trying to take up the slack of any falloff in U.S. supplies, but some key assets are American-made.
European countries and European Union institutions have allocated 237 billion euros ($266 billion) to support Ukraine, compared with 115 billion euros ($129 billion) from the U.S., according to Germany's Kiel Institute, which tracks assistance to Kyiv.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas on Tuesday questioned whether U.S. negotiators have been honest brokers in peace efforts. Ukrainian officials say the Trump administration has encouraged Kyiv to surrender land to Russia in return for peace.
"Although American negotiators have been trying to push Ukraine into surrender for ... one and a half years now," Ukraine has not surrendered on Putin's terms "because Europe has been supporting Ukraine," Kallas said.
Four people were killed and 27 others wounded, including children, in Russian missile and drone attacks on the Kyiv region over the past day, regional police said.
Three were killed and six were wounded in the Obukhiv district, where warehouses were damaged, police said. In the Bucha district, one woman was killed and 21 people were wounded, eight of them children, while hundreds of buildings were damaged, according to police.
On Tuesday morning, three people were killed and four injured when two vehicles caught fire in a Russian attack on the Kyiv-Odesa highway, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said. The dead included the driver of a shuttle bus that was hit. The bus transports people from Kyiv to the National Military Memorial Cemetery.
Two more people were killed in a Russian attack Tuesday on warehouses on the outskirts of Dnipro in central Ukraine, authorities said.
National grid operator Ukrenergo reported power outages in 12 regions of Ukraine following the Russian attacks.
The Russian Defense Ministry said in a statement that its forces carried out drone strikes on logistics centers, port infrastructure and three cargo ships in the port of Reni in the Odesa region. It said that another bulk carrier was hit at sea on its way to Odesa.
Meanwhile, air defenses intercepted 136 Ukrainian drones over multiple Russian regions overnight, the ministry said.

articles.title: Israel unveils new space warfare unit amid Gaza genocide
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Israel unveils new space warfare unit amid Gaza genocide
Israel has established a new military Space Division to expand its surveillance and warfare capabilities, raising questions about how the technology could be used against Palestinians amid its genocide in Gaza and continuing military occupation of the West Bank.
The Israeli military announced on Monday that Brigadier General "Shin", identified only by his first initial in Hebrew, had been appointed to command the division, which will operate under the military's Planning Directorate.
The new body will oversee space-related military operations, coordinate training and intelligence, and develop capabilities for what Israel increasingly regards as a separate arena of warfare.
The military said the division was established after it concluded that "the space domain has become an active combat domain" and would play an increasingly important role in future conflicts.
Welcoming the announcement on Tuesday, Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz described the initiative as part of his ambition to transform the country into a major military space power.
"The goal set for the IDF and the defense establishment is to make Israel one of the world's leading countries in the field of space security," Katz said, describing the project as "Star Wars, made in Israel."
He said Israel wanted the "ability to monitor, defend and attack from space any target across vast areas", arguing that such capabilities would strengthen its military dominance and deter adversaries.
Satellite surveillance and the war on Gaza
However, the expansion also carries significant implications for Palestinians, who have long been subjected to Israel's extensive military surveillance and intelligence operations.
Israel already operates a network of military reconnaissance satellites whose imagery is processed by Unit 9900, a specialised military intelligence formation responsible for visual and geospatial intelligence.
The unit's work includes identifying military targets and providing intelligence to support Israeli operations, including attacks in Gaza.
Its capabilities form part of a broader Israeli intelligence infrastructure that has been deployed during the war on Gaza, where surveillance technologies and digital targeting systems have come under growing scrutiny over their role in attacks that have killed large numbers of Palestinian civilians.
Human rights organisations have raised serious concerns about Israel's use of digital intelligence and automated targeting technologies during the war, including the reliability of information used to identify suspected targets and the risks posed to civilians.
Human Rights Watch warned in 2024 that Israel's reliance on digital targeting tools in Gaza raised concerns about inaccurate data and the potential for unlawful attacks.
Although the precise responsibilities of the new Space Division remain unclear, an expansion of Israel's satellite intelligence capabilities could further strengthen the military's ability to monitor Palestinian territory, track movements and identify potential targets.
Such technology could also be used to monitor roads, border crossings, infrastructure and changes in the urban landscape across Gaza and the occupied West Bank.
There is no confirmation that the new division will directly oversee operations against Palestinians, but its establishment could consolidate capabilities already used by Israel's military intelligence services.
The distinction is significant because satellite surveillance is not merely a means of observing territory. When integrated with military intelligence and targeting systems, it can contribute directly to decisions about where and when strikes are carried out.
Expanding Israel's military reach
Israel has continued to invest heavily in reconnaissance satellites, including its Ofek series, which provide imagery for intelligence gathering and military planning.
Until now, responsibility for space-related operations, including satellite launches and ballistic missile defence, has largely rested with the Israeli Air Force, while Unit 9900 has controlled military intelligence satellites after their deployment.
The Israeli military has not clarified which responsibilities will be transferred to the new division.
According to the military, several projects involving space-based sensors and space warfare capabilities have already been approved over the past year.
A new frontier for warfare
Israel's announcement also reflects intensifying international competition over the militarisation of space, with the US, Russia, China and India developing technologies intended to protect their own satellites or disrupt those operated by adversaries.
The 1967 Outer Space Treaty prohibits the placement of nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction in orbit but does not comprehensively prohibit conventional military activities in space.
Israel has also identified Iran's developing space capabilities as a potential threat.
During its conflict with Iran in March, the Israeli military claimed to have destroyed a facility in Tehran involved in military satellite development, alleging that it was also working on technology capable of attacking satellites.
The claims could not be independently verified.
Alongside the Space Division, Israel announced the establishment of a new Robotics Division under its Depth Corps, which conducts operations beyond the country's borders.
Military chief Eyal Zamir has also outlined plans to expand the military's use of unmanned systems and artificial intelligence, reflecting a wider effort to integrate advanced technologies into Israeli warfare.
The announcements come as Israel continues to expand its military capabilities despite mounting international scrutiny of its conduct in Gaza and the occupied Palestinian territories.

articles.title: Zelenskyy says if Trump can't stop Putin, help Ukraine do it
articles.body:
Ukraine's Zelenskyy says if Trump "cannot rein Putin in," at least clear interceptor missile shipment
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in an interview published Tuesday that if President Trump "cannot rein Putin in," he should provide long-requested interceptor missiles so Ukraine can defend itself, as the war of words between the two leaders continues to escalate.
"If you cannot rein Putin in, then give us interceptor missiles so I can protect our energy infrastructure," Zelenskyy told the Italian newspaper Corriere Della Sera, referring to Russia's autocratic President Vladimir Putin.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said later Tuesday that Mr. Trump has been "frustrated" by what he described as false accusations that "he is doing things to deliberately harm Ukraine." He insisted that nothing had been "deliberately denied to Ukraine," but added: "It's simply, it's a balance between our obligations to other partners and frankly our own ... requirements for our own facilities as well."
The exchange came as Zelenskyy prepared to meet U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff in Norway on Tuesday, with his fellow envoy, Mr. Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, expected to join remotely.
Zelenskyy has accused the Trump administration this week of delaying shipments of interceptor missiles to Ukraine, as well as constraining Starlink satellite data that is vital to Ukrainian forces' ability to intercept incoming Russian attack drones.
Ukraine has nearly run out of the U.S.-made Patriot air defense interceptors used to take down Russian ballistic missiles, and Zelenskyy has long pleaded for more. This week he said the U.S. was delaying delivery of Patriots already purchased by European nations for Ukraine.
Rubio, on a visit to India, said "every other country in the world" also wanted Patriots.
"I also talked to Saudi Arabia today. They'd like interceptors. Israel would like interceptors. We would like interceptors. Every country in the world would like interceptors," he said. "It's probably the most in-demand product right now in the defense field. So, when a country doesn't get interceptors from the United States, it's not because we're denying."
The meeting comes as daily Russian drone and missile attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities continue claiming civilian lives, and as relations between Kyiv and Washington appear more strained than they have been since Zelenskyy's tumultuous February 2025 meeting in the Oval Office.
The Ukrainian president said Monday that his country had suffered another night of Russian strikes, "and again there was no warning from partners." At least four people were killed in the capital in the latest attacks, Kyiv officials said Tuesday.
Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store said Finnish President Alexander Stubb would also join the talks in Oslo, with "the aim to put diplomatic efforts on a more constructive path," according to a statement from the prime minister's office.
Starshield and Patriots
Mr. Trump on Friday waived some sanctions against Russia, reducing penalties for its energy sales in a bid to ease rising U.S. gas prices caused by the ongoing war with Iran — a policy Zelenskyy says could embolden Moscow to step up its four-and-a-half-year invasion of Ukraine.
Mr. Trump has criticized Zelenskyy for saying he would resume strikes on Russian refineries in retaliation for the latest Russian onslaught.
Zelenskyy said Saturday that Ukraine was still unable to use Starshield — the military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite network — to intercept Russian drones.
The Trump administration has denied ordering Starshield restrictions. A senior Pentagon official told CBS News Monday that there had been "no change to Department of War policy regarding intelligence sharing or any capabilities we are enabling Europeans to provide to Ukraine."
In recent days, Mr. Trump has intensified his public criticism of Zelenskyy, saying in a Truth Social post that the Ukrainian leader "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did," and telling reporters, "maybe it's time for Zelenskyy to get somebody else to negotiate."
Mr. Trump has never publicly acknowledged that Russia started the war against its neighbor, which initially began in 2014, and has at times blamed Zelenskyy for the full-scale invasion ordered by Putin on Feb. 24, 2022.
Ahead of his Tuesday meeting with Mr. Trump's envoys, Zelenskyy said he had a "substantive conversation" with Rubio the previous day in which he stressed that Starshield "needs to be restored" and ballistic missile interceptors "are needed to protect lives."
Zelenskyy told a bipartisan group of U.S. lawmakers via video call on Monday that "the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles" already paid for by European countries. He said Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth hadn't signed off on the shipment.
Multiple European countries were waiting for U.S. approval to transfer their own Patriot interceptors, he added, saying he believed "some political decision has been made to slow down ... support for us."
Rubio said Tuesday that it could be accurate that a batch of interceptors purchased for Ukraine had not been delivered, but he told reporters: "I think the important takeaway for you is that there has not been some deliberate political directive to go out and harm Ukraine."
Rubio also said Mr. Trump was "frustrated because, first of all, he doesn't like to be blamed for things that aren't true, including accusations that somehow he had ordered intelligence sharing to be cut off. And that's not true. He's said that repeatedly."
"I think the president, more than anything, is responding to the insinuation that somehow he is doing things to deliberately harm Ukraine — which is not fair and not true," he added.
In his interview with the Italian newspaper, published hours earlier, Zelenskyy said Ukraine had built its relationship with Washington "on honesty, fairness, and, most importantly, transparency."
"When you lie while your people are at war, it is very painful. That is why I have always wanted to hide nothing and never lie to the President of the United States," Zelenskyy told the paper, adding: "We would like to continue having the same open, honest, and pragmatic relations with America that we have today."
"The Russians are striking. America cannot stop them," he said. "Let's believe that America really wants to, but cannot. Then, as a partner, I am willing to meet President Trump halfway: if they strike us and we cannot strike back — that is neither honest nor fair — but if this is what you need, if you cannot rein Putin in, then give us interceptor missiles so I can protect our energy infrastructure."
Trump-Xi-Putin summit on Ukraine?
U.S.-led efforts to end the nearly five-year conflict have stalled in recent months, with Washington more focused on its war with Iran.
Mr. Trump recently said he was ready to meet with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in China next month for talks that could include discussion of the Ukraine war.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has confirmed that "the topic of such a hypothetical has indeed been mentioned."
Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said this week that any such meeting on his country's fate, without Ukraine at the table, would "only encourage Putin to continue this war."

articles.title: Russia has stockpiled up to 700 ballistic and thousands of cruise missiles – Ukraine's Defence Intelligence
articles.body:
Russia has stockpiled up to 700 ballistic and thousands of cruise missiles – Ukraine's Defence Intelligence
Russia has stockpiled up to 700 ballistic missiles, several thousand cruise missiles of various types and over 6,000 strike drones for attacks on Ukraine as of October.
Source: Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU), as reported by NV
Details: DIU estimates that Russia currently has a stock of around 115 Iskander-M ballistic missiles and can produce up to 65 a month. Russia is also continuing to develop an upgraded version of the system with a projected range of 550-700 km, up from the current 500 km.
Kh-101 cruise missiles remain one of Russia's main weapons for large-scale strikes against Ukraine. Russia aims to produce more than 80 of them each month.
Russia is estimated to have over 450 Kalibr cruise missiles in its stockpiles and produces approximately 29 more each month. DIU said that, because Ukrainian air defences have proved highly effective, Russia is directing most newly manufactured missiles towards strategic reserves and naval forces.
Moscow's stockpiles include up to 400 RM-48U ballistic missiles, which have been adapted from the S-300PM and S-400 air defence systems for use against ground targets. Russia produces around 40 of these missiles each month.
The stockpile of modernised Oniks missiles, featuring an extended range and a more powerful warhead, exceeds 600. More than 55 were produced between January and July 2026.
The Russians' stock of Zircon hypersonic missiles is estimated to be over 120. Their production has been low, at just over 30 since the beginning of the year. Meanwhile, production of Kinzhal ballistic missiles has been temporarily halted due to accuracy issues, and manufacturing capacity has been shifted to conventional ballistic missiles.
Russia has also significantly expanded its capacity to produce long-range kamikaze drones at the Alabuga Special Economic Zone in Tatarstan. This year's state order for Geran-type attack drones and decoy drones exceeds 100,000 units. DIU says this "shows that the enemy is systematically seeking to wear down Ukrainian air defences".
Russia's operational reserve currently stands at around 6,200 Geran-type drones of various modifications, including jet-powered variants. Monthly UAV production has reached 10,000 units.
Since the summer of 2026, Russia has focused on manufacturing Geran-4 and Geran-5 jet-powered drones, assembling up to 4,000 units per month.
Russia also continues to produce up to 2,000 Geran-2 drones a month, alongside hundreds of cheap Gerber decoy drones made of plywood and foam. The decoys are designed to wear down Ukrainian air defences and help locate air defence missile systems.
Background:
- In June 2026, DIU reported that Russia was capable of launching up to 100 ballistic missiles per month while maintaining stockpiles at a stable level.
- On 10 August, Vadym Skibitskyi, Deputy Head of DIU, said Russia was increasing missile production for strikes against Ukraine, with output for the main types of Russian missiles reaching 110-120% of monthly targets, meaning pauses in strikes should not be expected.
- On 20 August, Ukrainska Pravda, citing intelligence data, reported that Russia had a stockpile of over 600 Oniks missiles, 450 Kalibrs and 120 Zircons. Meanwhile, the Russians had reoriented primary production capacity to boost output of 9M723 ballistic missiles for the Iskander-M system.
- On 8 September, at a meeting of the Ukraine-NATO Interparliamentary Council, Skibitskyi said that Russia was planning to test a new type of ballistic missile with a range of up to 800 km by the end of 2026.

articles.title: Rubio insists the US isn’t trying to hurt Ukraine
articles.body:
The Ukrainian president complained about delayed air defense deliveries, the U.S. no longer warning of ballistic missile attacks and a slowdown in crucial Starlink services.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the country had not changed its policy on sharing early warnings of Russian missile attacks with Ukraine and that the Pentagon was not deliberately withholding air defense missiles.
"There's nothing being deliberately denied to Ukraine," Rubio said during a visit to India Tuesday, calling reports that the U.S. was not giving Ukraine early warning of Russian ballistic missile attacks "outrageous."
"Everything they've been doing with Ukraine remains the same," he said of U.S. Department of Defense policy. "That has not changed. Nothing has changed."
Advertisement
Rubio's comments come as Russia escalates its attacks and Washington moves toward positions more favorable to Moscow, raising European concerns that the U.S. is not a dependable source of support for Ukraine.
Rubio was speaking shortly after the EU’s top diplomat Kaja Kallas accused Washington of trying to force Ukraine to surrender to Russia. "American negotiators have been trying to push Ukraine into surrender for already almost two years," she told the European Parliament on Tuesday morning.
On military equipment, Rubio said Ukraine's urgent appeals for more interceptors for Patriot air defense systems had to be balanced against U.S. needs — which are trying to restock thanks to the war against Iran— as well as the demands of other allies.
"I know one of the things that President Zelenskyy has been talking about is that he's been trying to buy interceptors. And I understand. So does every other country in the world," Rubio said. "I also talked to Saudi Arabia today. They'd like interceptors. Israel would like interceptors. We would like interceptors. Every country in the world would like interceptors."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Monday accused the U.S. of holding back on sending air-defense missiles paid for by allies under the NATO-led Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List program.
“Unfortunately, the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles that our partners have already paid for through the program PURL,” Zelenskyy said during a video briefing to U.S. lawmakers.
Advertisement
Zelenskyy also said that the U.S. is not always alerting Ukrainian authorities about incoming Russian ballistic missiles; such attacks have become more frequent and are killing people across Ukrainian cities.
"Unfortunately, we did not receive an early warning from our partners about the first wave of the Russian ballistic missile attack last night. And we are still facing speed restrictions on Starlink and Starshield services in various sectors of the front. The U.S. side has not provided Ukraine with any explanations regarding either of these two issues," Zelenskyy said in the Monday call.
U.S. early warning "always worked and then suddenly it malfunctioned. Nobody in Ukraine believes in this,” an official familiar with the matter told POLITICO on condition of anonymity. “Americans first said it happened because of weather conditions, then it was a software malfunction, then something else … They do not provide an official explanation.”
However, Rubio said the U.S. was looking into why Ukraine had problems with information about Russian missiles on Oct. 13 and 18, saying, "perhaps it was an internal issue in terms of them being able to take the information that was being provided and systemize it and react to it."
"I think the important takeaway for you is that there has not been some deliberate political directive to go out and harm Ukraine," Rubio said.
Ukraine is also complaining that Elon Musk's Starlink has throttled back speeds on its internet connections in Ukraine, making it difficult to intercept Russian drones.
Advertisement
Zelenskyy said Tuesday that he had raised the issues with Rubio.
"I am grateful for his willingness to help and his clear position. First, it's about interceptors against ballistic missiles, which are needed to protect lives. Second, it's about early warning of Russian ballistic missile attacks, which is vital. Third, it's about the situation around Starlink/Starshield, which needs to be restored," he said in a social media post.
The growing frictions with the U.S. come as President Donald Trump ramps up pressure on Kyiv to stop hitting Russian oil refineries and to reach a peace deal with Moscow.
“Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine ... They have not been doing that much,” Trump told reporters on Monday.
Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff traveled to Norway on Tuesday for a new round of talks on ending Russia's war against Ukraine.
U.N. Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine said that 328 civilians were killed and more than 2,000 wounded across Ukraine last month, an 85% increase from September 2025. The U.N. said that the first two weeks of October were among the deadliest for civilians in years, driven by intensified missile and drone strikes.
This story has been updated. Seb Starcevic contributed reporting.

articles.title: Ukraine wants F-16 repairs at more sites, tells Lockheed
articles.body:
- Ukraine’s defense minister and army chief met Lockheed Martin Aeronautics President Orlando Sanchez Jr. to discuss F-16 support and PAC-3 interceptor supplies.
- Kyiv wants to expand F-16 maintenance to more sites in Ukraine, including through localization, to keep as many jets flying as possible.
Ukraine’s Defense Minister Evgeniy Khmara and Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapatyi met a Lockheed Martin delegation led by Orlando Sanchez Jr., president of Lockheed Martin Aeronautics, to press for steady weapons deliveries, more PAC-3 interceptors for Patriot and wider F-16 maintenance across Ukraine, the Ukrainian Defense Ministry said.
The talks centered on the F-16, which the ministry described as one of the Ukrainian Air Force’s key tools against Russia’s new jet-powered attack drones, and on Kyiv’s push to service the jets at more locations inside the country, including through local production.
“The F-16 is part of Ukrainian aviation. Ukraine is committed to a long-term partnership with Lockheed Martin. It is important to increase weapons deliveries and do everything we can to ensure that as many F-16s as possible remain in service and operate in Ukrainian skies,” said Ukrainian Defense Minister Evgeniy Khmara.
The meeting followed President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s own talks with a Lockheed Martin team in Kyiv on Oct. 19, when he praised the F-16’s record against Shahed drones and said Ukraine is counting on the program continuing. Sources at Lockheed Martin have told The Defence Blog that the company is promoting the idea of a special F-16 version tailored to Ukraine, with longer range, a new AESA radar to spot low-flying drones and cruise missiles faster, and deeper integration of European weapons, although no formal talks on such a variant are underway.
Lockheed Martin systems already make up a large share of Ukraine’s long-range firepower and air defense, from the HIMARS rocket launchers that have struck Russian logistics hubs since 2022 to the F-16 fighters and the PAC-3 interceptors that Patriot batteries fire against Russian ballistic missiles. The F-16 has become the backbone of the Ukrainian Air Force since the first jets arrived in 2024, and the type now flies roughly 80 percent of all Ukrainian Air Force sorties, with one wing alone credited with downing more than 1,000 Russian drones and cruise missiles.
Keeping those aircraft flying is a growing challenge, since Ukraine’s F-16s are older airframes donated by European NATO members and fly near-daily combat missions, which wears down engines and structures far faster than peacetime training. Expanding maintenance to more sites inside Ukraine would cut the time jets spend out of action and reduce the risk of concentrating them at a few bases that Russian missiles and drones could target, while localization would give Ukrainian industry a direct role in sustaining the fleet.
The PAC-3 request reflects Ukraine’s most urgent air defense need, since Patriot is the main system in its inventory able to intercept Russian ballistic missiles such as the Iskander-M and the Kinzhal. Lockheed Martin is ramping up production of PAC-3 MSE interceptors, and Zelenskyy said after his own meeting that Kyiv hopes to buy part of the increased output to protect more cities from ballistic attacks.
The ministry said Ukraine is ready to share its combat experience with Lockheed Martin to make the company’s weapons more effective in modern warfare, and the talks come as Lockheed Martin offers Ukraine its own version of the F-16, a variant that sources at the company told The Defence Blog would bring longer range, a new AESA radar to detect low-flying drones and cruise missiles faster, and deeper integration of European guided bombs and cruise missiles.

articles.title: Hegseth Highlights Defense Manufacturing Push with Visit to Future ‘Doomsday’ Planes
articles.body:
DAYTON, Ohio, and EAU CLAIRE, Wis.—Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth took his Arsenal of Freedom tour to the swing states of Ohio and Wisconsin on Oct. 20, highlighting efforts to boost defense manufacturing before the midterm elections next month, including by visiting future E-4C “Doomsday” planes.
“We plan to spend even more in the future,” Hegseth said during a visit to the Sierra Nevada Corporation in Dayton, Ohio, where he praised President Donald Trump and Sen. Bernie Moreno, an Ohio Republican.
“We are providing larger and longer and more predictable contracts to companies so that they can deliver at scale and at pace,” he added. “That means more jobs, more reliable jobs, high-paying jobs as companies invest in their people. We’re going to reward leaders who invest in their workers, who expand their capacity, and who share our utter sense of urgency.”
Sierra Nevada purchased five Korean Air 747-8i jetliners and plans to convert at least four into the new E-4C Survivable Airborne Operations Center, or SAOC. Hegseth championed the company, which won a $13 billion contract to build America’s next-generation nuclear command-and-control aircraft over Boeing. Shield AI was recently awarded a contract to integrate artificial intelligence into aircraft. And there are signs the Air Force may choose to grow the fleet.
Speaking to reporters, Hegseth discussed his recent trop to the Middle East, where he visited U.S. fighter units and Airmen, among other service members, and told Air & Space Forces Magazine he met with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. He declined to say what he had discussed with the Israeli leader, including the possibility of renewing attacks on Iran, but added that the Israeli military “has great capabilities.”
“We’ve worked with the Israeli military quite a bit,” Hegseth said. “They’ve been good partners.”
Hegseth also told Air & Space Magazine the Pentagon had not ordered a slowdown of SpaceX’s Starlink or its military version, Starshield, for Ukraine—Ukrainian officials say their access to the space internet service has been throttled, hampering their drones and air defenses.
“We haven’t changed our posture in any way to all the Ukrainians,” Hegseth said. “We haven’t pulled anything back. There are terms of service that ultimately need to be complied to, and that’s where Starlink has the option to make those decisions. But nothing’s changed from our view. We haven’t made any directives or anything like that. And we wish the Ukrainians, obviously, success.”
The Wall Street Journal reported later on Oct. 20 that the move to slow Starlink was decided by Elon Musk, the chief executive of SpaceX.
But Hegseth’s trip was mainly intended as an opportunity for him to make his case for more defense spending and the Pentagon’s push to help the defense industry.
“We’re asking for a $1.5 trillion investment to make a generational investment to ensure that we remain the strongest and most powerful military in the world,” Hegseth said after touring SNC’s facilities with Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink. “And those types of investments translate directly into high-paying jobs for American manufacturers.”
The aircraft being overhauled by Sierra Nevada Corporation are due to replace the four aging E-4B National Airborne Operations Center aircraft, which are on average over 50 years old.
Boeing was eliminated from the competition to modernize the E-4 nuclear command and control fleet in 2023, leaving SNC as the sole competitor; the E-4C airframe itself is still based on Boeing’s 747-800i.
That gave SNC its largest contract in six-decade history, which is also one of the largest aircraft modernization deals given to a company that isn’t the plane’s original manufacturer. The E-4C flew its first test flight last year.
”In a doomsday scenario, SAOC provides the president with unbreakable command and control. No other nation on planet earth has these types of capabilities, serving as our nation’s ultimate insurance policy in a no fail mission,” Hegseth said.
Hegseth also touted his Future of War initiative, Project Meridian, and his plans for a new four-star Autonomous Warfare Command—and, he said, the effort he has embarked on over the last year to champion American manufacturing.
Hegseth then jetted to Wisconsin to visit the rural congressional district of Rep. Derrick Van Orden, a close administration ally, who is currently locked in a tight reelection battle predicted to be a toss-up. Hegseth’s visit to the small business Riverside Machine and Engineering, alongside Small Business Administrator Kelly Loeffler, highlighted an effort to invest in small defense companies. The company is a small subcontractor that builds parts that go in radars and other equipment for BAE Systems and Lockheed Martin, including the F-35.
“Tens of thousands of small businesses are the core of our defense industrial base,” Hegseth said. “Any supply chain is only as weak as its weakest link, and if you can’t make a critical subcomponent, then ultimately that F-35 doesn’t fly or ultimately that radar isn’t working.”

articles.title: Britain sends Typhoons to guard Saudi cities from Houthis
articles.body:
- Britain will deploy Royal Air Force Typhoon jets to Saudi Arabia to intercept Houthi missiles and drones, without striking targets inside Yemen.
- The UK already supports Saudi Arabia with a Voyager refueling tanker, air defense equipment and personnel, and is extending the tanker mission by 90 days.
Britain will send Royal Air Force Typhoon fighter jets to Saudi Arabia to shoot down Houthi missiles and drones aimed at Saudi cities and critical infrastructure, the UK Defense Ministry said on Oct. 20.
CNN reported that the jets will fly defensive counter-air missions over the kingdom, and a spokesperson for the prime minister’s office said they will intercept incoming threats and will not carry out strikes inside Yemen.
The government has not said how many Typhoons are going, where they will be based or when patrols will begin. The jets join UK support already in place in the kingdom, including air defense equipment, British personnel helping counter missile and drone attacks, and a Royal Air Force Voyager tanker that has been refueling Saudi fighters since September.
“The continuing attacks from the Houthis on our ally Saudi Arabia are absolutely despicable. The targeting of the airport in Riyadh in particular shows the lengths the Houthis are going to escalate the situation in the region,” said UK Defense Secretary Wes Streeting.
Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport has been hit repeatedly this month. The deadliest strike, on Oct. 10, wounded more than 300 people, and while Saudi civil aviation authorities put the death toll at 12, CNN has since reported 13 killed, making it the deadliest attack on Saudi Arabia in more than a decade. The Houthis have also fired ballistic missiles and drones at oil facilities, and on Sept. 16 the group claimed to have shot down a Saudi F-15 over Marib, a claim Saudi authorities have not confirmed.
The fighting escalated after the Houthis announced in July that they would target Saudi shipping in the Red Sea and infrastructure inside the kingdom, following a Saudi strike on the Houthi-held airport in Sanaa. Last month the group pushed down Yemen’s western coast and took the port of Mocha and Mayyun Island in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, the narrow southern entrance to the Red Sea.
Saudi Arabia has asked regional and Western partners for air defense help. France has agreed to send military personnel and equipment, and more than 100 U.S. military advisers are providing intelligence and targeting support under a newly formed joint forces command. Pakistan already has troops in the kingdom, and Egypt’s parliament is debating a deployment after President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi called an emergency session.
The Typhoon is a familiar aircraft in the region, since the Royal Saudi Air Force has flown it since buying 72 jets in a deal agreed in 2006. Britain previously sent its Sky Sabre ground-based air defense system to Saudi Arabia earlier this year during the war with Iran.
The Associated Press reported that Britain is also extending its Voyager refueling mission by 90 days. Downing Street has described the support as defensive and limited in scope, while Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces press a counteroffensive that has so far failed to dislodge the Houthis from key positions.

articles.title: US-Iran mediation persists with both sides prep for war
articles.body:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told US media that a peace deal with Iran is extremely difficult and economic pressure will continue until Tehran stops attacking shipping in Hormuz. Meanwhile, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told the media Hormuz will remain closed until Washington accepts Tehran’s conditions
The war in Yemen intensifies between the Iran-backed Houthis and the internationally recognised Yemeni government forces as strikes reported by both sides
Oil prices climb further, inching past $110 per barrel
Israeli attacks continue on Gaza, occupied West Bank, south Lebanon and southern Syria
And so we continue our live coverage of the day...
French President Emmanuel Macron landed in Riyadh where he is due to meet Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman on Wednesday, in a surprise "solidarity" visit after weeks of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.
Macron is the first Western leader to visit the kingdom since Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis intensified their attacks this month.
The trip is part of a Gulf tour to secure diesel and petrol supplies as Macron seeks to bring down energy prices following violent protests in France sparked by rising living costs that have created a political crisis for the president.
"The president of the republic is travelling to Saudi Arabia this afternoon to meet with Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman," a statement from Macron's office said.
The visit aimed to "demonstrate France's solidarity with the kingdom in the face of the attacks carried out by the Houthis against its territory, and to continue efforts undertaken on securing and diversifying hydrocarbon supplies", it added.
France to hold Lebanese army conference after Israeli polls
French President Emmanuel Macron said Wednesday that his country would organise a conference to support the Lebanese army after Israeli elections this month, decrying what he called untenable pressure on Beirut.
Israeli troops currently occupy a swathe of south Lebanon after invading in March, while Lebanese authorities are under pressure to disarm militant group Hezbollah.
"We will coordinate to carry out this work in support of the Lebanese Armed Forces and a conference will be set up in the coming weeks by France," Macron told reporters during a visit to Qatar.
"I think it is useless to do it before the Israeli elections, but we will organise such a conference because it is unavoidable," he said.
Israel is set to go to the polls on Tuesday.
An international conference in Paris in support of Lebanon's army was planned for March but was delayed after Israel's invasion of Lebanon.
The poorly equipped Lebanese army has struggled to carry out its mission. [Getty]
With Israel's occupation entrenched, Hezbollah rebuilding its military capabilities, and the Iran war unresolved, the threat of a new conflict looms, writes Dario Sabaghi.
Yemen's Houthis on Wednesday targeted a military base at an airport in the southern city of Al Mukalla, which is controlled by Yemen's Saudi-backed government, two military officials told AFP.
"The Houthis used missiles and drones to target a military base housing forces from the Saudi-led coalition at Al Rayyan airport," said one of the officials, speaking on condition of anonymity.
Turkey, Qatar, Pakistan, Indonesia sign defence cooperation
Turkey, Qatar, Pakistan, and Indonesia signed an agreement on Wednesday aimed at boosting defence cooperation and strengthening defensive capabilities, the Turkish Defence Ministry said.
In a statement, the ministry said the accord signed in Doha would also support military exercises and training, cooperation on research and development, and contribute to joint efforts to improve the countries' respective defence industries.
Iran FM: ready for diplomacy, but will 'defend ourselves'
French President Emmanuel Macron said Wednesday that he had secured gas from Qatar during his Gulf tour, as he seeks to bring down the price of energy following violent protests sparked by rising living costs.
"We secured during the winter period the equivalent of two terawatt-hours per month of LNG, which was important for us and which will allow us to move forward," he told reporters in the Qatari capital Doha.
US cannot blockade, threaten while expecting diplomacy: Iran
The US cannot expect dialogue with Iran while blockading and threatening it, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said on Wednesday according to state media, a day after Pakistan's army chief visited Tehran to discuss mediation efforts and regional developments.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis said on Wednesday it had intercepted five drones launched towards the kingdom, including in the Medina region home to one of Islam's holiest cities.
"Four drones launched towards the kingdom have been intercepted and destroyed," coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki posted on X, adding in a second post that the interceptions took place in Saudi Arabia's Eastern region as well as Medina.
Al-Malki, who did not specify who was behind the launches, later said another drone had been intercepted, also in the Eastern region.
The Houthis denied having targeted the kingdom, with military spokesman Yahya Saree saying their forces had not carried out any "deep" operations in Saudi territory.
Saudi Arabia has this month come under sustained attack from the Iran-backed Houthis, including a strike on Riyadh's international airport that was the kingdom's deadliest in years, as the war with the group escalates.
Medina, the burial place of the Prophet Mohammed and home to the Prophet's Mosque, is one of Islam's holiest cities alongside Mecca, both of which the Houthis have promised to spare.
Yemen's Houthis say targeted Saudi position in Aden
Yemen's Houthis said they attacked a Saudi position in the city of Aden on Wednesday, with smoke seen rising near the airport, in the third attack in a week on the seat of power of Yemen's Riyadh-backed government.
"Our armed forces were able to target the Saudi enemy's operations room in the Badr camp in Aden with a ballistic missile," Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said in a statement.
A police official in Aden earlier told AFP there had been a blast "caused by a Houthi missile", speaking on condition of anonymity for security reasons.
Two other security sources in the city told AFP the attack targeted a site near the airport that belonged to forces from the Saudi-led military coalition that has been battling the Houthis.
Unknown projectile hits tanker west of Oman's Bukha: UKMTO
An unknown projectile struck a tanker about 11 nautical miles west of Oman’s Bukha, near Hormuz, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported.
UKMTO said a fire that erupted was extinguished and all crew were safe.
An explosion was heard in the Yemeni city of Aden and smoke seen rising near the airport on Wednesday, a police official and an AFP journalist said, as fighting intensifies between government forces and the Iran-backed Houthi group.
The official said the blast was "caused by a Houthi missile", speaking on condition of anonymity for security reasons.
Missile hit Iranian Kurdish group camp near Iraq's Erbil
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi stressed that the best solution in the region is diplomacy and reaching a negotiated solution during an interview with an Iraqi news channel.
"Our negotiations with the US side through mediating countries, including Pakistan and Qatar, are continuing continuously," he said.
"We previously presented an initiative to the US side known as the 'Seven Day Plan,' in which we clearly explained our conditions. The Strait of Hormuz was supposed to be completely opened on the sixth day of this plan. The Americans informed us that they agree to these conditions, but they would like to add some other provisions,” he added.
In response to a question about the nature of these conditions and whether they are security or economic, the Iranian minister explained that some of them are related to issues that were previously discussed during previous negotiations.
"What we want from the American side is to adhere to all the terms of the memorandum of understanding previously signed with Islamabad. After their commitment to these terms, we can enter into negotiations on other files. In the final stage of negotiations, any issue or problem raised by either party can be discussed and a final agreement can be reached," he said.
Araqchi reiterated Tehran's assertion that the Strait of Hormuz will not be opened until an agreement or understanding is reached regarding it, adding: "We also said that the American side must accept our conditions for opening the Strait to ships. Before such an understanding or agreement is reached, the strait will naturally be closed, and the movement of ships in it and the current sea routes will face difficulties."
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu planned to carry out strikes against Iran earlier this month, but President Donald Trump opposed reigniting the fighting before the US midterms, according to a report by the Financial Times.
Three people familiar with the matter tell the newspaper that the IDF was ready to carry out strikes on the weekend of 10 October to target Iranian nuclear facilities and regime sites, as well as civilian infrastructure including energy plants.
However, the unnamed sources say that Trump decided not to restart the conflict before the US midterms on 3 November.
The sources say the strikes would have been more intense than those carried out by the US and Israel in February.
Iraq has closed the Sheeb border crossing with Iran to passengers, vehicles and commercial trucks until further notice, two sources at the crossing said on Wednesday.
Another source said the decision has been taken to reconsider the security arrangements inside the crossing.
Gaza rescuers, hospitals say Israeli strikes kill seven
Israeli strikes on separate locations in the Gaza Strip killed seven Palestinians on Tuesday, according to the territory's civil defence rescue service and several hospitals.
Two men were killed in Israeli strikes in the town of Al-Zawaida and the Wadi Gaza area in the central Gaza Strip, according to Mahmoud Bassal, spokesperson of the civil defence, a rescue force operating under Hamas authority, and the Al-Aqsa Martyrs' Hospital.
An Israeli strike in the Jabalia al-Balad area in northern Gaza killed one person, according to Bassal and Al-Shifa Hospital, which reported it had received another victim of a strike in the Zeitoun neighbourhood southeast of Gaza City.
In another Israeli strike, a man and a woman, identified by Al-Shifa Hospital as Akram Yassin and his wife, were killed and several others injured in a residential block near the hospital in the Al-Rimal neighbourhood, west of Gaza City.
Nasser Hospital reported that it had also received the body of a teenager killed by Israeli gunfire south of Khan Younis in Gaza's south.
Iran's Nournews says Qatari delegation arrives in Tehran
Iran has not received a response from Saudi Arabia or Yemen's Houthis to its offer to help broker talks to end the fighting between them, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said in a television interview aired on Tuesday.
Araqchi offered to help facilitate dialogue as the Iran-aligned Houthis intensified strikes on Saudi Arabia earlier this month.
In the interview with Iraq's Al Ekhbariya TV, Araqchi also responded to the possibility of Egypt joining Saudi Arabia in the war against the Houthis.
"Any foreign intervention would complicate matters," he said, adding Cairo has previously told Tehran that it would "not directly" interfere in the Yemeni conflict.
Egypt has said it is ready to provide Saudi Arabia with the support it needs to defend its security, potentially raising the stakes in the region.
A vote in the Egyptian parliament on a possible move against the Houthi fighters by the country's military, one of the Arab world's largest, was delayed until 26 October.

articles.title: Israel's occupation, Hezbollah's arms: A looming war in Lebanon?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Israel's occupation, Hezbollah's arms: The road to a new war in Lebanon?
On 5 October, Lebanon’s Internal Security Forces stopped a van with two people on board at the Dahr al-Baydar checkpoint.
When searched, authorities discovered and then seized about 780 kg of explosives, including TNT and Composition C-4 plastic.
The two people arrested were reportedly linked to Hezbollah. They were tasked with transporting the cargo from the Bekaa region to Beirut.
The reported involvement of Hezbollah members in the explosives seizure prompted a wave of accusations from the group’s political rivals, with some suggesting they could be used for internal political assassinations.
Lebanese Forces leader Samir Geagea called the seizure “the most dangerous incident in years”, saying the weapons were probably meant for use inside Lebanon.
Kataeb leader Samy Gemayel wrote they were probably intended for a new wave of assassinations like those between 2004 and 2008, including that of former prime minister Rafic Hariri in 2005.
Lebanon’s prime minister, Nawaf Salam, also noted that C-4 had been used in previous assassinations and promised a full investigation.
However, on 15 October, Hezbollah MP Hassan Fadlallah acknowledged that the vehicle and its cargo belonged to the group. He denied allegations of an assassination plot and stated that the explosives are part of the capabilities Hezbollah uses against Israel, demanding the return of the shipment.
On the same day, US Secretary of State Marc Rubio reportedly called Lebanon’s President Joseph Aoun, urging him not to return confiscated explosives to Hezbollah.
Hezbollah’s demand for the return of the explosives has further strained its relationship with a government that has banned the group’s military activity and is pushing to disarm it.
Israel's occupation creates openings for Hezbollah to rebuild
The discovery of explosive materials comes as Israel continues to occupy swathes of southern Lebanon and launch near-daily strikes despite a US-brokered ceasefire agreed in June.
Hezbollah has halted its attacks since then, but the seizure of explosives points to efforts to rebuild its military capabilities as the risk of renewed US-Iran conflict threatens to reignite the Lebanese front.
It is not uncommon for Hezbollah to use ceasefire windows to rebuild its capabilities following a conflict with Israel.
Between the November 2024 ceasefire that ended the Israel-Hezbollah war linked to Gaza and March 2026, reports indicate that the group has rebuilt its command structure and rearmed with assistance from Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
David Wood, senior Lebanon analyst at the International Crisis Group (ICG), said that Israel’s continued occupation and attacks in Lebanon also contribute to the conditions that enable the group’s rebuilding.
“While it might be true that Hezbollah continues to operate militarily, despite the Lebanese government wanting to have a state monopoly over arms, it would be much harder for Hezbollah to do that if Israel were more willing to grant actual concessions as part of its negotiations with Lebanon and to create a viable and fair security arrangement between the two countries,” he told The New Arab.
The US-brokered framework signed in June between Lebanon and Israel has yielded limited results. Lebanon demands an end to Israeli attacks and occupation, the release of detainees, and the return of the displaced. Israel ties these conditions to Hezbollah’s disarmament, which the group rejects.
Israel has continued its military operations in southern Lebanon, occupying more than 600 square kilometres of Lebanese territory while conducting near-daily airstrikes, artillery fire, and home demolitions.
It has mostly levelled 48 of about 60 occupied southern Lebanese towns and villages. In September, Israeli forces took control of the strategic Ali al-Taher ridge near Nabatieh. They previously captured Beaufort Castle and crossed the Litani River.
Lebanon’s Health Ministry says more than 4,300 people have been killed since 2 March, following Hezbollah’s entry into the wider US-Iran war. Nearly 9,000 have been killed since 2023. Almost 330,000 people remain internally displaced.
Nicholas Blandford, a non-resident senior fellow with the Atlantic Council’s Middle East Programmes, told The New Arab that daily shelling and drone surveillance are ongoing, along with efforts to prevent reconstruction south of the Litani River, even outside the occupied zone.
“So in effect, the Israeli occupation extends far beyond where they are physically deployed. It's been quite intense over the last month,” he said.
Israel is also escalating threats to expand its southern Lebanon occupation. Last week, Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz warned that Lebanon would lose Nabatieh and the Litani area to permanent Israeli control if Hezbollah joins Iran in attacking Israel.
A renewed Iran war could draw Lebanon back into conflict
In fact, US President Donald Trump is weighing fresh strikes against Iran, with Israel reportedly pushing for renewed hostilities. Iran is likewise preparing for war, and the conflict in Yemen further fuels regional escalation.
RANE’s lead MENA and defence analyst Freddy Khoueiry explained that repeated interceptions of weapons transfers in Syria and recent seizures of Hezbollah-linked material inside Lebanon show that the group is "clearly attempting to reconstitute parts of its military capability" to rebuild supply lines and replenish stock.
“Hezbollah is likely attempting to restore enough capability to at some point defend against a potential Israeli preemptive campaign and at the same time preserve the option to participate in another regional conflict involving Iran,” he told The New Arab.
For example, Khoueiry explained that seized TNT and C-4 could be used in explosive-drone payloads, rocket and missile warheads, and roadside bombs, mines and demolition charges against Israeli forces in southern Lebanon if conflict resumes.
Dual-use items like fibre-optic cables for drones could enter Lebanon through standard commercial channels, providing Hezbollah with an alternative route to Syria.
Hezbollah may be prioritising experimenting with and expanding the use of low-cost, fibre-optic-guided FPV drones, heavily deployed against Israeli troops in southern Lebanon before the June ceasefire, as they offer a cheap, effective, and hard-to-intercept option.
On the ground, the presence of Israeli troops in southern Lebanon may give Hezbollah an opening to use guerrilla tactics, such as small units staging hit-and-run attacks from familiar terrain. Its drone operations there could also expand the pool of trained drone operators.
Wood said that while Israel has vast military superiority, Hezbollah, this year, “has still managed to make a nuisance of itself”, demonstrating that “while it can't win a military victory over Israel, it can still inflict casualties”. Hezbollah drone attacks have reportedly killed at least 12 Israeli soldiers.
However, what Hezbollah’s role would be if the US and Israel resume strikes on Iran remains to be seen.
Blandford said that Hezbollah’s involvement would depend on Iran’s ability to absorb renewed US and Israeli attacks.
“The Iranians may conclude that if they can absorb fresh Israeli and US strikes, they don’t need to involve Hezbollah,” he said. However, if Iran deems additional pressure necessary, it may activate Hezbollah to engage Israel along the border, stretching and diverting Israel's resources.
Khoueiry further explained that Hezbollah’s weakened capabilities and fragile domestic position may limit its initial involvement, though opening a Lebanese front could pressure Israel and strengthen Hezbollah’s and Iran’s negotiating leverage.
“Hezbollah could specifically seek to link pressure on Israeli military presence inside of Lebanon and potentially northern Israel again to demand an Israeli withdrawal from Lebanon, while Tehran could again attempt to incorporate the Lebanese front into a broader regional ceasefire or negotiating framework,” he said.
However, other kinds of pressures are also likely to shape Hezbollah’s calculations. The Shia community, estimated at 32% of Lebanon’s population, has borne much of the war’s human cost during the war. Last week, Hezbollah announced plans to financially help families in Lebanon whose homes were destroyed or rendered uninhabitable.
Polls diverge on Shia support for Hezbollah’s weapons, with a May poll finding that most respondents opposed disarmament and a September survey finding that most favoured placing their weapons under state control, reflecting the complexity of the group’s relationship with its constituency.
Wood said that Hezbollah weighs the suffering of its constituency but, at the same time, also weighs its deep alliance with Iran.
The group also argues that disarmament would leave the Shia community and Lebanon “wide open to Israeli abuses,” and at times, it “has used those factors to justify its decision to enter conflict in Lebanon, in the knowledge that the Shia will first and foremost pay the price”.
Blandford also argued that if Hezbollah loses Shia support, “then the game is over.”
“It doesn't matter how many weapons or how much money the Iranians give Hezbollah; if they haven't got the support of the Shia community, it's finished.”
Dario Sabaghi is a freelance journalist interested in human rights
Follow him on X: @DarioSabaghi
Edited by Charlie Hoyle

articles.title: Covert CIA and Mossad operations inside Iran ahead of a possible new war - opinion
articles.body:
Middle Eastern wars do not always begin with the first missile. Their outcomes are often shaped weeks or months earlier, inside intelligence headquarters, through clandestine networks, and across the unseen battlefield of covert operations.
As the prospect of renewed conflict between the Islamic Republic of the criminal Shi’ite ayatollahs and the United States and Israel grows, the critical question is not who will strike first, but how much of the intelligence war is already unfolding inside Iran.
After eight months of war and severe military and economic losses, the Islamic Republic continues to pursue its survival through nuclear blackmail, threats to global energy security, and protracted negotiations.
President Donald Trump faces a strategic choice: accept a deal that allows Tehran to rebuild or sustain pressure until its security threats are verifiably constrained. In this confrontation, the CIA and Mossad’s intelligence capabilities, particularly their ability to identify and assess vulnerabilities within Tehran’s security establishment, may prove decisive.
Tehran has abandoned none of its tactics of intimidation, deception, and extortion. While speaking of peace, its officials impose unrealistic conditions on Washington. Mohsen Rezaei, a former IRGC commander associated with the Islamic terrorist cult of Mansouroun, insists that not a single gram of enriched uranium will leave Iran.
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has likewise conditioned reopening the Strait of Hormuz on acceptance of Tehran’s proposal. These demands reveal not a willingness to compromise, but a calculated effort to preserve leverage, prolong the confrontation, and buy time.
In intelligence warfare, time does not necessarily favor the side prolonging futile negotiations. Tehran may calculate that rising oil prices, American voter anxiety, and the November 3 midterm elections will pressure Trump into concessions.
Yet a prolonged crisis may also give Washington and Israel valuable opportunities to collect intelligence, assess military capabilities, and expose vulnerabilities within the Islamic Republic’s security apparatus. This remains a strategic assessment, not confirmation of ongoing covert operations.
Israel’s intelligence campaign against Iran’s nuclear program has already demonstrated the depth of Tehran’s counterintelligence vulnerabilities. Mossad’s 2018 seizure of Iran’s nuclear archive, sabotage attributed to Israel at nuclear facilities, and the 2020 assassination of Mohsen Fakhrizadeh exposed serious weaknesses in the regime’s security defenses.
Although the CIA’s direct involvement in these operations remains publicly unverified, US-Israeli intelligence cooperation is well established. Their shared strategic interests, however, should not be confused with evidence of joint participation in every operation attributed to Mossad.
Iran’s greatest vulnerability
For Tehran’s Shi’ite caliphate, the greatest danger extends beyond American air superiority or Israeli missile capabilities.
It is the prospect of intelligence penetration into the institutions sustaining the regime: the IRGC, counterintelligence agencies, national security decision-making centers, nuclear networks, and the increasingly compromised Intelligence Ministry.
A regime unable to protect its secrets, personnel, and command structure remains strategically vulnerable regardless of its military arsenal. Ideological loyalty and internal repression cannot compensate for counterintelligence failures.
The Strait of Hormuz represents another dimension of this asymmetric confrontation. The IRGC claims Iranian naval mines blocked three oil tankers, although independent verification remains lacking. Tehran’s broader objective is to weaponize maritime insecurity and energy-market uncertainty.
It need not win a naval battle to impose economic costs on Washington; threats to shipping can raise insurance premiums, transportation costs, and oil prices. Accurate intelligence on Iran’s actual maritime capabilities is therefore essential to distinguishing credible threats from coercive bluffing and preventing strategic miscalculation.
The Islamic Republic’s asymmetric warfare extends far beyond the Persian Gulf. For decades, Tehran’s outlaw regime has relied on terrorist militias, intelligence networks, cyberoperations, and terrorist proxies to project power and threaten adversaries.
