While allegations must be distinguished from verified intelligence, Washington cannot afford to view Tehran’s transnational threat solely through the nuclear lens.
Tehran’s refusal to relinquish its enriched uranium raises a critical question: If the regime genuinely seeks to resolve international concerns, why preserve one of its most dangerous strategic bargaining chips?
Enrichment alone does not establish an intention to build nuclear weapons. Yet uranium stockpiles, centrifuge capacity, and independent verification remain central to assessing nuclear breakout risks. Any agreement that leaves these vulnerabilities unresolved risks granting Tehran the time and strategic breathing space to rebuild.
For the CIA and Mossad, the strategic imperative is to deliver precise, independent intelligence that exposes Tehran’s capabilities, vulnerabilities, and intentions. Covert operations, however successful, cannot replace a coherent national strategy or independently guarantee regime collapse.
Intelligence achievements can degrade an adversary’s capabilities, but lasting strategic change requires political, economic, social, and security pressure working together.
Trump must distinguish between ending military operations and neutralizing the Islamic Republic’s criminal ruling apparatus. Destroying weapons, damaging facilities, and degrading IRGC capabilities does not necessarily dismantle the regime’s command structure, political will, or capacity to regenerate.
Tehran has repeatedly exploited periods of reduced pressure to rebuild its military, intelligence services, and proxy networks. American success must therefore be measured not merely by silenced missiles or a temporarily reopened Strait of Hormuz, but by the enduring degradation of the regime’s capacity to threaten regional and international security.
One strategic distinction must remain clear: Iran is not the Islamic Republic. Iranians have endured decades of repression, systemic corruption, isolation, and the regime’s regional adventurism.
Washington must not mistake the regime’s survival for Iran’s stability or sacrifice the Iranian people’s right to determine their political future in a closed-door security bargain. The demand for regime change among significant elements of the Iranian opposition deserves consideration in any serious diplomatic assessment.
This does not justify an unlimited war. Washington must weigh the human, economic, and military costs of another prolonged conflict. But avoiding war must not mean accepting a weak agreement.
Any settlement requires verifiable nuclear restrictions, independent monitoring, maritime security guarantees, and enforceable consequences for violations. Diplomacy must reduce threats, not reward their continuation.
Tehran is betting that rising oil prices, public exhaustion, and approaching US elections will force Trump to concede. Yet its leadership cannot know the full extent of American and Israeli intelligence assessments or the options under consideration. That uncertainty is a strategic factor in itself.
Covert operations may already be underway, but their existence and scope cannot be established from publicly available evidence, nor is another war inevitable.
History will judge this confrontation not by bombs dropped or facilities destroyed, but by whether a persistent security threat was durably contained. Tehran must not regain through diplomacy what it lost militarily without meaningful security concessions.
Trump must ensure that ending the war does not allow the Islamic Republic to rebuild its capacity for aggression. The intelligence battle may precede the first missile, but strategic victory requires lasting results.
The CIA and Mossad’s intelligence capabilities remain central to understanding and confronting Tehran’s intelligence apparatus. Whether their operations contribute to regime change remains uncertain, but their documented achievements deserve serious recognition.
For those seeking an end to the Islamic Republic, dismantling its machinery of repression and external aggression remains a fundamental objective. The regime’s continued existence offers no inherent guarantee of regional peace, stability, or international security.
The writer is a Middle East political analyst. His latest book, Tehran’s Dictator, examines the theocratic era of Ali Khamenei (1989-2026). @EQFard

articles.title: DIU: Russia has accumulated up to 700 ballistic missiles and more than 6,000 drones
Putin welcomes Witkoff with fresh Ukraine peace talks in offing
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin hosted U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff Wednesday to discuss new proposals for ending the war in Ukraine, amid Washington's latest push to stop Europe's bloodiest conflict since World War II.
The talks in St. Petersburg, Witkoff's ninth meeting with Putin, included a goodwill gesture from Russia: the release of a retired U.S. schoolteacher held in Russia.
The encounter prompted concerns in Kyiv and among its allies that the United States is backing away from Ukraine, at times holding back real-time intelligence on Russian attacks and hobbling Ukraine's military communications.
The latest talks came more than two years after President Donald Trump promised in his election campaign to end the Ukraine war within 24 hours.
Witkoff flew into St. Petersburg Wednesday morning, a day after conducting what a U.S. official called "constructive" talks in Oslo with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the leaders of Finland and Norway, and European and NATO representatives. President Donald Trump said it was time for Ukraine to end the war or face "a very bad thing."
U.S.-Ukraine ties have deteriorated sharply since Trump announced a diesel export deal with Russia earlier this month, which he said would help lower prices in the United States.
Since the diesel deal, Ukraine has complained of disruption to some intelligence sharing and to its use of the Starlink military satellite system, though Zelenskyy said Tuesday's Oslo meeting had reached an agreement to resolve those issues.
Citing U.S. officials and people familiar with the matter, The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday that billionaire Elon Musk ordered last week the slowdown of a military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite service that Ukraine relies on to track Russian ballistic missile strikes.
Reuters could not immediately verify the report.
Musk has said any such decision is made by the U.S. military or the president. Trump has said he was not responsible. U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth signaled Tuesday that the problem lay in the terms of service Kyiv needed to comply with.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Wednesday that Witkoff's meeting with Zelenskyy was positive and that Witkoff would share the results with Russia. He also reiterated that Washington had not pulled back Kyiv's ability to access Starlink.
"He will now, armed with those ideas, be able to go to St. Petersburg and share them with the Russian side, and let's see if we can make some progress," he said.
Despite the apparently cordial nature of Tuesday's meeting in Oslo, Trump, in comments Tuesday at the White House, remained frustrated with Zelenskyy, whom he has repeatedly rebuked and suggested should be replaced.
"He's going to have to want to make a deal, because I don't think his people are going to stand for it any longer," Trump told reporters on the eve of the talks in Russia.
Putin, who has shown few signs of compromising on his central war aims – which include full Russian control of the Donetsk region in eastern Ukraine and no NATO membership for Kyiv – received Witkoff in the Constantine Palace, an imperial edifice in his home city.
Kirill Dmitriev, Putin's special investment envoy and his key liaison for potential economic and financial deals with the U.S., also attended the meeting with Witkoff, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said.
A U.S. official said Ukraine brought new ideas and proposals to the Oslo talks, which made "meaningful progress" toward a coordinated approach to engaging with Russia.
The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said the talks covered "key elements of a comprehensive peace framework," including security guarantees for Ukraine, a postwar economic plan and a broader European security architecture.
Witkoff aimed to "create a pathway toward direct trilateral and broader multilateral negotiations," the official said. Zelenskyy said he hoped to discuss key issues on how to end the war during a trilateral meeting with Putin and Trump.
The Kremlin has repeatedly said that any Putin-Zelenskyy meeting would need to be painstakingly prepared by aides to make it worthwhile and that much legwork would be required for an overall agreement.
Trump said Tuesday he raised the idea with Putin of freeing Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old retired U.S. schoolteacher being held in Russia on mercenary charges he denies.
Putin told Witkoff that Hubbard was at the airport waiting to fly back to the U.S. with him. Witkoff thanked Putin for the goodwill gesture.
Hubbard was first detained in April 2022 and later sentenced to six years and 10 months on charges whose veracity his family and U.S.-based lawyer question.

articles.title: Kremlin Rejects Energy Ceasefire But Says Full Peace Deal Requires Ukraine’s Participation
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin is not considering an energy ceasefire with Ukraine, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said, claiming Moscow wants a broader peace agreement instead.
“Russia needs peace, not a ceasefire,” Peskov said, according to Russian state news agency TASS.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Peskov’s comments came as a rebuke to US President Donald Trump’s recent announcement of an energy truce between Kyiv and Moscow.
Peskov added that a full resolution of the war was impossible without Ukrainian officials’ participation.
“Someone there needs to make a responsible decision,” he said without specifying whom he meant.
Russian leader Vladimir Putin has reportedly proposed a trilateral summit with his US and Chinese counterparts in November to discuss a settlement in Ukraine without Kyiv’s participation.
Both the US and Russia also cast doubt on President Volodymyr Zelensky’s legitimacy despite most Ukrainians expressing trust in the leader in recent polls.
Peskov also commented on recent remarks by Finnish President Alexander Stubb, who said Ukrainian, US and European delegations identified new ideas for ending the war during Tuesday’s talks in Norway, ahead of Trump envoy Steve Witkoff’s visit to St. Petersburg.
Stubb said the proposals would be conveyed to the Kremlin for consideration.
“In my experience, peace requires patience, but unfortunately, war does not wait. People are dying every day. Our task is to do everything possible to put an end to this. And I believe that today was a step in the right direction,” Stubb said.
Russia Has Up to 700 Ballistic Missiles, 6,200 Attack Drones Ready to Strike Ukraine, Intelligence Says
But Peskov dismissed the remarks once again, saying that simply repeating the general European position on Ukraine was “unlikely to be a constructive contribution to a settlement.”
Peace on whose terms?
While all parties – including the US and Europe – have called for peace in Ukraine, the terms have been polarizing.
Europe has sided with Kyiv, arguing that Russia is responsible for the invasion and that any peace should be just and lasting, rather than a temporary ceasefire – similar to Moscow’s wording, except that Europe says this is necessary to prevent another Russian invasion.
Russia has long cast its own Ukraine invasion as a war against NATO, initially demanding that Ukraine be demilitarized and barred from joining the alliance, and recently reiterated demands for Kyiv to voluntarily withdraw from eastern Ukraine’s Donbas region, to which Moscow has laid claims via unrecognized referendums.
Kyiv, meanwhile, called for a freeze along the contact lines, arguing that ceding the Donbas region could weaken its own security and allow Russia to recuperate for another invasion against the rest of Ukraine.
Ukraine’s recent Operation Vivaldi also reversed much of Russia’s gains in the region throughout 2026.
While the previous US administration backed Ukraine’s sovereignty, the Trump administration has pursued economic incentives to bring Moscow to the negotiating table, with Zelensky saying in March that Washington had pressured Kyiv to give up the Donbas in exchange for security guarantees.
Energy truce in words only
Trump had claimed on Oct. 11 that both Kyiv and Moscow had agreed to halt attacks on energy infrastructure. Neither Kyiv nor Moscow immediately confirmed the truce’s terms or how compliance would be monitored.
The announcement followed Zelensky’s statement that Kyiv was ready to suspend long-range drone strikes on Russian oil refineries if Moscow agreed to a reciprocal, verifiable halt to attacks on Ukraine’s electricity and heating networks.
The proposed truce came amid growing tensions between Washington and Kyiv after Trump announced a deal allowing Russian diesel sales and criticized Ukraine’s strikes on Russian refineries.
On Oct. 18, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha accused Russia of exploiting diplomatic efforts while intensifying attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. He said Russian forces had carried out 76 targeted strikes on energy facilities in the week following Trump’s announcement.
During the same period, Russian forces launched nearly 2,700 strike drones, 1,700 guided aerial bombs and 66 missiles across Ukraine, Sybiha said.
Sybiha warned that easing sanctions or offering economic concessions without changes in Russia’s conduct would provide the Kremlin with additional revenue to finance its war. He urged Kyiv’s allies to increase pressure on Moscow rather than ease the economic costs of its aggression.

articles.title: Israeli plans to strike Iran before election raise fears of wider regional war
articles.body:
A report that Israel planned to strike Iranian civilian infrastructure earlier this month, only to be stopped by U.S. President Donald Trump, has renewed questions about the strategic justification for another war with Tehran, particularly with Israeli elections less than a week away.
The Financial Times reported Wednesday that Israel had planned to attack Iranian infrastructure on Oct. 10, including power plants, nuclear facilities and other targets associated with the Iranian government, before Trump intervened to prevent the operation.
The report has raised concerns about why Israel would consider launching another major military campaign against Iran when previous rounds of fighting have failed to topple the Iranian government or permanently eliminate its military capabilities.
Israel has spent much of the past three years engaged in intensive fighting on multiple fronts, while damage from previous confrontations with Iran and fighting along its northern and southern borders has yet to be fully repaired.
Iran, meanwhile, continues to demonstrate its ability to disrupt shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, attacking vessels and affecting the global economy. Gulf states have largely absorbed the consequences without launching direct military responses.
Against that backdrop, questions remain over whether Israel has a clear strategic plan for another confrontation and what objectives a renewed campaign could realistically achieve.
Danny Citrinowicz, a former head of the Iran branch in the Israeli Military Intelligence Directorate's Research Division and now a senior researcher specializing in Iran and the Shiite axis at the Institute for National Security Studies (INSS), told ynet that there was no immediate military justification for launching another war.
"There's absolutely nothing that justifies a war now, either before the elections or afterward," Citrinowicz said.
"Iran is rebuilding its strength and restoring its missile capabilities. On the nuclear front, there are no indications whatsoever that they have resumed enrichment. There are the same indications that they moved certain materials to Pickaxe Mountain, but nothing beyond that."
Pickaxe Mountain, also known as Kuh-e Kolang Gaz La, is a mountainous site near Iran's Natanz nuclear complex that has attracted international scrutiny over suspected underground nuclear-related construction.
Citrinowicz questioned why Iran remained capable of launching substantial missile attacks after two previous wars that Israeli officials had described as major military successes.
"We also need to understand why, after two wars against Iran, we're still seeing them launch dozens of missiles," he said. "Apparently, they're not afraid for their arsenal."
'No justification for another campaign'
Citrinowicz said the reported Israeli interest in attacking Iran's energy infrastructure appeared to rest on two possible strategic assumptions, neither of which he considered convincing.
"What is the strategic objective of another war?" he asked. "According to various reports, Israel wants to attack Iran's energy facilities for one of two reasons: Either they think that will bring down the regime, which it won't, or they want to turn Iran into a failed state. And it's clear that would lead to a very broad Iranian campaign against Israel."
He said Iran's continued military buildup did not, by itself, justify an immediate attack.
Iran has continued replacing senior officials killed in previous confrontations, including some whose successors have adopted even more hard-line positions.
Earlier this week, Mehrdad Akhlaghi was appointed Iran's new defense minister. Like his predecessors, he warned that Iranian forces remained ready to respond to threats.
But despite the rhetoric and continued rearmament, Citrinowicz said there had been no dramatic change in Iranian behavior in recent months.
He argued that Iran's efforts to rebuild its capabilities were comparable to those of other Israeli adversaries, including the Houthis in Yemen, Hezbollah in Lebanon and pro-Iranian militias in Iraq.
Another war against Iran, he warned, could reignite fighting across all those fronts.
"The point is that there is no justification requiring a military campaign at this time," Citrinowicz said. "We need to monitor the situation and see what develops. If Iran makes a breakout toward a nuclear weapon tomorrow, then we need to attack. But right now, nothing is happening."
He described the possibility of an Israeli strike just two weeks before the election as deeply troubling.
"What's happening now is sheer madness — attacking two weeks before elections. For what?" he said.
"Iran is not on the verge of developing a nuclear weapon, and with all due respect to its missile arsenal, it still hasn't returned to where it was before Operation Rising Lion and Operation Roaring Lion," he added, using the Israeli names for the previous bouts of direct fighting against the Islamic Republic.
"There is no operational or strategic need to attack now," Citrinowicz said. "There is an attempt to incorporate political considerations, and that is serious."
The former intelligence official also questioned the lasting achievements of the previous military campaigns, noting that Iran's leadership remained in power and its military continued rebuilding.
"Yes, another strike would cause damage, but the consequences for the international system would be insane," he said. "They would set the entire Gulf ablaze."
He criticized what he described as an apparent willingness to launch another campaign without first examining why earlier operations had failed to achieve their declared objectives.
"It's as if we don't care. Just attack again. But for what?" he said.
"And this is after we were promised tremendous, unprecedented achievements in two wars, that we had 'pushed the threat back for generations.' How did we push the threat back for generations if they can attack again?"
He added that Israeli officials had previously emphasized achievements against Iran's missile capabilities, yet Iranian missiles continued to pose a threat.
"The most serious thing is the mixing of political considerations," he said. "Ultimately, there is no justification for launching a campaign two weeks before elections."
US midterm elections complicate diplomatic efforts
The prospect of another confrontation also comes as Washington approaches its midterm elections in early November, a political milestone that Citrinowicz said could influence both Iranian calculations and Trump's willingness to pursue military action.
"The elections in the United States are extremely significant because the Iranians want Trump to lose," he said. "They want to demonstrate the price of confronting them to any American president: Mess with us and you'll lose the elections."
Citrinowicz said Tehran remained open to a negotiated agreement but continued to insist on conditions unacceptable to the Trump administration.
"The Iranians are prepared to return to an agreement, but the conditions they're presenting are conditions Trump will not accept," he said.
He dismissed recent reports in the Qatari newspaper Al-Araby Al-Jadeed suggesting a diplomatic breakthrough was imminent.
"With all due respect to the reports in Al-Araby Al-Jadeed, there is no diplomatic breakthrough whatsoever," he said.
He pointed to remarks made Tuesday by Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, during a meeting with Pakistan's army chief, Asim Munir.
According to the account, Rezaei insisted that all enriched nuclear material would remain in Iran.
"All enriched nuclear materials will remain in Iran," Rezaei said, describing them as "a central asset and national wealth of the Iranian people, intended for use within the country."
Rezaei also said Iranian officials and the public agreed that negotiations should not resume until Washington took steps to rebuild trust.
"The Iranian people and officials agree that there will be no negotiations as long as the United States does not take confidence-building measures," he said, adding that the prerequisite for restoring trust was meeting Iran's stated conditions.
Citrinowicz said the statements underscored the distance between Washington and Tehran despite those reports of diplomatic progress.
He also warned that the period between November's U.S. elections and the seating of the new Congress in January could prove especially volatile.
"I think the period between November and January is very dangerous because it's the transition between Congresses," he said. "During those two months, Trump will want to do something."
However, he suggested Trump's preferred course of action might differ substantially from Israel's reported objectives.
"Perhaps he wants to deliver a single blow, then end the whole affair and declare victory," Citrinowicz said. "I'm not sure he wants to return to the idea of toppling the regime."
He described the possibility of Israel initiating another military campaign under the current circumstances as highly irresponsible.
Israeli fighter jet activity raises escalation fears
Citrinowicz also expressed concern over a Fox News report that Israeli fighter jets had flown over Syria and Iraq toward Iran as part of a military exercise.
He warned that such activity, if accurately reported, could be interpreted by Tehran as preparation for an imminent attack, potentially provoking an Iranian response.
"If that's true, it's an extremely dangerous development," he said. "We're on the brink of war, and we're conducting a simulated strike in Iraq?"
Citrinowicz questioned the logic of staging an exercise resembling an attack on Iran during a period of heightened tensions.
"Do we want to force the Iranians to fire missiles at us?" he asked.
"There's no logic in simulating an attack on Iran at the height of tensions, other than a desire to push the Iranians into attacking us, to have them fire the first shot so we'll have an excuse to respond."
He warned that another Israeli-Iranian confrontation would almost certainly spread beyond the two countries.
"Any war with Iran will once again be a regional war," he said. "Certainly involving the Houthis, certainly the militias in Iraq, and I believe ultimately Hezbollah as well."
Citrinowicz said the regional security environment had changed in ways that could make another confrontation particularly dangerous.
He pointed to the absence of a U.S. military presence in Iraq, which he said would make it easier for pro-Iranian militias to operate, as well as the presence of Houthi elements in the country.
"We'll once again find ourselves stuck in a regional war," he said.
He also highlighted concerns about Israel's and the United States' supplies of missile interceptors, which would be essential to defending against sustained Iranian attacks.
"We know we have a problem with interceptors. That's no secret. And the Americans have a problem with interceptors as well," he said.
Those shortages, he suggested, could become particularly consequential in a prolonged conflict involving multiple fronts and repeated missile barrages.
'We cannot separate Netanyahu's political considerations from Israel's strategic interests'
Citrinowicz said his central concern was the possibility that domestic political calculations were influencing decisions with potentially far-reaching consequences for Israeli national security.
"The most serious aspect of this entire situation is that it's impossible to separate Netanyahu's political considerations from the strategic considerations of the State of Israel," he said.
"That's extremely dangerous. This would be another war with Iran."
He warned that previous confrontations had demonstrated the economic and social costs of fighting Iran, with military operations disrupting daily life and economic activity across Israel.
"We know that every war with Iran paralyzes the Israeli economy and brings activity here to a standstill," he said. "And for what? What strategic objective would this war serve?"
He argued that another campaign would be especially difficult to justify given the limited prospects of removing Iran's leadership through airstrikes alone.
"We understand very clearly that we are not going to topple this regime from the air," he said.
Rather than rushing toward another confrontation, Citrinowicz called for a thorough examination of Israel's previous campaigns, including the objectives they failed to achieve and whether additional military action would serve the country's long-term interests.
"Launching a campaign two weeks before elections is madness," he said.
"Before Israel launches a campaign for which there is currently no immediate need, we must ultimately analyze what we failed to achieve in the previous campaign and why."
He said policymakers should also consider whether military force was the only available option and whether another confrontation would advance Israel's strategic interests.
"Is the kinetic solution the only one, and will it serve the interests of the State of Israel?" he asked.
Citrinowicz emphasized that Israel should preserve close strategic coordination with Washington, describing it as the foundation of Israeli policy toward Iran.
"We certainly need to maintain strategic coordination with the United States," he said. "That's a significant issue because it's the basis of all Israeli policy toward Iran."
But he stressed that coordination with Washington should not replace an independent Israeli assessment of the risks and benefits of military action.
"With all due respect to the Americans, the State of Israel needs to examine what's right for it," he said.
He concluded that Israel should not embark on another potentially more dangerous war without first understanding why previous operations had failed to achieve their stated objectives.
"Right now, it's clear that the war's objectives were not achieved," Citrinowicz said.
"Before we analyze why they weren't achieved, we shouldn't jump into another campaign, one that could potentially be even more dangerous than the previous one, because it would be extremely violent and the Iranians are learning from every confrontation."

articles.title: Kremlin warns of ‘extremely dangerous’ nuclear arms control vacuum
articles.body:
Kremlin warns of extreme nuclear danger
Russia and the US urgently need to resume dialogue on strategic stability and arms control, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said. The absence of a treaty-based framework in this areas is creating a very dangerous situation, he added.
The New START treaty, the last remaining bilateral agreement limiting US and Russian strategic nuclear arsenals, expired in February without an extension or replacement.
Signed in 2010 and extended in 2021, the treaty capped each side at 1,550 deployed strategic nuclear warheads and 700 deployed delivery systems, while providing for transparency and on-site verification measures.
Following the treaty’s expiration, Russia suggested maintaining caps on warheads for another year if Washington reciprocated, but the initiative went unanswered, according to Moscow.
Russia is convinced that talks must resume soon, Peskov told reporters on Tuesday. “This is an extremely important issue,” he said. “For the first time in a long while, the world has been left without this treaty-based legal framework.” He described the situation as “extremely dangerous.”
Peskov urged an early start to negotiations, warning that they would inevitably be complex and lengthy.
The Trump administration has long insisted that any future nuclear arms control agreement should include China as well. In February, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington will press for trilateral talks with Beijing and Moscow.
On Monday, US President Donald Trump said he is open to discussing nuclear disarmament at a potential meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of next month’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China.
“We would have it to talk about nuclear weapons and denuclearization,” he told reporters. “If President Xi wants to have it, I’d have it. I’m sure we’d talk about other things like trade too.”
Peskov said Russia cannot disregard the nuclear arsenals of European NATO members, particularly Britain and France, in future strategic stability talks with the US.
Earlier this year, President Emmanuel Macron announced a “forward deterrence” initiative that could see French nuclear weapons deployed to other European countries. In March, he said France would no longer disclose the size of its arsenal, arguing that “to be free, we have to be feared.” He also outlined plans to increase its nuclear arsenal, which is currently just under 300 warheads, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI).
Moscow has warned that the strategy could backfire, saying it cannot “ignore an obvious buildup of the nuclear component of NATO’s joint potential.”
In August, NBC reported that the Pentagon was also working on a nuclear strategy that would give the US president a wider range of nuclear options in a potential conflict with Russia or China. The approach would reportedly pivot towards shorter-range tactical nuclear weapons instead of relying primarily on long-range strategic nuclear weapons.
Russia updated its nuclear doctrine in 2024, stating that aggression by a non-nuclear state backed by a nuclear power would be treated as a joint attack and that nuclear weapons could be used if conventional aggression posed a critical threat to the sovereignty or territorial integrity of Russia or its ally Belarus. Moscow also criticized the US nuclear weapons deployment to Europe as part of NATO’s nuclear-sharing arrangements.

articles.title: Ukraine, Lockheed Martin discuss F-16 upkeep, PAC-3 supply
articles.body:
Defense Minister Yevheniy Khmara and Armed Forces Commander in Chief Mykhailo Drapaty met a delegation of the American defense company Lockheed Martin, led by Lockheed Martin Aeronautics President Orlando Sanchez Jr., and discussed the importance of stable arms supplies and further cooperation, the Defense Ministry said.
"We count on mutually beneficial cooperation with Lockheed Martin for years ahead. Ukraine is ready to share unique combat experience so that together we can make defense solutions more effective in modern war," the ministry said on Telegram on Wednesday after the meeting.
The sides separately discussed the value of F-16 aircraft for the Air Force, and the ministry said it is now important for Ukraine to widen the geography of their maintenance, including through localization.
"The F-16 is part of Ukrainian aviation. Ukraine is committed to a long-term partnership with Lockheed Martin. It is important to increase arms supplies and do everything to keep as many F-16s as possible in service and working in Ukrainian skies," Khmara said.
The sides also discussed scaling up supplies of PAC-3 interceptor missiles to counter Russian ballistic missile strikes.
The ministry said Lockheed Martin products are already working to defend Ukraine, not only the F-16 and PAC-3 missiles for Patriot air defense systems, but also HIMARS rocket systems.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met the company's team in Kyiv earlier this week.
"The company is now increasing production of ballistic interceptors. We expect to be able to buy some of them to protect more lives. We are also trying to do everything so that F-16 maintenance and repair take place in Ukraine," he said after the meeting on Monday.
Zelenskyy said Patriot systems and F-16 aircraft from this company play an important role in defending against Russian ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones, and that the sides discussed ways to widen and increase supplies.
"It is important that Lockheed Martin is present in Ukraine. We are doing everything on our side to expand our partnership," he said.

articles.title: Brother Munir! The Ball Is in the US Court
articles.body:
Brother Munir! The Ball Is in the US Court
Pakistan's army chief came to Tehran to break the deadlock, but the US has repeatedly derailed mediation with fantasies like Iran's surrender
TEHRAN – Field Marshal Asim Munir, Pakistan’s army chief, arrived in Tehran on Tuesday for consultations with Iranian officials. It is General Munir's fifth visit to Tehran since the start of the US-Israeli war against Iran on February 28.
In continuation of the Pakistani government's sincere mediation, the country's army chief arrived in Tehran yesterday and held talks with senior Iranian officials. Islamabad's efforts come as Iran has always given credibility to mediators, but in recent years it is the US that has consistently neutralized those efforts and discredited them. Iran gave the four European countries the opportunity in the JCPOA to appear as international actors, but when Trump withdrew from the JCPOA in his first term, those countries failed to honor their commitments to Iran and even aligned themselves with the US policies and anti-Iran actions. After that, Iran engaged with Oman, and Muscat also sincerely tried to untie the knot between Washington and Tehran, but in the end Trump even threatened to bomb Oman, leaving observers stunned.
Pakistan's sustained efforts in the ongoing war also led to the Islamabad MoU and placed Pakistan in the position of a major international actor, but once again it was the US that destroyed it only weeks later with adventurism in the Strait of Hormuz and violation of the memorandum's provisions.
Tehran was the first country to recognize Pakistan's independence and has always had warm and close relations with Islamabad. Islamabad knows well that the Islamic Republic of Iran is a strong barrier against the sinister intentions of the Israeli regime, and if Tel Aviv's malign actions are not contained, they know no limits. Tehran and Islamabad have many common interests, and Pakistan's role and efforts in resolving the ongoing conflict are welcomed by Tehran. But has the US had, and does it have, the same view of mediators?
Pezeshkian: Iran does not trust the US
President Masoud Pezeshkian, in his meeting with the Pakistani army chief, recalling the record of US bad faith and breach of promises – attacking our country in the middle of negotiations and martyring the Supreme Leader of the Revolution, scientists and innocent schoolchildren without any legal justification – said: All the problems created in the region, from escalation of tension and conflict to disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, all stem from the warmongering nature of the US. All their claims against our country lack legitimacy, because we had proven our goodwill both with regard to negotiations and inspections in the nuclear file within the framework of international laws and regulations.
Emphasizing that the US must first show it will lift threats and sanctions so that conditions for dialogue can be met, Pezeshkian stated: You cannot increase sanctions and pressure day by day and close routes and roads to our country, and then claim you seek dialogue and negotiation. What kind of dialogue is this?
Noting that we know war benefits neither us, nor the region and the world, nor even the US, the President added: It is the US that must answer why it started the war in the first place, entangling itself and the world in problems and difficulties?
Pezeshkian noted: We have been and are ready for dialogue, but the US must first remove threats and sanctions and then we will talk, because if they are truly seeking dialogue and agreement, such behavior is completely in contradiction with their claim and is not logical.
The President, further pointing out that they imposed all these criminal acts on our country and our region under the false claim of nuclear weapons, while they martyred our Leader who had repeatedly stressed the prohibition of nuclear weapons, and drove the region into deadlock, said: They will certainly not achieve their objectives through war and will only bring destruction and damage, not only for Iran but for the entire region; something we do not want to happen.
Stressing that they must prove to our nation that this time they do not want to lie to us, Pezeshkian said: Our nation today does not trust the US and believes that if we negotiate, they will attack us again.
The President added: They constantly propagate in the media that they want to attack our country to frighten our people, while our nation has no fear of martyrdom. You, as our Muslim brothers, must make them understand that this is not how one treats Muslims. We do not want to impose our will on anyone, but we will not submit to coercion.
Field Marshal Asim Munir, in the meeting expressed pleasure at meeting Pezeshkian, presented a report on diplomatic actions and efforts to reduce tensions, and while expressing concern over a renewed outbreak of war, stressed the importance of resolving issues through diplomatic solutions and Pakistan's readiness to help settle matters in this regard.
He, while regretting the non-implementation of the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, said: Negotiation never means weakness and acceptance of submission to the US, because the Iranian nation has repeatedly shown its dignity, authority and power to the world; rather it is an opportunity to resolve issues through a path other than war, conflict and insecurity.
Iran will not take out its uranium
General Munir also met in Tehran with the Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council. Major General Mohsen Rezaei, the Representative of the Supreme Leader and Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, in his meeting with Asim Munir, stressing that all enriched nuclear material will remain in Iran, said: Not even an ounce of enriched nuclear material will leave Iran, and this material is a great asset and the national wealth of Iranians for use inside the country.
Major General Mohsen Rezaei stated: All the Iranian people and officials have unanimously and with one voice concluded that until confidence-building is done by the US, there will be no negotiation, and the start of this confidence-building is the fulfillment of Iran's conditions. He also stressed the fraternity of the Iranian and Pakistani nations.
Asim Munir, emphasizing the reopening of the border between Iran and Pakistan, said the Iran-Pakistan border problem has been resolved and the border has been reopened as of Tuesday.
Referring to the courageous defense and resistance of the Armed Forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran in the 40-day war, he stressed regional cooperation between the two countries without the presence of foreigners.
US threats have no effect on our decisions
The Pakistani army chief also met with Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Speaker of Parliament, in Tehran. In the meeting, Ghalibaf, while appreciating the support of the Pakistani government and nation for Iran in conditions of war and negotiation, stressed the fraternal relations of the two countries. Asim Munir also announced the reopening of the two countries' border as of today and described border issues as temporary and technical.
Referring to Iran's deep distrust of the US and the Trump administration's violation of the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, Ghalibaf stressed that the US can win Iran's trust only by implementing Iran's seven conditions presented in New York.
He also said that Iran is not warmongering but is fully prepared to defend the homeland and national dignity, stressing that threats and military moves cannot change the strategic decisions of the Islamic Republic, and that it is the US that must act to get out of the quagmire of war.
A deadlock that is not easy to break
General Munir's visit to Tehran took place while negotiations between Iran and the US have reached a deadlock, and Tehran's seven-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz could not untie this knot either. The deep divide between the two sides' views of the balance of conflict and tension is one of the main reasons mediation efforts have failed. While the US is a short distance from the midterm elections and the Republican Party is not in good shape in the polls, Trump is trying to force Iran into submission through threats. Iran, by tightening control over the Strait of Hormuz and dealing with violating vessels seeking to pass through the strait without permission, has increased pressure on the US, and oil prices have even exceeded 110 dollars. In the latest developments, two tankers carrying a total of 4 million barrels of crude oil hit mines over the weekend; one caught fire and the other came to a halt.
The diesel deal with Putin, although it faced enormous criticism inside the US, failed to have any particular effect on prices or calm angry US consumers.
Trump has so far taken varied and sometimes contradictory positions on the midterm elections and their link to the war with Iran. He has tried to deflect the rise in fuel prices onto the Ukraine war and Biden's record by shifting blame. Meanwhile, he has at one point spoken of the insignificance of these elections for his Iran policy and even said the elections and their outcome do not matter to him at all, but in practice he behaves differently. From the 5,000-dollar promise to every US adult and personal appearances at campaign rallies in various states, telling people to imagine they are going to the ballot box to vote for him, all show how vital this election is for him.
The US President recently said he would not start a new round of confrontation with Iran until after the elections, but evidence does not necessarily confirm this claim. The secret trip of Pete Hegseth, the US Secretary of War, to Israel and his consultations with Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli Prime Minister, held with the participation of officials from the UAE, has increased doubts about the future plans of the US and Israel.
Iran is ready for the next round of war
 
In Iran too, senior military officials speak of full readiness for a new round of war. Sardar Hossein Mohebbi, in his recent interview with the Tehran Times, did not rule out the possibility of a new US attack aimed at manufacturing an achievement on the eve of the elections, stressing that such an attack would bring no achievement for the US and that even if limited, Iran's response would be very severe and would confront the world with a serious energy crisis.
The IRGC spokesman, in other remarks, named data cables on the floor of the Persian Gulf as one of the possible targets in a new round of war – something that Mohsen Rezaei, the Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, had also pointed to before him.
Major General Abdollahi, Chief of the General Staff of the Iranian Armed Forces, also said: Our enemies possess modern and new equipment, and we must, when necessary, respond to the enemy with different methods and asymmetric equipment, as happened in the two recent wars.
In the event of any renewed miscalculation by the enemy, we will neutralize the effect of the enemy's expensive and advanced equipment with a wide range of cheap but effective equipment, and this will be painful, worrying and costly for the enemy.
It seems Trump is seeking even a temporary achievement to pass easily and triumphantly through the upcoming elections, but whether he loses or wins this election, it is unlikely to fundamentally affect his strategy toward the war with Iran. Trump has openly and fully endorsed Netanyahu in the Israeli elections, and Netanyahu has explicitly stated that his goal is the destruction of Iran. The Israeli Prime Minister spoke by phone with Trump on Monday and, by his own account, stressed in it the need to achieve this goal. In such circumstances, there is no doubt about the real intentions of the Donald-and-Bibi duo toward Tehran, and this very fact undermines any mediation and proposal.
Trump is not after a deal
While some unofficial sources in the region have said Pakistan and Qatar have prepared a proposal covering part of both sides' demands that could be agreed by Tehran and Washington, evidence shows that from Tehran's perspective, Trump is merely seeking to pass through the difficult strait of the midterm elections, not to end an unjustified and costly war whose declared objectives have changed repeatedly.
Tehran has no doubt about Islamabad's sincerity in resolving the current situation, but the point is that the ball is in Washington's court, not Tehran's. Until the US government abandons the illusion of forcing Iran to surrender and imposing its unilateral conditions – whether through negotiation or military aggression – this conflict and tension will not end.
It is worth noting that concurrent with General Munir's presence in Tehran, Mohammad Ishaq Dar, Pakistan's Foreign Minister, announced at the Shanghai Cooperation Organization meeting in Tajikistan that Islamabad continues to work to reduce tensions and mediate between Tehran and Washington.
Stressing that dialogue and diplomacy are the most effective way to resolve regional disputes, he said: "Pakistan will continue to support dialogue and the peaceful settlement of disputes to achieve lasting peace and stability."

articles.title: Lockheed Martin offers Ukraine its own version of the F-16
articles.body:
- Lockheed Martin is promoting a Ukraine-specific F-16 version with longer range and a new AESA radar, sources at the company told The Defence Blog.
- Zelenskyy met a Lockheed Martin team in Kyiv on Oct. 19, praising the F-16’s role against Shahed drones and calling for the program to continue.
Lockheed Martin is promoting the idea of a special version of the F-16 fighter built around Ukraine’s needs, with longer range, a new AESA radar and stronger air defense capabilities, sources at the company told The Defence Blog.
The idea is being floated as the U.S. defense giant expands its work with Kyiv, and it surfaced days after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met a Lockheed Martin team in Kyiv on Oct. 19 to discuss F-16 support and pilot training, the President’s Office said.
According to the sources, one option under consideration is a new F-16 variant with extended range and an AESA radar that would let pilots detect low-flying drones and cruise missiles earlier and faster than the radars on Ukraine’s current jets allow. The company is also looking at deeper integration of European weapons on the aircraft, including guided bombs and cruise missiles, which would give Ukraine more options than the mix of Western munitions its F-16s carry today.
No concrete negotiations on a new version are underway, the sources said, but the Ukrainian side has shown interest in an affordable, versatile fighter that its pilots have already mastered in combat. Lockheed Martin is counting on numerous joint projects with Ukraine, the sources added, and Zelenskyy said after the meeting that Kyiv wants the F-16 program to continue.
“It has been working from the first day the F-16 was used and still is today. Especially ahead of a difficult winter, during massive attacks with Shaheds, the F-16s destroy them. And we have a very good rate of destroying Shaheds. That is why we are very proud that we have this capability. Thank you very much. We are counting on the program continuing,” said Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
The F-16 has become the backbone of Ukraine’s air force since the first jets arrived in 2024, and the type now flies roughly 80 percent of all Ukrainian Air Force sorties, as we reported last year. One Ukrainian F-16 wing alone has been credited with downing more than 1,000 Russian Shahed-type drones and cruise missiles, and its vice commander told a U.S. audience that what Ukraine needed most was newer Block 70 jets and more missiles.
That request goes to the heart of the radar issue, since the F-16s that Ukraine received from European NATO members are older airframes upgraded under the Mid-Life Update program, which still rely on a mechanically scanned radar. Newer Block 70 aircraft use an AESA radar that can track more targets at longer range and is better at picking out small, low-flying objects such as drones and cruise missiles against the ground, which is the main threat Ukrainian pilots face during Russia’s mass overnight attacks.
At the Oct. 19 meeting, Zelenskyy also discussed work to let Ukraine service and repair its F-16s on its own territory, as well as larger deliveries of the anti-ballistic interceptors that Lockheed Martin builds for the Patriot air defense system, which the company is ramping up and part of which Kyiv hopes to buy. A Ukraine-specific F-16 would sit alongside the country’s other fighter plans, which include 16 Gripen E jets ordered from Sweden in June with deliveries from 2029 and a separate donation of Gripen C/D fighters, we reported at the time.
The sources did not say how much a dedicated Ukrainian variant would cost, how many aircraft could be involved, or which European weapons Lockheed Martin would prioritize for integration, and any such program would need approval from Washington before talks could move beyond the idea stage.

articles.title: Poland has no Patriot missiles to spare for Ukraine
articles.body:
Poland has no Patriot missiles to spare for Ukraine
Poland does not have enough Patriot air defense missiles to hand over to Ukraine, Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski has said, urging other NATO members to supply Kiev with the scarce interceptors.
In an interview with the Polish Press Agency published on Monday, Sikorski warned of growing pressure on Western air defenses, citing the US-Israeli bombing campaign against Iran.
“Following the attacks on Iran, the shortage of interceptor missiles has indeed increased, and Russia is producing more missiles than we have interceptors to neutralize them. This is a real problem,” he said.
“There are NATO countries that still have such resources to contribute, but Poland is not one of them,” Sikorski said, adding that Warsaw “can only join the calls for countries possessing Patriot missiles to share them with Ukraine.”
The issue sparked a political scandal in Poland in July, when the government came under fire over the transfer of Patriot interceptors to Ukraine as part of a wider NATO-backed aid package. Opposition politicians accused Warsaw of sacrificing its own security to arm Kiev, while Prime Minister Donald Tusk insisted the deliveries would not compromise the country’s defenses.
Poland has emerged as one of the EU’s most rapidly militarizing nations, with defense spending reaching 4.7% of GDP. Warsaw has also been one of Kiev’s staunchest backers, pouring billions into military and other aid while serving as a crucial hub for Western arms shipments.
Yet Poland now faces delays in replenishing its own arsenal, with deliveries of US-made PAC-3 MSE Patriot interceptors pushed back as the war with Iran drains American weapons stocks, Polish General Ireneusz Nowak warned earlier this month.
Relations with Kiev have also soured over Ukraine’s honoring of Nazi collaborators linked to the World War II-era Volhynia massacres, in which Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) militants associated with the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN) killed an estimated 100,000 ethnic Poles. Warsaw recognizes the killings as genocide, while Kiev continues to honor figures including OUN leader Stepan Bandera.
Tensions flared again this year after Zelensky awarded a Ukrainian military unit the honorary title “Heroes of the UPA.” Polish President Karol Nawrocki subsequently stripped him of the country’s highest honor, politicians on both sides renounced state decorations, and Warsaw threatened to obstruct Ukraine’s EU accession.
The ammunition crunch is spreading across NATO. In July, the Netherlands said it had exhausted its capacity to supply Ukraine with Patriot missiles from its own stocks, having already provided interceptors and helped assemble a complete Patriot system for Kiev.
Meanwhile, Kiev is facing a critical shortage of air defense ammunition as Russia intensifies strikes on Ukrainian military and energy infrastructure. Moscow has said the attacks are in retaliation for Kiev’s continued strikes on Russian territory, including civilian targets and energy facilities.
Vladimir Zelensky has requested 300 Patriot interceptors from European backers and complained that Washington has approved only some of the missiles purchased through a NATO-backed initiative. The White House has also delayed approving additional transfers as US President Donald Trump presses Ukraine to reach a negotiated settlement with Russia.
Moscow has repeatedly maintained that Western weapons deliveries prolong the conflict, obstruct peace efforts, and risk drawing NATO countries into a direct confrontation with Russia.

articles.title: Round-the-clock Russian terror: how much longer will the enemy be able to attack Ukraine continuously
articles.body:
Round-the-clock Russian terror: how much longer will the enemy be able to attack Ukraine continuously
Kyiv • UNN
Russia has intensified its drone attacks, seeking to exhaust air defenses and pressure Ukraine. Stronger defense and strikes against Russia's military-industrial complex could reduce the attacks.
Russia continues its massive drone attacks on Ukraine and is attempting to cover as large an area as possible with its strikes. Military expert Oleh Zhdanov told a UNN journalist more about why the Russian Federation is relying on massive air attacks, how they are connected to political pressure on Ukraine, and what could force Russia to reduce the intensity of its strikes.
Details
Russian drone attacks are taking place virtually around the clock, but the nature of the air strikes changed at the end of October. According to the military expert, whereas reactive drones predominated earlier, Russia is now once again actively using conventional attack drones. In addition, the enemy is attempting to simultaneously cover as much of Ukrainian territory as possible with its attacks.
It is very strange that now "our old song is starting again—we are starting it all over again." In the sense that they are now going to attack 24/7. And what have they been doing all this time? Even now, if you look out the window, air raid alerts are in effect 24/7 across most of Ukraine. And we made it through the whole of September like that
Russia plans to increase drone production: Politico learned the details21.09.26, 10:29 • 5874 views
At the same time, Oleh Zhdanov noted that at the end of September, short intervals began to appear between drone raids. In particular, in Kyiv and other cities, there was sometimes approximately an hour between successive attacks, but at the end of October, Russia once again intensified its attacks.
The difference at the end of October is that they began trying to cover all of Ukraine. They have returned again: whereas in September they were mostly reactive, now they have once again added conventional "Shaheds" and "Geran-2" drones. And their number is greater—more than half of the drones in these continuous raids at present
Ballistic missiles also remain a separate threat; their launches, Oleh Zhdanov emphasizes, are more difficult to predict. He explains that recently Russia has used them at intervals of approximately once every 7–10 days. Moreover, the intensity of such strikes may vary, so Ukraine must also be prepared for combined attacks.
Will Russia have enough resources for continuous attacks
The expert notes that Russia is using the means of destruction at its disposal, while the scale of drone use depends, in particular, on production capabilities.
They can provide a large number of drones—and they do. Note that in September they were stockpiling conventional "Geran-2" drones. In fact, they used very few of them for a month, and then in the first ten days of October they carried out two powerful strikes, when the number of conventional drones exceeded 500 units. And now they are launching them within the limits produced by their enterprises
At the same time, Oleh Zhdanov believes that Russia has limited capacity to accumulate large stockpiles of weapons, so it is forced to constantly replenish the resources it has used. However, this does not mean that the intensity of the attacks will necessarily decrease in the near future.
They are essentially operating straight from the production line; there are very few stockpiles at present. And I say again, we have two options: the first is to destroy their production facilities, but we cannot reach them, plus they have now begun burying the same "Geran" drones in the ground. So the second option is to build an air defense system in a new, modern sense, rather than according to the old approaches of the Soviet Union or the Second World War
Why Russia is relying on drones
Massive drone attacks allow Russia to exhaust Ukrainian air defenses over a prolonged period and create a constant threat to the civilian population and infrastructure. In the expert's view, the Kremlin seeks to use these strikes as an instrument of pressure on Ukrainians in order to secure concessions on its own terms.
The objective is one and only one—to break public opinion so that people agree to capitulate on the terms of the Russian Federation. And now, by the way, negotiations are underway in Norway, and it is the same old song: "Surrender, and everything will be fine for you. If you do not surrender to us, we will continue the shelling." That's all
The expert also links the intensity of Russian attacks, in particular, to the upcoming midterm elections in the United States and negotiations on ending the war, in order to increase pressure on Ukraine precisely during periods of important international events.
Absolutely. putin always ties powerful shelling of Ukraine and massive combined strikes to political events. Today, the midterm elections in the United States are at the top of our agenda. And in fact, in my view, both Trump and putin have simultaneously gone all in. They are applying pressure in every way they can, - with all available forces and means
What could force Russia to reduce the number of strikes
The expert identifies strengthening Ukraine’s air defense as one of the key areas for countering Russian attacks. In his opinion, it is necessary to improve the ability to intercept targets at short and medium ranges, as well as to develop weapons capable of destroying threats before they are used. In addition, strikes against Russia’s military-industrial enterprises also play an important role.
Sanctions are a long song. And the most effective sanctions are our missiles and our drones. Unfortunately, our strikes against military-industrial complex enterprises are not as powerful as one would like, because even a drone carrying 100 kilograms of explosives is not a missile carrying 300 or 500 kilograms of explosives
Oleh Zhdanov also drew attention to the importance of ballistic weapons, which, according to him, could enhance Ukraine’s ability to strike Russian launchers and other military targets. At the same time, the effectiveness of countermeasures depends not only on the availability of such weapons, but also on the ability to detect targets in a timely manner and strike them. The expert believes that the development of indigenous missile technologies could become one of the factors deterring Russian attacks.
If we had ballistic missiles, we would take out the launchers or at least drive them away from the border so that they could not reach our territory. There is very little time to hit a launcher at its launch position or in the loading area. That is why Russia is very afraid of Ukraine acquiring ballistic weapons

articles.title: Maybe it’s personal: Europeans worry Trump just likes Putin more than Zelenskyy
articles.body:
Maybe it’s personal: Europeans worry Trump just likes Putin more than Zelenskyy
After 20 months of upheaval in transatlantic relations, EU officials fear the U.S. president dislikes Ukraine’s leader too much to push for a fair peace.
U.S. President Donald Trump and Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy are pictured on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Sept. 22, 2026. | Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images
In a throwaway comment this week, Donald Trump made clear that he does not regard the war in Ukraine as a conflict with fault on both sides. “Russia frankly has been fine on Ukraine,” the U.S. president said. “They have not been doing that much.”
To residents of Kyiv — who have endured weeks of intensifying bombardment — and Ukraine’s allies across Europe, the remark confirmed a growing impression that the U.S. is taking Russia leader Vladimir Putin’s side in the war.
“American negotiators have been trying to push Ukraine into surrender for already almost two years,” the EU’s top diplomat Kaja Kallas told the European Parliament on Tuesday. The reason Ukraine hasn’t “surrendered on Putin’s terms” so far is because Europe has been providing so much support, she added.
Advertisement
As they scratch their heads for explanations for Trump’s latest turn against Ukraine, some European officials and diplomats think it comes down to the president’s personal preferences, as much as his country’s political aims.
“I do think it’s a personal thing,” said former British Cabinet minister David Lidington, now distinguished fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, a leading security think tank in London. “Trump is self-centered — his personal predilections for dictators and autocrats, his desire to give opportunities to U.S. businesses … are very important parts of his motivation.”
In private, EU officials agree. “Trump doesn’t like [Ukrainian President Volodymyr] Zelenskyy. He just doesn’t like him,” said one government official who has observed both men closely. “That makes it harder to get the U.S. to help on peace. Everything is a rational business deal with Trump, until it’s not.”
A diplomat from an EU country — granted anonymity, like others in this report, to discuss sensitive matters — said the inconsistent Trump could change his mind again and reverse recent moves against Ukraine. The U.S. president has chopped and changed on many issues, “except one thing,” the diplomat said. “He seems to be supportive of the Russians.”
“He’s been critical of Ukraine, the EU, NATO, but hardly ever said anything critical about Putin. It is striking. We have to deal with an administration that seems to be more pro-Russian than anything else,” the diplomat said.
The White House didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
Advertisement
Mounting losses
For Ukraine and its European allies, the idea that nothing can or will change Trump’s feelings about Zelenskyy is a bleak one. After four-and-a-half years of war, Kyiv is running low on funding, air defenses and — amid swelling support for Europe’s populist right — facing a potential loss of political support in the months ahead.
Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff met the Ukrainian president and the leaders of Norway and Finland for talks in Oslo on Tuesday, and will head to St. Petersburg to discuss peace proposals with the Russian leadership on Wednesday as the White House pushes hard for a ceasefire. One option Putin will be offered is a three-way leaders’ summit with Trump and Zelenskyy.
Previous efforts to get the Russian president to attend such a meeting have failed, however, and EU diplomats do not believe Putin is showing any genuine desire for a ceasefire. That is partly what makes Trump’s hostility toward Zelenskyy so problematic.
“There is a clear consensus across Europe that Putin does not want peace,” a second EU diplomat said. “He will need to be forced into peace.”
Trump greets Russian President Vladimir Putin as he arrives for talks in Anchorage, Alaska, on Aug. 15, 2025. | Andrew Harnik/Getty Images
But instead of making demands of Putin, Trump has ratcheted up his pressure on Zelenskyy, even amid escalating Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities this month. Ukraine’s leader is feeling the strain, as he told his EU counterparts in private meetings in Brussels last week, according to the first diplomat.
In a succession of highly critical comments in recent days, Trump has said Zelenskyy “doesn’t care” and “doesn’t want to end this war;” and should be replaced as leader or as Ukraine’s negotiator. “President Putin would like to see a settlement,” Trump said. “President Zelenskyy could have solved this war, or he could have made a deal, many times.”
Advertisement
The Oval Office beating
Trump’s animosity may date back to an incident during his first term in 2019, when he urged the Ukrainian leader to help with an investigation into Joe Biden, who eventually defeated Trump in the following presidential election, Lidington said. A succession of hostile encounters in the years since — including in the Oval Office in February 2025 — have reinforced the impression, he said.
“It was clear that in the infamous meeting in the White House that Trump and [Vice President JD] Vance had planned that public beating-up of Zelenskyy and it struck me then that there was a strong personal element to this,” said Lidington.
“I think there’s another element, which is that if you look at the people Trump tries to court, it tends to be autocratic strongman — and it is ‘man’ — leaders,” Lidington said.
He recalled attending a dinner with world leaders in 2018 to mark the centenary of the end of World War I in Paris. French President Emmanuel Macron and the German chancellor at the time, Angela Merkel, were playing joint hosts “at the top table,” but Trump was not interested in making small talk with either of them, Lidington said.
“It was pretty obvious from the body language that Trump was impatient with them and one of the people he really wanted to talk to was [Turkish leader Recep Tayyip] Erdoğan and other people who were a bit more in that strongman image that he likes to portray himself,” he observed.
‘Strange stories’
A senior official from a European country familiar with the Ukraine talks said Trump’s motives were partly political, partly about calculating what would be profitable and partly about personalities.
Advertisement
“They are currently in an election cycle and need someone to blame for rising prices,” the official said. “In general, Trump tends to like various types of people and leaders. He actually has a fondness for successful and cheerful people.”
In recent days, Zelenskyy has warned his country is suffering more civilian casualties because the U.S. has cut back on support, including Starlink and Starshield services that help Ukraine defend itself against Russian attacks and plan operations. “We still have no explanation for this, just different strange stories,” Zelenskyy told U.S. congressmen on Monday.
This month, the advanced warnings of incoming Russian missile attacks from U.S. partners have failed to come through as normal. Ukraine is also running low on Patriot missile interceptors, he said.
The Pentagon has not issued an official comment on the Ukrainian complaints. The U.N. Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine said 328 civilians were killed and more than 2,000 wounded across Ukraine last month, an 85% increase compared to September 2025. The U.N. said that the first two weeks of October were among the deadliest for civilians in Ukraine in years, driven by increased missile and drone strikes.
The first EU diplomat quoted above said many European governments were irritated that Trump had cut them out of his conversations with Putin so far. “There is probably much more dialogue between the Americans and the Russians than we might know,” the diplomat said.
Tuesday’s meeting with Witkoff in Norway raised the possibility that direct engagement with Putin might be back on the cards, for Zelenskyy at least.
“Today was a good day for peace,” Finland’s President Alexander Stubb said after attending the talks in Oslo. “On a substantive and technical level we have actually made a lot of progress under the radar in the past week or so,” Stubb said.
The process is now going in the right direction again, he added. “Hopefully, we don’t do any backtracking.”

articles.title: Trump may completely halt the supply of Patriot missiles to Ukraine – NATO warns of the risks

Trump may completely halt the supply of Patriot missiles to Ukraine – NATO warns of the risks
Kyiv • UNN
NATO fears a complete halt to U.S. arms deliveries to Ukraine due to tensions between Zelenskyy and Trump. Patriot deliveries are already being delayed.
NATO representatives warned Ukrainian officials about the risk of a complete halt to the supply of U.S. weapons, including missiles for Patriot systems, due to deteriorating relations between Presidents Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Donald Trump. Details
According to the publication, the Alliance's leadership fears that relations between Kyiv and Washington could deteriorate completely. The PURL program, under which European countries purchase U.S. weapons for Ukraine, is a particular concern. The United States currently supplies only about 12 Patriot interceptor missiles per month, four times fewer than during Joe Biden's presidency.
U.S. delaying deliveries of missiles already paid for by European allies
Zelenskyy previously stated that U.S. missiles were arriving irregularly, despite European partners having already paid for the corresponding deliveries. In addition, according to him, the Pentagon failed several times to warn Ukraine about Russian missile attacks.
The situation is complicated by limited stocks of U.S. interceptors.
