articles.title: U.S. Navy taps portable reactor to power Indiana base
articles.body:
- The U.S. Navy selected Radiant to install a 1-megawatt Kaleidos microreactor at Naval Weapons Station Crane in Indiana under the U.S. Army’s Janus Program.
- The Department of War wants the Navy’s first shore-based microreactor operating at Crane no later than September 2028.
The U.S. Navy has selected Radiant to install its Kaleidos nuclear microreactor at Naval Weapons Station Crane in Indiana, putting a commercial company in charge of the service’s first shore-based advanced reactor, which the Department of War wants running no later than September 2028.
Radiant announced the selection on Oct. 20, about six weeks after the Department of War named Crane as the site for the Navy’s first microreactor without saying which vendor would build it.
Kaleidos is a factory-built reactor that produces 1 megawatt of electricity and is designed to be moved by truck, ship or aircraft and set up at a customer’s site without cooling water, major excavation or extensive construction. Each unit runs for up to five years before it needs refueling, over a planned service life of 20 years, and at Crane it is meant to keep power flowing to the base independently of the regional grid, which matters for an installation where the Naval Surface Warfare Center, Crane Division, works on microelectronics, high-voltage systems and weapons.
The reactor will be installed under the U.S. Army’s Janus Program, the Pentagon effort to put commercially owned and operated microreactors on military bases so they can keep critical facilities running through grid outages. Before it reaches Crane, the project still has to move through design refinement, prototype testing, environmental review, site preparation and coordination with the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, with technical support from the Naval Nuclear Propulsion Program, the organization that runs the reactors on the Navy’s carriers and submarines.
“The Janus Program was built from day one to deliver real, reliable hardware and systems to solve energy resilience challenges across all of the Services,” said Dr. Jeff Waksman, Principal Deputy Assistant Secretary of the Army for Installations, Energy and Environment. “We are excited to partner with the Navy to place a Janus reactor at NWS Crane, and by doing so to deliver the state of Indiana its first advanced microreactor.”
Crane is the second military base Radiant has lined up this year under Janus. In August, the U.S. Army awarded contracts worth up to $2.2 billion to five reactor makers, with Radiant receiving the largest share, up to $750 million to deploy 15 Kaleidos units by 2030, as we reported, starting with three reactors at Fort Benning in Georgia that will back up Lawson Army Airfield and other critical facilities, we reported in September. The company also has a deal with the Defense Innovation Unit and the Department of the Air Force to deliver a Kaleidos unit by 2028, and it now says it is the only nuclear company working with the U.S. Army, U.S. Navy and U.S. Air Force at once.
“Our installations are foundational warfighting platforms and ensuring their resilience is essential to supporting the Fleet,” said Vice Adm. Brad Collins, Commander, Navy Installations Command. “By investing in advanced capabilities like this microreactor at Crane, we are providing our Shore infrastructure with the resources needed to sustain the mission and empower our warfighters.”
Radiant has not yet proven the design at full scale, and the reactor is now going through a year-long test campaign at the Idaho National Laboratory’s DOME facility, where the Department of Energy gave the company exclusive access after a competitive selection. The company says the test uses the same reactor design and the same type of fresh fuel that will go to military customers, running at full power for an extended period to show the performance and reliability needed before deployment.
The Navy brings decades of reactor experience to the project, since the Naval Nuclear Propulsion Program, founded in 1948, has logged more than 7,500 reactor-years of operation and over 171 million miles under nuclear power without a reactor accident.

articles.title: Ukraine hits Russian heavy rocket launcher near Black Sea coast
articles.body:
- Ukraine’s Prymary drone unit destroyed a Russian Tornado-S rocket launcher near Skadovsk in occupied Kherson Oblast, hitting it with several kamikaze drones.
- OSINT analyst Dominik geolocated the strike to Ulyanivka, while HUR said the unit also hit a Buk-M3, an Orion drone and four radars.
Ukrainian drones have destroyed a Russian 9K515 Tornado-S heavy multiple launch rocket system in occupied Kherson Oblast, hitting the launcher with several different kamikaze drones in succession in a strike carried out by the Prymary unit of Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence (HUR), which released the footage on Oct. 20.
OSINT analyst Dominik geolocated the strike to the village of Ulyanivka just outside Skadovsk, at coordinates 46.189524, 32.964916, which places the launcher close to the Black Sea coast and well behind the Dnipro River front line.
The video shows the Tornado-S being struck by drones of different types one after another, a method Ukrainian operators use against high-value vehicles so that a second or third drone can finish off a target that survives the first hit before the crew can drive it away. HUR did not give the exact date of the strike, saying only that it took place over the past month, and Russia has not commented on the loss.
The Tornado-S is one of the most valuable launchers in Russia’s rocket artillery, since it is a modernized version of the Soviet 9A52 Smerch that fires 300 mm (11.8-inch) rockets from a 12-tube launcher mounted on an eight-wheeled Kamaz truck. Built by NPO Splav in Tula, part of the state-owned Rostec group, the system uses digital fire control and GLONASS satellite navigation so its three-person crew can prepare and fire a full salvo without leaving the cab, and its guided rockets can reach targets up to 120 km (75 miles) away.
That range lets Russian crews fire on Ukrainian cities from deep inside occupied territory, and in the south the system has repeatedly been used against Kherson and other towns along the Dnipro from positions in the occupied part of the region. Ukrainian units put a high price on each launcher they destroy, and after a drone strike on a Tornado-S in the Huliaipole sector in July, the Pomsta Border Guard Brigade estimated the vehicle’s value at more than $15 million.
The Skadovsk strike is the latest in a series of Tornado-S losses this year as Ukrainian drones reach further behind Russian lines. In February, the Ptahi unit of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces destroyed a launcher in occupied Zaporizhzhia Oblast with FP-2 strike drones guided by reconnaissance drones, we reported at the time, and in March a long-range Fire Point drone hit three Tornado-S launchers and a transport-loader near Karakul in occupied Crimea, as we reported. Two more launchers were hit near Melitopol within a few days in late April, followed by the July strike in the Huliaipole sector.
“Big names, formidable specifications and the millions invested in military equipment do not guarantee the occupiers’ immunity,” Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence said in its statement.
The Tornado-S was the centerpiece of a wider monthly report from Prymary, which HUR said also hit a Buk-M3 air defense system, an Orion reconnaissance and strike drone, a Kasta-2E low-altitude radar, a Nebo-U long-range surveillance radar and two P-18 early warning radars. The unit also struck a drone assembly and repair site and a building housing troops of the 4th Air Assault Battalion of the 108th Air Assault Regiment, although HUR gave no dates or locations for those strikes and did not say whether every target was destroyed or only damaged.

articles.title: Pentagon deploys USS Theodore Roosevelt to Middle East as Trump weighs Iran strikes - report
articles.body:
The Pentagon is sending the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group and the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit to the Middle East, two US officials confirmed to Fox News on Tuesday.
This follows a US official telling The Jerusalem Post on October 1 that the aircraft carrier and a unit of US Marines would be sent to US Central Command (CENTCOM)'s sphere of operations.
The USS Makin Island amphibious ready group also departed San Diego, carrying the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit, the Post reported at the time.
According to Fox's report, the aircraft carrier group is due to arrive in the Middle East by the end of November.
Currently, two other US aircraft carriers are deployed in the region, namely the USS George H. W. Bush, which arrived in April, and the USS George Washington, which arrived in August to replace the USS Abraham Lincoln.
However, US Naval Institute News reported that the USS Theodore Roosevelt was moving to US Central Command's area of operations in order to relieve the USS George Washington.
In addition, the USS Boxer amphibious ready group is deployed in the Arabian Sea, carrying the 11th Marine Expeditionary Unit, alongside the USS Portland and USS Comstock.
Additional naval deployments could provide Trump with more options if strikes on Iran ramp up after midterms
"This will provide more options for the US as President [Donald] Trump is reportedly considering ramping up strikes on Iran after the [November 3] Midterms," Fox News's Chief National Security Correspondent Jennifer Griffen wrote.
The Jerusalem Post also assessed on October 1 that, after this latest deployment, Trump will have significantly greater military capabilities and a wider range of options to act against Iran.
Meanwhile, the US military has been conducting routine troop rotations in recent weeks, and additional troops and aircraft are expected to arrive in the coming weeks as part of preparations for an escalation in the Middle East, security sources told Walla on October 4.
Some 3,000 US troops are currently stationed across Israel. Their duties include operating air defense systems, serving as pilots and support crews, and handling logistics and headquarters operations.
Amichai Stein, Idan Kweller, and Amir Bohbot contributed to this report.

articles.title: Putin, Witkoff meet in Russia for Ukraine war talks
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Putin, Witkoff meet in Russia for talks on Ukraine war
Russia's Vladimir Putin began talks with US envoy Steve Witkoff on ending the Ukraine war in Saint Petersburg on Wednesday, with the American official saying he had brought "ideas" for a possible peace deal.
Witkoff travelled to Russia from Norway, where he met Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky in talks Washington described as "positive."
The meeting is taking place as the United States pushes an end to Europe's worst conflict since World War II, with Russia pounding Ukrainian cities ahead of winter and amid a bitter feud between Donald Trump and Zelensky.
As Witkoff touched down in Putin's home city, Russia announced it would soon begin shipments of diesel to the United States under a deal with Trump, and that it had freed a US citizen—Stephen Hubbard—held by Moscow since the start of the war on allegations of fighting as a "mercenary" for Ukraine.
"We've brought some papers. It's really some ideas, some sort of peace deal between Russia and Ukraine, and you'll read that at your leisure," Witkoff—Trump's business partner and envoy—told Putin in Saint Petersburg's Konstantinovsky Palace.
Putin thanked Trump for his efforts to resolve the war and said he was eager to be informed about the US meeting with Zelensky.
The longtime Russian leader has repeatedly refused to hold face-to-face talks with Zelensky and said that Moscow intends to seize the rest of eastern Ukraine.
Witkoff told Putin he hoped trilateral talks can resume.
"I'm hoping that you might consider that as a next step in the peace process so we can begin to have technical teams discussing what are those next steps," he told the Russian leader.
Putin thanked Trump for his "attention" to the conflict and said the US leader had "insisted that it was necessary to end this conflict" in their last phone call.
Russia's war against Ukraine has killed hundreds of thousands of troops on both sides as well as thousands of civilians.
As Witkoff arrived in Saint Petersburg, Kyiv said Moscow's strikes killed at least four people —including two in the capital and an elderly couple in the eastern Kharkiv region.
'Momentum' in talks
Meeting Putin, Witkoff described his talks with Zelensky as "productive."
"I think there's some degree of momentum and I hope that today can be another step forward in the peace process and discussing how we resolve the Ukrainian conflict," he said.
Zelensky on Tuesday thanked Washington for the resumption of US intelligence sharing on Russian strikes.
The Witkoff-Zelensky meeting in Norway followed days of friction between Washington and Kyiv, with Zelensky urging the US not to side with Russia and Trump calling for the Ukrainian leader to be replaced.
Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner is also due to participate in Wednesday's talks with Putin remotely.
US-led talks on the conflict have so far not led to a breakthrough and Moscow insists it intends to press on with its offensive.
Witkoff also told Putin that Washington was "grateful" for a diesel deal—met with astonishment in Kyiv and across Europe—that saw US sanctions on Moscow eased to allow Russian fuel to flow to the United States.
The deal has been seen as a way to try to lower fuel prices for American consumers ahead of testing midterm elections in the US next month.
Washington was interested in further "business and economic cooperation" with Russia when the war ends, Witkoff said.
"We even talk about it now openly with the Ukrainians to give them some sort of sense about what the possibilities will be when this whole conflict is over," he said.
Kyiv has pleaded with Western countries to put more pressure on Moscow and not lift sanctions.
Ahead of the talks, Putin announced that Stephen Hubbard, an American taken captive by Russian forces in Ukraine in 2022 and later sentenced to almost seven years in prison, had been freed.
Trump had asked the Russian leader to free Hubbard, a retired English teacher in his 70s who had always denied the charges he was a "mercenary" fighting for Ukraine.
Witkoff hailed the move and called Putin a "humanitarian".
Trump later said that Hubbard was on his way to the Unites States and that the release had not been part of a swap deal.

articles.title: Kallas lashes out at US over Ukraine peace efforts
articles.body:
Kallas lashes out at US over Ukraine peace efforts
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas has accused Washington of trying to force Ukraine to surrender to Russia, attacking President Donald Trump’s diplomatic efforts to end the conflict.
Speaking to the European Parliament in Strasbourg on Tuesday, Kallas credited Europe’s military and financial backing of Kiev with prolonging the conflict and preventing Ukraine from accepting Moscow’s terms.
“American negotiators have been trying to push Ukraine into surrender for already almost two years, one and a half years now,” she said, as quoted by Euronews.
Moscow has cited Kiev’s aggressive posture and the hostile position of its European backers as major obstacles to a peace settlement. Ukraine has consistently rejected Russia’s conditions, insisting on joining NATO and restoring control over all territories it claims.
Kallas’ remarks came a day after US President Donald Trump said negotiations were making “great progress,” defending his decision to ease economic pressure on Russia to keep diplomacy moving.
Trump has stepped up his criticism of Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky, describing him as “more difficult to deal with” than Russian President Vladimir Putin. He has accused Zelensky of prolonging the conflict and taking Washington’s extensive support for granted, and has criticized Kiev’s continued attacks on Russian refineries for disrupting global diesel markets. Zelensky has said he feels betrayed by Trump.
Trump lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports earlier this month to curb rising energy prices ahead of the US midterm elections. On Friday, he suspended tariffs targeting China, India and other major buyers of Russian oil and gas. Trump defended the measures, saying he did not want to drive Moscow away from the negotiating table. The decisions drew criticism from European officials, with Kallas describing the diesel agreement as a “gift to Putin.”
US special envoy Steve Witkoff held talks in Oslo on Tuesday with Zelensky, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store, with Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner joining remotely. Witkoff is expected to travel to St. Petersburg on Wednesday for another round of discussions with Russian officials, according to Store.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Monday that Moscow “highly appreciates” Washington’s continued mediation efforts.
Russia has insisted on a long-term peace deal that addresses the root causes of the conflict, rejecting the idea of a temporary truce. Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has accused Zelensky of repeatedly undermining negotiations, suggesting that any agreement acceptable to Moscow and Washington would threaten the Ukrainian leader’s hold on power.
Further financial support for Kiev has also become a source of disagreement within the EU. At Friday’s EU summit in Brussels, Zelensky demanded another €70 billion ($78.5 billion) for next year, in addition to €90 billion already pledged by the bloc to bankroll Kiev’s war effort.

Ukrainian Partisans Cut Moscow Military Comms to Help Drones Slip Through Russian Air Defenses
Agents of the ATESH partisan movement are sabotaging Russian military communications around IXcellerate, one of Moscow’s largest commercial data centers, in an effort to disrupt air-defense coordination and help Ukrainian drones reach their targets, the group said on October 21.
“We are disabling enemy channels, disrupting command and control, and helping UAVs reach their targets,” ATESH said.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
IXcellerate is a major part of Moscow’s digital infrastructure, supporting banking applications, card payments, telecommunications operators, and business services.
ATESH claims that Russia’s Defense Ministry also uses infrastructure connected to the facility for military communications and air-defense command systems, effectively embedding military traffic within civilian server networks.
According to the movement, drone strikes depend not only on the aircraft themselves but also on disrupting the communications networks that connect Russian air-defense crews and command posts.
Cutting those links on the ground, ATESH says, can delay target information and reduce coordination between air-defense units.
Without stable communications, Russian air-defense crews can lose situational awareness, receive targeting information too late, and struggle to cover the routes used by incoming drones, the group said.
ATESH claims its agents are identifying military communications infrastructure concealed within civilian facilities and disrupting those networks from inside Russia.
The group said Moscow’s attempts to hide military traffic inside civilian server infrastructure have not prevented partisan cells from locating and targeting the communications links supporting Russian military operations.
Previously, ATESH claimed responsibility for sabotaging a critical electrical substation in Azov, Russia’s Rostov region, disrupting power to a defense manufacturing facility that produces guidance systems and other components for Russian missiles.

articles.title: Report: Netanyahu planned massive Iran attack, but Trump blocked it
articles.body:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu planned to launch a major new military offensive against Iran earlier this month, but President Donald Trump blocked the operation over concerns about restarting the war ahead of the November 3 U.S. midterm elections, the Financial Times reported Wednesday, citing three people familiar with the plans.
According to the FT, Netanyahu instructed the Israeli military to prepare a multi-day bombing campaign for the weekend of October 10, targeting Iranian nuclear facilities, power plants and other civilian infrastructure, as well as sites associated with the regime. The planned offensive was intended to surpass the intensity of the joint U.S.-Israeli military campaign launched in February.
The operation was ultimately shelved because of Trump's opposition, although both leaders have continued threatening renewed military action against Tehran. One person familiar with the discussions told the FT that another round of strikes in the coming weeks remained a realistic possibility, potentially involving both Israel and the United States.
"There will either be a deal or an attack," the person said, suggesting that Washington hopes to force Iran into an agreement addressing its nuclear program and control of the Strait of Hormuz, the strategic waterway through which much of the world's oil passes.
The report said Israeli officials had presented their American counterparts with an updated list of Iranian targets based on newly collected intelligence. The list reportedly includes civilian infrastructure sites that were not attacked during the previous campaign.
U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth visited Israel on Monday for talks with Netanyahu and other senior officials, according to an Israeli official cited by the newspaper. It remains unclear whether Washington had been expected to participate directly in the operation originally planned for October 10.
Another person familiar with the matter suggested that Israel's military preparations could also have been intended to increase pressure on Tehran during negotiations, emphasizing that the ultimate decision on renewed hostilities rested with Trump.
Deputy White House spokesperson Anna Kelly told the FT that Iran was in extremely poor economic and military condition and that U.S. efforts to blockade Iranian ports while facilitating Gulf oil exports were succeeding. She explicitly ruled out American strikes before the midterm elections.
The revelations come amid heightened military readiness in Israel ahead of the October 27 parliamentary election. IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir has ordered troops to remain on their bases beginning Thursday, suspending leave through election day to ensure voting can proceed safely.
Trump has meanwhile publicly endorsed Netanyahu's re-election bid and intensified his warnings to Tehran. On Sunday, he suggested that Washington could be forced to confront Iran without Israeli support if Netanyahu lost, while threatening further military action unless Iran changed course.
In a video released Monday from an Israeli air base, Netanyahu told Trump that they had unfinished business to complete together. Trump responded by praising the Israeli prime minister and expressing confidence in their partnership.
According to the FT, current and former Israeli security officials fear that a new war launched so close to the election could undermine the democratic process. Even if Netanyahu loses, he could remain caretaker prime minister for weeks while coalition negotiations proceed, retaining the legal authority to order military action.
The prime minister's office did not respond to the FT's requests for comment, while the IDF declined to comment.

PARIS — Suspicious drones flew over military facilities in southeastern France earlier this month, the French navy said on Wednesday.
During a large-scale armed forces exercise that lasted from Oct. 5 to Oct. 16, "unauthorized drones were detected in the no-fly zone, near and above military sites," the navy said in a press statement.

The French navy's statement confirms local media reporting about drone sightings around Toulon. The southeastern town is home to one of France's largest naval bases, which hosts the country's aircraft carrier Charles de Gaulle as well as attack submarines.

articles.title: New energy shock hits Germany
articles.body:
New energy shock hits Germany
Petroleum product prices have soared in Germany, with gasoline and diesel nearly 49% more expensive and heating oil nearly doubling over the past year, according to official figures.
The surge comes as Europe’s largest economy continues to grapple with the fallout from its break with Russian energy in 2022, now compounded by the US-Israeli war against Iran.
Prices for refined oil products jumped 51.3% year-on-year in September and 8.2% from August, the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis) reported on Tuesday. Heating oil surged 91.8%, motor fuels rose 48.6%, and naphtha, used in chemical manufacturing, climbed 53.8%.
The figures reflect producer prices rather than those paid by consumers at the pump.
The shock spread across the energy sector. Producer energy prices rose 14.9% year-on-year, with natural gas distribution costs up 15% and electricity 8.2%.
Germany’s crude oil import bill also surged despite slightly lower purchases. In the first eight months of 2026, the cost jumped 21.7% to €30 billion ($33.6 billion), while volumes fell 0.6% to 49.1 million tons. Destatis attributed the increase to higher crude oil prices amid the Middle East conflict.
The pressure has spread across German industry. Overall producer prices rose 6.7% year-on-year in September, the sharpest increase since March 2023. Manufacturing materials and components became 6.4% more expensive, while machinery and equipment rose 2.4%. Excluding energy, producer prices were up 3.2%.
The Iran war has severely disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital route for global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies, driving up energy prices worldwide. Brent crude topped $111 a barrel on Tuesday, a five-month high, while US benchmark WTI exceeded $104.
Although Gulf crude oil shipments have reportedly recovered to around 80% of pre-war levels, new Iranian attacks on vessels have kept markets on edge. Escalating fighting between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis has added pressure, with strikes on Saudi oil infrastructure and renewed clashes near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait threatening another key shipping route linking the Red Sea to global markets.
Germany’s energy troubles, however, predate the Middle East crisis. The country has faced high costs since abandoning cheap Russian energy following the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022, forcing energy-intensive manufacturers to seek more expensive alternatives.
Before the break, Russia supplied 55% of Germany’s natural gas imports. Direct imports from Russia have since fallen to zero, with Germany reportedly paying five times as much for gas. Norway (44%), the Netherlands (24%), and Belgium (21%) have become its main suppliers, with US liquefied natural gas (LNG) accounting for much of the remainder.
Berlin has spent around €50 billion to cushion the price shock since cutting Russian gas imports, German media reported last month. Yet the economy remains sluggish, with corporate insolvencies hitting a 13-year high in the first half of 2026. Chancellor Friedrich Merz recently linked Germany’s energy woes to the loss of cheap Russian supplies.
Meanwhile, Berlin committed €96 billion in Ukraine-related support, launched a €100 billion rearmament drive, and pledged to raise core defense spending to 3.5% of GDP by 2029.
Amid criticism that increased military spending is at the expense of domestic needs, Merz’s approval rating sank to a record-low 10% in a poll in October. His Christian Democratic Union (CDU) has suffered major electoral setbacks against the right-wing Alternative for Germany (AfD), which has overtaken the CDU-led bloc in national polling. The AfD has called for Russian gas imports to be restored.
Moscow has long argued that Western energy sanctions are counterproductive, redirecting Russian exports while forcing Europeans to pay more for alternative supplies. Russia has offered to cover shortages and resume deliveries, but says its proposals have gone unanswered.

articles.title: Witkoff urges Putin to restart trilateral talks on Ukraine
articles.body:
United States special envoy Steve Witkoff has proposed that Russian President Vladimir Putin consider resuming trilateral talks involving Ukraine, the United States and Russia at the level of technical groups, and has handed over documents setting out approaches to a peace settlement of Russia's war against Ukraine, Russian media reported.
"I also hope you will consider resuming trilateral talks involving Ukraine, Russia and the United States, within which we could discuss next steps toward a settlement," Witkoff said at a meeting with Putin in St. Petersburg on Wednesday.
The talks could involve representatives of technical groups and experts who would work through the relevant issues in detail, he said. Witkoff expressed hope that the sides could discuss the proposal even if they do not reach a final decision at the current meeting.
The American envoy also said he had brought documents setting out approaches to a peace settlement and asked Putin to look at them. United States special envoy Jared Kushner was to join the meeting by phone, and, according to Witkoff, also wanted to present a few ideas.
After the Oslo talks on October 20, attended by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Witkoff and European representatives, Finnish President Alexander Stubb said the sides had discussed security, the economy, air defense, energy infrastructure and a partial ceasefire, including in the context of energy and food security.
Zelenskyy said the proposals worked out by Ukraine and its European partners provide for a move to a potential trilateral meeting of leaders to resolve issues that require decisions at the highest level. He said Witkoff was to pass these proposals to the Russian side.

articles.title: Mother of all bombs or father of all missiles?
articles.body:
Mother of all bombs or father of all missiles?
In a note, Etemad examined US rhetoric about using the “Mother of All Bombs” and Iran’s response that it could employ the “Father of All Missiles.” The paper argued that Iran’s statements do not necessarily mean such bombs would be ineffective, nor that Tehran has publicly revealed the nature or scope of any potential response. Political declarations, deterrent warnings, and military operational plans are three distinct matters.
The verbal clash between the “Mother of All Bombs and the Father of All Missiles” reflects a battle of narratives more than a definitive answer to a military question. Washington seeks to intimidate through displays of destructive power, while Tehran emphasizes its retaliatory capabilities and the costs of any attack. Ultimately, the impact of either narrative will depend not on the names of bombs and missiles but on real military capabilities, political decisions, and the consequences of any confrontation.
Khorasan: Iran has achieved many of its war objectives
Khorasan argued that Iran has already achieved many of its goals in the conflict. According to the paper, many of the developments currently unfolding in Europe are a result of Iran’s actions. While Western governments had intended to dedicate significant financial resources to supporting their populations, they have instead been forced to return to older policies to manage the economic consequences of the war. This has led to growing public dissatisfaction and notable social reactions. The newspaper claimed that Iran has already attained a large portion of its objectives: it succeeded in limiting the conflict from a national to a regional level, forcing its foes to operate under those constraints. It also asserted that Iran overcame infrastructure-focused warfare, severely suppressed enemy agents within the country, and maintained overall domestic stability by preventing major shortages and deep economic stagnation.
Ettelaat: Which side will compromise, Iran or the US?
Ettelaat discussed the lack of progress in ongoing negotiations between Iran and the United States, citing former Minister of Culture and Islamic Guidance Ali Jannati. He argued that diplomacy has not failed, because opportunities for negotiation remain available even under the most difficult circumstances. Over the past month, Qatari mediators have reportedly conveyed Iranian proposals to the United States and delivered Washington’s responses back to Tehran. According to Jannati, the talks have stalled because Iran proposed seven principles as the basis for negotiations and the United States broadly accepted the framework but strongly disagreed over the sequence in which the provisions should be implemented. Washington wants the nuclear issue to be addressed first, whereas Tehran views it as the final matter for discussion. He suggested that both sides continue to insist on their positions and that little progress is likely unless one party shows flexibility and makes concessions. Otherwise, he warned, the possibility of renewed war remains.
Vatan-e-Emrooz: France bowed to Hormuz
Vatan-e-Emrooz analyzed protests in France and comments made by President Macron. According to the paper, Macron acknowledged in a televised address that French citizens had reason to be upset about rising fuel prices linked to developments in the Persian Gulf. The newspaper noted that Macron had previously stated that France was living with the consequences of the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. It linked current economic pressures to events eight months earlier, when US and Israeli attacks on Iran led to the closure of the strategic waterway. The paper argued that the disruption of oil shipments through Hormuz triggered increases in fuel costs, inflation, and living expenses worldwide. It contended that these economic effects have fueled ongoing protests in France, which began in mid-September over shortages of teachers and inadequate school facilities but have continued for more than a month due to broader concerns about the cost of living.
Shargh: Repeated US threats aim to weaken social resilience
In an interview with Shargh, Seyed Jalil Mirmohammadi Meybodi, a member of the Iranian Parliament’s Industries and Mines Committee, discussed the main source of “psychological warfare” against Iran by the Trump administration. He argued that it originates from US policy and Washington’s extensive media capabilities. Psychological warfare is one of America’s principal tools in its confrontation with Iran, and Tehran faces an enemy that controls powerful global media networks. He claimed that the United States has failed to achieve its objectives and has therefore resorted to new threats and attempts to project victory. He said that Donald Trump continually seeks to portray himself as victorious and might use a major military action, such as a large-scale bombing campaign, to claim success. Meybodi also argued that any new military action against Iran would be met with a reciprocal response. In his view, frequent public discussion of war often makes actual conflict less likely, and recurring threats may be intended more to influence Iran’s political and psychological calculations than to signal an imminent military operation.

articles.title: Israel may be forced to act as Iran rebuilds military capabilities before election, officials warn
articles.body:
Israel is monitoring Iranian efforts to rebuild its military capabilities following the damage Tehran sustained during Operation Roaring Lion, with security officials warning that developments could force Israel to defend itself despite Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's desire to avoid escalation ahead of the elections, according to assessments discussed in recent Israeli security consultations.
Intelligence indicating that Iran is working to restore its military capabilities following the blows it sustained during Operation Roaring Lion was examined during security discussions held in Israel.
In recent weeks, Iranian measures indicating renewed military preparations have been identified. Israeli officials believe that the completion of these preparations could significantly strengthen Iran's combat capabilities. Previous assessments have also highlighted the speed of Iran's military recovery following the conflict.
According to officials familiar with the discussions, "Netanyahu wants the elections to take place as planned and on schedule, something that would not be possible if Israel were in a state of emergency involving fighting against Iran."
Nevertheless, the officials stressed that the situation is changing in accordance with the pace of Iran's military preparations and activities, and that Israel's security assessments are being updated as developments unfold.
Israel does not rule out renewed military action against Iran
"It is impossible to completely rule out a situation in which developments on the ground would require Israel to defend itself," the officials said, despite the desire to avoid escalation ahead of the elections.
US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth made a brief, unannounced visit to Israel on Monday, during which he met with Netanyahu at the Israeli Air Force's Ovda Airbase in southern Israel. The meeting between Netanyahu and Hegseth took place amid heightened security discussions.
The meeting was also attended by Defense Minister Israel Katz, National Security Council head Shmuel Ben Ezra, and other senior officials.
Possible renewal of strikes against Iran
The previously unannounced visit took place amid ongoing Israeli-US security consultations concerning Iran and the possibility of renewed military operations against Iranian nuclear and military facilities.
Neither the Prime Minister's Office nor the Pentagon has issued an official statement regarding the content of the discussions. Hegseth's arrival in Israel was not preceded by a public announcement or the release of an official agenda.
The meeting was held at a military base in southern Israel rather than at the Prime Minister's Office in Jerusalem or the Kirya military headquarters in Tel Aviv, against the backdrop of American military activity at the base and ongoing discussions between the two countries concerning Iran.

articles.title: Air Force’s Top Planner Lays Out Vision for Fighter Fleet Mix by 2035
articles.body:
Roughly two of every five fighters in the Air Force fleet could be F-35As by 2035, according to a new fighter force structure report the service submitted to Congress on Oct. 16.
Lt. Gen. David Tabor, deputy chief of staff for plans and programs, revealed the new estimate during an Oct. 20 media roundtable at the Pentagon as he explained the report’s estimates of the future force’s mix of different types of fighters.
The Air Force did not provide a full copy of the report to reporters.
About 40 percent of the fleet could be F-35s, Tabor said. Another 20 percent would be a combination of F-22 Raptors and F-47s as the sixth-generation fighter replaces the Raptor. The Air Force built 186 operational F-22s, and Tabor said the Air Force still plans to replace them with roughly an equivalent number of F-47s. The remaining 40 percent of the fleet would likely be split evenly between F-15 Eagle variants and F-16 Fighting Falcons, Tabor said.

Currently, the fighter fleet—not counting A-10s—is split roughly 45 percent F-16s, 30 percent F-35s, 15 percent F-15s, and 10 percent F-22s.
Beyond the mix of the fighters, the force structure report also provides a new estimate of the total number of fighters the Air Force says it will need in the years to come: 1,509 combat-coded aircraft by 2035.
That’s up from the 1,271 the service estimated it would have in 2026 and the 1,369 combat-coded fighters it was shooting for by 2030 in last year’s report, Tabor said. The additional 140 jets would be a mixture of F-35s, F-15EXs, and F-47s.
The data used for the previous report was “pretty old,” Tabor said, so the service’s researchers set out to compile fresher and more accurate information. This analysis was going on before combat operations against Iran broke out earlier this year, he said, and was not driven by the war.
The Air Force’s analysis was based on geographic combatant commanders’ reported requirements to achieve their goals at “medium risk,” Tabor said, and he cautioned that is based on their subjective assessments of what they will need—and will likely change in the future.
“Certainly, world events and changing requirements in the combatant commands will change that number,” Tabor said. “Capabilities that we bring on to platforms will change the number, and I think really importantly, technology will change the number.”
Getting to the new 2035 goal depends on two key factors falling into place, Tabor said. First, Congress will need to provide the funds the Air Force needs to buy the jets. And the defense industrial base—in particular, prime contractors Lockheed Martin and Boeing—must produce enough aircraft in time.
Top Air Force officials have for years said the service needs to buy 72 new fighters each year to replace its older, retiring jets and modernize the fleet. The fiscal 2027 budget request doesn’t reach that level, proposing 38 new F-35s and 24 F-15EXs for a total of 62. Tabor said those purchases can “ramp over time” to hit the numbers the Air Force needs.
“The question is, can industry produce at those levels?” Tabor said. “They’ve assured us that they can, and we believe them, but we also actually need to see it manifest.”
Right now, 2027’s funding levels remain a big question mark. The administration’s strategy for funding the Pentagon this year relies on a budget reconciliation bill to add additional funding priorities on top of the proposed “base” appropriations.
The Air Force’s proposed budget counted on $2.34 billion coming through reconciliation to pay for 14 of those 38 new F-35s. If reconciliation doesn’t pass, Tabor said, the Air Force is not out of options. It could try to find money in the base budget to pay for more F-35s, he said—though that would require pulling billions from other critical programs.
“We just lose 14 times [an] F-35’s worth of other capabilities that we were planning on,” Tabor said.
Or, he said, the purchases could be pushed out to 2028, which would further put the Air Force behind on reaching its fighter fleet goals.
“It is really imperative that we get the resourcing we need in order to modernize the Air Force the way we want it to be,” Tabor said. “We need it all.”
In the meantime, the clock is ticking on large portions of the Air Force’s fleet such as older F-15s and F-16s, which are aging and reaching the end of their lifespans.
The Air Force is considering buying a new version of the F-16, which is tentatively being referred to as the F-16G. But the Air Force has not yet made any decision on that, Tabor said, “and we’re not in a position where that decision has to be made immediately.” That decision likely won’t be made as part of the 2028 budgeting process, he said, but perhaps the years that follow.
Older F-16s will reach the end of their lifespans in the mid-2030s, Tabor said, and “we are very conscious of that.” The simple—“and maybe the lazy”—way to approach that problem, Tabor said, is to automatically replace them with new F-16s. But that might not be the best strategy, he said.
“There is a spectrum of capability that we might want to replace the F-16s with,” he said. “It’s not urgent, frankly. What we don’t want to get to is a point where it is urgent, and we haven’t done the homework and decided ‘hey, this is really the right place to be.’ We do have time to churn through that and make sure that we have a good option going forward.”
One advantage to buying more F-16s, which Lockheed Martin now builds in Greenville, S.C., is that “it’s practically a ready-made aircraft,” Tabor said—if the Air Force wants to stick with the same type of capabilities.
Another potential wrinkle is the Pentagon’s push to expand its multiyear procurement authorities. The Air Force is eyeing such agreements for the F-35 and F-15EX, though its request is pending before Congress. More multiyear procurement deals will help provide industry more financial stability, Tabor said, which could make it easier for them to expand and stabilize production of fighters.
But while the Air Force is rapidly preparing to add hundreds of autonomous drone fighters known as Collaborative Combat Aircraft to its fleet—the goal is 500 airframes by 2032—Tabor said they’re not yet changing the service’s calculus on what fighter force it will need in the future.
“CCA is very much a reality,” Tabor said. “It is going to be a part of our future, and there is absolutely a world in which the incorporation of CCAs into the force will mitigate the requirement for the number of fighters. That’s not the CCA that we have right now, but it is advancing very, very rapidly. We’re confident that it will play a major role in future versions of the fighter force structure report.”

articles.title: China and Russia push Japan’s jet scrambles to 4-year high
articles.body:
- Japan’s Air Self-Defense Force scrambled fighters 442 times from April to September 2026, up from 265 in the same period of 2025.
- Scrambles against Russian aircraft rose from 59 to 152, while those against Chinese aircraft and drones climbed from 198 to 285.
Japan’s Air Self-Defense Force scrambled fighter jets 442 times between April 1 and Sept. 30, about two-thirds more than the 265 scrambles in the same period last year, according to Joint Staff Office figures reported by USNI News. The rise came as Chinese and Russian military aircraft flew near Japan far more often, and the six-month total for the first half of Japan’s 2026 fiscal year is the highest first-half count since fiscal 2022, when JASDF fighters launched 446 times.
None of the flights crossed into Japanese sovereign airspace, and the report lists no airspace violations during the period. Japan scrambles fighters against foreign aircraft approaching the country and entering its Air Defense Identification Zone, a monitoring area that reaches well past the 12-nautical-mile (22 km) territorial limit into international airspace.
Chinese aircraft and drones accounted for 285 scrambles, or about 65 percent, up from 198 a year earlier. The sharper change came from Russia, as JASDF fighters launched 152 times against Russian aircraft compared with 59 in the first half of fiscal 2025, which is more than in the first half of any of the four previous fiscal years listed in the report. The remaining five scrambles were classed as “other.”
The Joint Staff Office pointed to three patterns behind the numbers: Russian Il-20 intelligence-gathering flights over the Sea of Japan and the Pacific, Chinese Y-9 intelligence flights over the East China Sea, and long-range joint flights by Chinese H-6 and Russian Tu-95 bombers. Japan reported Y-9 flights on five consecutive days from Sept. 3 to Sept. 7, after we reported on an Aug. 12 Y-9 sortie through the same corridor between the Danjo Islands and Okinawa.
The southwest, which faces Taiwan and the East China Sea, remained the busiest sector, with the Southwestern Air Defense Force logging 201 scrambles against 189 a year earlier. The Northern Air Defense Force, which covers Hokkaido and northern Honshu opposite Russia’s Sakhalin Island, more than doubled its count from 53 to 112. The Central Air Defense Force rose from nine to 27.
The steepest jump came in the Western Air Defense Force, which covers Kyushu, Shikoku and western Honshu and went from 14 scrambles to 102. USNI News, citing the Joint Staff flight-path map, attributed the increase to Chinese activity over the East China Sea and to Russian aircraft flying from the Sea of Japan to the East China Sea to link up with Chinese formations.
The largest single event came on June 27, when two H-6 bombers and two J-16 fighters flew from the East China Sea into the Sea of Japan. There they joined two Russian Tu-95 bombers, two Tu-142 maritime patrol aircraft and a Su-35 fighter. The combined group flew back to the East China Sea, where the Russian bombers and patrol aircraft met another two H-6s and four J-16s, passed between Okinawa and Miyako Island and continued on a long-range flight over the Pacific south of Shikoku.
South Korea also scrambled fighters that day after nearly 10 Chinese and Russian aircraft entered and left its own air defense zone, and Seoul lodged a protest with both countries the next day. It was the first joint bomber flight around Japan since a December 2025 mission that paired two Tu-95s with two H-6s and eight J-16s. Beijing and Moscow describe such patrols as normal cooperation, while Japan’s 2026 defense white paper says repeated joint activities are “obviously intended as demonstration activities against Japan.”
The report also lists 25 publicly announced cases of unusual flight activity during the six months. Chinese Y-9 flights account for 13 of them, twice accompanied by a TB-001 reconnaissance and strike drone, while Russian Il-20 flights appear 10 times. The only other bomber entry covers July 21, when a single Tu-95 and a Su-35 flew over the Sea of Japan.
The surge follows a quieter year. Japan recorded 595 scrambles in all of fiscal 2025, including 214 against Russian aircraft, and monthly counts climbed late in that year, reaching 79 in December 2025. That same month, Japan accused J-15 fighters from the carrier Liaoning of directing their radar at two JASDF F-15s southeast of Okinawa.
The pace held through the summer, with 90 scrambles in July and 76 in August, as Chinese intelligence aircraft and drones and Russian intelligence planes kept up flights around Japan.

articles.title: UAE-made armored vehicles seen again in Russia
articles.body:
- Russia’s Gyurza SOBR unit in the Moscow region has been seen with a Cobra-LAMV armored vehicle made by Emirati company Streit Group.
- Ukraine, the European Union, Switzerland and Canada have sanctioned Streit Group over vehicles supplied to Russia’s National Guard.
Armored vehicles built by Emirati manufacturer Streit Group have been spotted again in Russian service, this time with Gyurza, the special rapid response unit (SOBR) of Rosgvardia’s Main Directorate for the Moscow region, which was photographed operating a Cobra-LAMV 4×4. The light armored vehicle is built on a Toyota Land Cruiser chassis and marketed by Streit to police and internal security forces. It continues to turn up with Russia’s National Guard even though Ukraine, the European Union, Switzerland and Canada have all sanctioned the company over its vehicles reaching Russia.
Cobra vehicles first appeared in Russia in October 2024, when a Russian military blogger published video of a shipment of more than 20 Streit-built Spartan, Cobra and Cougar armored vehicles bound for Russian forces, as we were first to report. In September 2025, Rosgvardia units were filmed training with Spartan SUT vehicles, including one fitted with an 82 mm (3.2-inch) mortar in the rear compartment, we reported at the time. Every one of these deliveries reached Russia well after the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Ukraine was the first to respond, listing Streit Group in 2023, and the European Union and Switzerland followed in October 2025 before adding founder Guerman Goutorov personally to their sanctions lists in May 2026. Canada sanctioned the company in August 2026 for supplying vehicles to Rosgvardia, a move Russia’s ambassador in Ottawa dismissed as having no practical effect, and the new Moscow-region sighting shows that the vehicles keep reaching Russian units regardless.
The Canadian measures carry particular weight because Streit started out as a Canadian business founded in Ontario in 1992 by Goutorov, a Russian-born businessman who served five years in the Soviet police before emigrating to Canada in the early 1990s. He later moved the company’s headquarters to the Ras Al Khaimah free trade zone in the United Arab Emirates, where Streit grew into one of the world’s largest armored vehicle makers with production sites on several continents. Goutorov’s Canadian citizenship shields him personally from Ottawa’s sanctions, and he has appealed his listing in the European Union.
Streit’s links to Russia go well beyond finished vehicles, since the company opened an armored vehicle plant east of Moscow and another in Tatarstan in 2009 and kept trading with Russian suppliers after both the 2014 and 2022 invasions. Customs records show that between 2015 and 2022 it imported 41 shipments of parts from Russian truckmaker Kamaz and 38 shipments of VPK-Ural vehicle kits, including six from the sanctioned Arzamas plant in the two weeks before Russian troops crossed into Ukraine. The company also worked with Russia’s Military-Industrial Company on armored vehicles that were later used by Wagner Group fighters in several conflict zones.
Russia is far from the only controversial destination for Streit vehicles, which have repeatedly surfaced in conflict zones under arms embargoes or in the hands of armed groups. In Yemen, Houthi military media released footage of armored vehicles captured from Saudi-backed forces. In Iran, a Toophan MRAP displayed at the Eghtedar 40 military exhibition in Tehran in 2019 was photographed and described as the same design as Streit’s Typhoon, although Iranian sources present the vehicle as a domestic development.
UN expert panels have accused Streit of breaking arms embargoes on Libya and Sudan and criticized the sale of hundreds of its vehicles into South Sudan, as we reported in 2016. Its vehicles have since been delivered to Khalifa Haftar’s forces in eastern Libya and seen with riot police in Belarus and with Guinea’s military junta. In 2015, Streit’s U.S. subsidiary paid a $3.5 million fine and Goutorov personally paid $250,000 over unlicensed exports of armored vehicles to Afghanistan, Iraq, Nigeria and other countries.
Streit has denied wrongdoing every time its vehicles have surfaced in such places, insisting that it follows UAE export law, ships its vehicles without weapons and bears no responsibility for how buyers modify or use them after sale. The company has never explained how its armored vehicles continue to reach Rosgvardia units more than four years into Russia’s full-scale war against Ukraine.

articles.title: Canada can help Seoul counter North Korea’s new ‘ways of war’: Military chief
articles.body:
Canada’s Chief of the Defence Staff Gen. Jennie Carignan speaks during an interview with NK News at the Canadian Embassy in Seoul on Oct. 16, 2026. | Image: NK News
Canada can share lessons from training Ukrainian forces to help South Korea learn how to defeat the new “ways of war” that North Korea is mastering through Russia’s war, Canada’s top military commander told NK News.
Gen. Jennie Carignan, Canada’s chief of the defense staff, said in an exclusive interview in Seoul that North Korea’s growing combat experience is a concern for Canada and its allies. She pointed to drones and automated systems as a natural area for cooperation, and said both militaries must stay agile because the next war will not look exactly like the one in Ukraine.
Joon Ha Park is a correspondent at Korea Risk Group. He has previously written on issues related to the two Koreas at The Peninsula Report, and appeared on ABC News Australia, Deutsche Welle and Monocle Radio. He specializes in offering in-depth analyses of South Korea’s defense policy, security relations and domestic politics for Korea Pro.

articles.title: U.S. Army awards $308M for digital investigation software
articles.body:
- The U.S. Army awarded Authentic8 a $307.7 million modification to set up a department-wide contract for its Silo digital investigation software.
- The Army solicited a single bid for the sole-source deal, which covers secure browsing tools used for open-source intelligence and dark web research.
The Pentagon is spending up to $307.7 million on software that lets its analysts browse the darkest corners of the internet without leaving a trace, after the U.S. Army awarded California-based Authentic8 a department-wide deal for its Silo platform on Oct. 20.
Silo is designed for the kind of online detective work that military intelligence now depends on, from monitoring Telegram channels and extremist forums to tracking weapons sales on dark web marketplaces, while hiding the fact that the person on the other end works for the U.S. government.
The problem Silo tries to solve is simple: every time an analyst opens a website from an official network, that site can log the visit, fingerprint the browser and, in the worst case, push malicious code onto a military computer. Silo moves the whole browsing session onto Authentic8’s own cloud servers, so nothing from the website ever reaches the user’s machine, and it lets investigators choose where they appear to be connecting from, so a visit from an Army analyst in Virginia can look like an ordinary user in another country.
That capability has become more valuable as open-source intelligence has grown into a core part of modern warfare, with Russia’s war against Ukraine showing how much can be learned from soldiers’ social media posts, geolocated videos and commercial satellite images. Analysts who dig through that material regularly visit sites run by hostile governments, militant groups and criminal networks, where a careless click from a government address can tip off the target or expose the analyst’s own network to hackers.
The Army ran the purchase as a sole-source deal and received a single bid, after telling industry in August that its requirement was specific to Authentic8’s product and that it planned to buy directly from the company unless another firm could show it offered the same capability. The award gives commands across the Department of War one place to order Silo licenses, add-on tools and support, with the amount and location of the work decided order by order rather than fixed up front.
Authentic8 is already a familiar name in federal law enforcement and financial investigations, with the Department of the Treasury, the Internal Revenue Service and the U.S. Secret Service among the agencies that have bought Silo for secure browsing and dark web research. The new contract expands an initial award made in September into a much larger vehicle that the whole department can use, which puts the Redwood City company’s tools on track to become a standard part of the military’s online investigation kit.

articles.title: Ukraine hits data center of Russia’s top ban
articles.body:
Ukraine hits data center of Russia’s top ban
Ukraine continued striking Russian data centers this week, hitting one belonging to Sberbank, Russia’s largest bank. The state-owned lender is also a sweeping online conglomerate, developing its own artificial intelligence model and operating an extensive ecosystem of digital services. Although the strikes did not cause serious disruptions to banking services, the ongoing Ukrainian campaign could undermine Russians’ confidence in the banking system.
- Ukraine attacked a data center in the city of Balakovo, in the Saratov region, approximately 1,000 kilometres from Moscow. Sberbank has been building the facility since 2021 and described it as the largest in Russia. A week earlier, Ukrainian drones knocked out three of Yandex’s six major data centers. Yandex is one of Russia’s largest IT companies.
- Following the attack, users in Russia began complaining about problems with Sber’s services (the bank’s umbrella brand encompasses its digital products), the Samokat grocery delivery service, and the GigaChat AI service. Some other websites unrelated to Sber also experienced technical issues, including the Kontur business ecosystem and the Ozon marketplace. The disruptions peaked at 11:10 a.m. Moscow time on October 14, after which the number of error reports began to decline.
- Sberbank customers barely noticed the effects of Ukraine’s attack on the data center because the bank’s core banking systems are hosted at other sites, technology expert Anastasia Bezrukova told the business newspaper Vedomosti. According to her, the Balakovo data center was being built to expand existing infrastructure. It was also intended to house the country’s most powerful supercomputer and provide backup capacity for Gostekh, a cloud platform serving federal and regional government agencies. Sberbank has two other data centers that remain untouched: one in Moscow and another in Moscow Oblast.
- Earlier, following Ukrainian attacks on Yandex data centers, Russian users experienced serious disruptions to Yandex Pay, the company’s payment service. For several days, they were unable to make payments or transfers. Some users complained that the problems with Yandex Pay prevented them from making their monthly loan and mortgage payments.
- Strikes on data centers and the subsequent disruptions to banking services are unlikely to trigger a systemic crisis in Russia’s banking sector, but they could further erode public confidence in it. Amid mobile internet disruptions, rising taxes, and widespread anxiety fueled by rumors of a possible new wave of mobilization, Russians have been withdrawing increasing amounts of cash and using it to pay for purchases. According to September data from the central bank, the share of cashless transactions in retail turnover fell for the first time in the second quarter of 2026, dropping by 0.5 percentage points to 88.4%, the data shows. Previous crises — the pandemic, the beginning of the war against Ukraine, and Yevgeny Prigozhin’s attempted military mutiny in 2023 — led to noticeable increases in the amount of cash in circulation.
Why the world should care
A potential increase in cash in circulation could have two consequences. The first is an expansion of the shadow economy, which could potentially affect tax collection, although the impact is unlikely to be significant. The second is a liquidity shortage in the banking sector, which could affect banks’ financial results and slow the decline in lending rates as the key interest rate falls.

articles.title: Exclusive: Corbyn vows to pursue Gaza inquiry despite UK refusal
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Exclusive: Corbyn vows to pursue Gaza inquiry despite UK refusal
Jeremy Corbyn has vowed to continue pressing for an inquiry into Britain's possible complicity in Israel's genocide in Gaza after the UK government rejected his renewed calls for an investigation, the former Labour leader told The New Arab.
Corbyn, who now represents Islington North for Your Party, is seeking an independent public inquiry into Britain's military, economic and political cooperation with Israel since October 2023, including arms supplies, surveillance flights and the use of Royal Air Force (RAF) bases.
The former Labour leader first introduced the Gaza (Independent Public Inquiry) Bill in June 2025 before reintroducing the legislation in the 2026–27 parliamentary session. The latest version was published on 2 September and is awaiting its second reading.
However, the government has resisted calls to establish an inquiry, arguing that its policies and actions relating to Gaza have already undergone extensive parliamentary scrutiny.
"The UK's policy and actions relating to the conflict in Gaza have been subject of extensive parliamentary scrutiny through ministerial statements, debates, Select Committee scrutiny, and oral and written Parliamentary Questions," Middle East Minister Stephen Doughty said in a written response to Corbyn's request.
The refusal comes despite hopes that Prime Minister Andy Burnham's government would take a different approach after he apologised for his predecessor Keir Starmer's words and actions regarding Israel's genocide in Gaza.
"We're not going away, we're not giving up because I think this cause is far too important and far too great," Corbyn told The New Arab.
Corbyn said an inquiry could answer questions about Britain's supply of F-35 fighter jet components to Israel and RAF reconnaissance flights over Gaza.
UK companies manufacture around 15% of the components used in F-35 fighter jets, which Israel has deployed in its assault on Gaza, according to the Campaign Against Arms Trade.
Between December 2023 and July 2025, the RAF conducted more than 600 reconnaissance flights over Gaza, according to Action on Armed Violence (AOAV).
The Ministry of Defence maintained that the flights were conducted "solely to locate hostages", though AOAV questioned whether their scale and persistence were consistent with humanitarian aims.
"We do need a very profound apology to the Palestinian people for the way in which the British government has maintained a supply of arms and military corporation with Israeli Defence Force throughout this whole horrific period, particularly since October 2023," Corbyn said.
In 2016, while Labour leader, Corbyn apologised for the Labour Party's role in the Iraq War following the publication of the Chilcot inquiry's findings.
The inquiry found that Saddam Hussein did not pose an imminent threat to Britain at the time of the 2003 invasion and that intelligence about Iraq's alleged weapons of mass destruction had been presented with unjustified certainty.
Corbyn was among the Labour MPs who opposed the Iraq War and subsequently pushed for an inquiry into Britain's role in the invasion and its aftermath, which resulted in hundreds of thousands of deaths, according to various estimates.
"One day the British Prime Minister will say we need an inquiry. I hope it's soon," Corbyn told The New Arab.

articles.title: Exclusive: Mediators submit new peace proposal to Iran, US
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Exclusive: Mediators submit new peace proposal to Iran, US
Qatari and Pakistani officials submitted a new peace proposal to Iran and the US on Tuesday in a bid to prevent further escalation in the Middle East war, sources familiar with the mediation efforts told The New Arab.
The people described the plan as a "middle-ground proposal" that partially meets both sides' demands over Iran's nuclear programme and the release of Tehran's frozen assets. It has received positive responses from both Washington and Tehran, they said.
Pakistan's army chief Asim Munir delivered the proposal to Iranian officials in Tehran on Tuesday, according to the sources, who spoke to TNA on condition of anonymity.
Neither side has shown willingness to compromise over their demands, with the US still insisting Tehran must dismantle its nuclear programme and Iran demanding the immediate release of all its assets frozen abroad.
After agreeing to a temporary ceasefire in June, the two sides were supposed to begin negotiating a comprehensive peace deal covering the nuclear programme and Iran's frozen assets.
But since that truce fell apart the following month, no further negotiations have been held. Tensions have instead ratcheted up further in recent days, with Iran increasing its attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and Trump threatening to return to war after November's midterm elections.
The sources said that the latest proposal aims to extract minor concessions from both sides in a bid to build confidence for new talks. Under the deal, Iran would agree to a secret, unannounced visit by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) to inspect its nuclear sites. In return, the US would allow Tehran to receive the interest generated on its $6 billion of frozen assets held in Qatar.
On Monday, sources familiar with the negotiations told The New Arab that a breakthrough could be announced later this week.
The sources, who also requested anonymity, said efforts were continuing to narrow the differences between the two sides and encourage them to make mutual concessions to prevent the war from resuming.
Qatar and Pakistan are pursuing joint mediation efforts aimed at ending the seven-month regional war. Both countries mediated June's memorandum of understanding that briefly brought the conflict to a halt.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said on Tuesday that Iranian officials would discuss the peace negotiations with Munir.
Munir's visit comes amid mounting tensions over Iran's nuclear programme, the continued closure of the Strait of Hormuz and US demands for Tehran to curb its enrichment capabilities.
President Trump and other US officials have issued new threats to restart the war if Iran does not back down, while Iranian officials have said they are ready for renewed conflict. On Saturday, US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth warned that Iran would face "destruction" unless it abandoned its nuclear ambitions.
The mediation efforts also coincide with intensifying regional and international diplomatic activity, including Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov’s visit to Tehran on Monday.

articles.title: Exclusive: Iraq imposes restrictions on Houthis’ Baghdad office
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Exclusive: Iraq imposes restrictions on Houthis’ Baghdad office
Iraq has imposed restrictions on representatives of Yemen’s Houthi group in Baghdad, banning them from political and media activities amid regional tensions and efforts to strengthen ties with Saudi Arabia, sources have told The New Arab (TNA).
Houthi leaders and officials in Iraq have been instructed not to conduct any media or political “activities” from Iraqi territory, an Iraqi official who requested anonymity told TNA.
A senior official in the office of Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said the directive imposed a comprehensive ban on members of the group in Iraq holding meetings, organising press conferences and seminars, or moving outside the limits permitted under the country’s residency laws.
Since 2018, the Houthis have operated an office in Baghdad’s affluent Jadriya neighbourhood, known as the Representation Office of Ansar Allah. It is headed by Abu Idris al-Sharafi, a prominent Houthi representative with ties to Iraq dating back to 2016.
According to the Iraqi official, the government has designated residences for members of the Houthi representation and required them to provide advance information about their movements within Baghdad and other provinces.
The official added that the group’s members had been informed of the decision several days earlier.
The directive explicitly prohibits activities conducted from Iraqi territory against Saudi Arabia or other countries in the region, citing the principles of good neighbourliness and non-interference in the affairs of other states enshrined in the Iraqi constitution.
Houthi leaders have reportedly made several visits in recent months to political officials, as well as commanders from the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF) and other armed factions in Baghdad and several provinces. Iraq is home to numerous Iran-backed armed groups.
The Iraqi official said members of the Houthi group could no longer organise political or media activities relating to the ongoing war in Yemen.
The restrictions come about a week after al-Zaidi visited Saudi Arabia and met Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, holding talks on security, political and economic issues.
During the meeting, al-Zaidi assured the crown prince that Iraq would not allow its territory to be used to launch attacks against Saudi Arabia or other countries in the region, the Iraqi News Agency (INA) reported.
“Iraq’s firm position is not to allow its territory to be used as a launching pad for any attacks or actions that affect the security of the kingdom and the countries of the region, and to be keen on adhering to the principles of good neighbourliness and respecting the sovereignty of Iraq and brotherly and friendly countries,” al-Zaidi’s office said in a statement cited by INA.
During the Houthis’ lightning offensive in Yemen last month, Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline was struck by drones - forcing Riyadh to temporarily suspend operations along the export route, which Saudi Arabia uses as an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz.
Saudi Arabia said the drones originated in Iraq.
Baghdad conducted its own investigation and concluded that the strikes had been launched from Iraqi territory, although no group claimed responsibility.
Speaking to TNA, retired Iraqi Army Colonel Saad al-Jughaifi said the latest restrictions on Houthi representatives were consistent with international pressure to curb support for groups Washington describes as Iran’s regional proxies.
Al-Jughaifi also disclosed that measures introduced several months ago had restricted prominent members of Lebanon’s Hezbollah armed group and the Houthi movement from accessing Iraq’s financial transfer system, including banks, currency exchange and remittance companies.
He said restrictions had also affected their access to Iraqi Airways.
Al-Jughaifi added that the measures were intended to prevent Iraq from facing further financial, economic and political crises resulting from an adverse international classification.
He said that the Houthis had been hosted in Iraq under the government of Adel Abdul Mahdi in 2018, but their presence had since expanded in terms of personnel, headquarters and offices. Some members had also brought their families to live in Iraq.
Yemen’s civil war, in which Saudi Arabia has led a military coalition supporting the government since 2015, reignited in September following the collapse of a years-long truce.
The Houthis have tried to impose a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia, targeting its tankers and seizing large stretches of Yemen’s Red Sea coast, a key route for oil exports.
The conflict has also driven up energy prices, with the Houthis launching repeated missile attacks against the kingdom.
Saudi Arabia’s King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh has been targeted 20 times since the beginning of the month, with a recent attack killing 13 people and injuring more than 300.

articles.title: Ukraine has shown heroism, but military aid to it has depleted U.S. weapons stocks – Hegseth
articles.body:
Ukraine has shown heroism, but military aid to it has depleted U.S. weapons stocks – Hegseth
Kyiv • UNN
U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said that support for Ukraine under the Biden administration had depleted American weapons stocks. He did not provide specific data on the scale of the reduction.
U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth said that Ukraine had demonstrated heroism in confronting Russian aggression, but that the large-scale military assistance provided to Kyiv under the previous U.S. administration had depleted the United States' weapons stocks, UNN reports.
Details
According to the Pentagon chief, Ukrainian troops made significant efforts to defend their country and received substantial support from international partners, including the United States.
Ukraine made heroic efforts, and significant assistance was provided to it. So significant that under the previous administration, weapons stocks were depleted
The Pentagon spoke about the consequences of military assistance to Ukraine
In his statement, the American secretary linked the reduction in U.S. military reserves to the volume of weapons that Washington transferred to Ukraine during Joe Biden's presidency.
At the same time, Hegseth did not specify which categories of weapons he was referring to or the extent to which the corresponding stocks of the U.S. military had been reduced.
The United States remains an important weapons supplier to Ukraine. In particular, European partners continue to rely on American production when providing Ukrainian troops with the necessary systems and ammunition.
The Pentagon chief's statement is his assessment of the consequences of Washington's previous policy. The minister's quoted remarks contain no specific data that would make it possible to assess the scale of the alleged depletion of U.S. military stocks.

articles.title: Starlink slowdown makes Ukraine’s Shahed-hunting drone maker rethink air-launched interceptors
articles.body:
Ukrainian drone maker Wild Hornets is rethinking projects it is currently working on, including launching interceptors from aerial platforms, because of limits on SpaceX’s Starlink satellite internet. Spokesman Mike Orliuk told The War Zone (TWZ) this on 20 October. The company builds Sting interceptors, which it says destroyed over 15,000 Shaheds and Gerberas, a cheaper Shahed lookalike, in a year. Orliuk said Sting’s current operations are unaffected.
The stakes rise as Russia shifts to faster drones. Ukrainian defense technology adviser Serhii Beskrestnov counted more than 2,500 jet-powered Gerans, Russia’s version of the Shahed, in August. President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on 16 October that these drones fly faster than 400 km/h. He added that some Ukrainian interceptors chasing them work through Starlink. When the link was slowed, Ukraine could not intercept some of them, he said.
How Sting stays connected
“Our own communications system provides the basic connection to our interceptors,” Orliuk said. The company’s remote-control technology can draw on various internet sources, he added, though the military often uses Starlink. Even then, the terminal does not need to move at high speed. It only links the command center to a ground station, which Orliuk compared to a cell tower.
“For these needs, everything is operating normally with Starlink at the moment,” he said.
An air-launch project under review
“Some drones carry a terminal on board and need to fly at high speed with it,” Orliuk said. “In such cases, Starlink’s limitations make their operation impossible.”
That is why the company is rethinking the air-launch project. Wild Hornets has made no clear decision yet but will test alternatives, Orliuk said. He declined to describe them.
“I believe, in any case, depending on a single solution is very risky,” he said.
Musk pointed at the US military over Ukraine’s satellite limits. Now a US official says the administration had nothing to do with them
Other firms share the concern
Orliuk said he has spoken with other companies that rely far more on Starlink and have expressed concerns. He pointed to growing interest in Europe’s Eutelsat network, though “creating something like Starlink won’t be easy.”
Who ordered the slowdown remains unclear. The order to slow Ukraine’s Starshield service came from inside the White House, two US officials and a Western official said. A US official told TWZ the president never made such a request. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on 17 October that the slowdown had “nothing to do with the White House” and called “a report on that” “categorically false,” without saying which report he meant.
