articles.title: Nuclear safety risk grows: Russian-occupied nuclear plant’s cooling pond keeps sinking, Russia runs short of diesel and staff, Ukraine says
articles.body:
The Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant is short of cooling water, diesel, and qualified staff, Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence (HUR) said on 20 October, warning of rising risks to nuclear safety. The water level in the plant’s cooling pond fell to 12.27 meters on 12 October, down from 12.86 meters in July, while the plant needs at least 15 meters to fully meet its needs, according to HUR. Russian managers are also considering cutting the number of backup generators kept on automatic standby, which would inevitably raise the risk of emergencies, the intelligence agency said.
Europe’s largest nuclear plant has been under Russian control since March 2022. Its six reactors have been in cold shutdown since April 2024, but they and their spent fuel still need constant cooling, which depends on water, on a single remaining external power line, and on diesel generators as the last resort. The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) warned on 16 October that depleted diesel reserves increase the risk that nuclear safety is challenged if the plant loses power again, and that the situation may become acute in winter.
A pond with no source to refill it
The cooling pond has been sinking since Russia destroyed the Kakhovka dam in June 2023, cutting off the reservoir that fed it. Energoatom, Ukraine’s state nuclear operator, recorded 15.70 meters in October 2023. By June 2025, the level had fallen below 14 meters against a norm of above 16, Oleh Korikov, head of Ukraine’s State Nuclear Regulatory Inspectorate, said.
HUR’s figures show the decline continuing this year, from 12.86 meters in July to 12.63 in early August, 12.55 at the end of August, and 12.34 at the start of October. In 2025, the IAEA said groundwater wells on site were supplying cooling water for the safety systems. Its team had not been allowed to inspect a new dam in the cooling channel, access IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi called essential to assess the cooling water situation.
Diesel for a blackout that Russia cannot supply
If the plant loses external power, its diesel generators would burn about 150 metric tons of fuel a day in a prolonged blackout, HUR said. The occupation administration cannot deliver enough, so reserves stay minimal. Russian managers are also looking for covert fuel supplies, including low-quality fuel, without informing the IAEA mission, according to HUR.
The IAEA has already reported fewer generators on automatic standby. Since late September, only four of the plant’s 20 emergency generators would start automatically in a blackout, with the rest needing manual connection, which Grossi said deviates from normal practice. No diesel deliveries have reached the plant since March, the agency said on 16 October.
The plant spent nearly three weeks on generators after losing its last external line on 20 August, EP reported, until the Ferosplavna-1 line was restored under an IAEA-brokered ceasefire. The main 750 kV Dniprovska line remains out. HUR said the Kremlin rejected Ukraine’s proposal to supply power through it, which raises the nuclear safety risks.
Russia blacked out Europe’s largest nuclear plant 15 times since occupying it in 2022
A plant short of the people who know it
About 5,000 people now work at the plant, against roughly 11,000 before the full-scale invasion, and only 1,450 were on site, HUR said. The plant lacks specialists who know its equipment, as well as the experts needed for repairs and for reconnecting it to external power. Russian managers plan training courses for applicants from Russian regions to replace Ukrainian staff, according to HUR.
In Enerhodar, the city where the plant’s staff live, mobile, internet, electricity, and water supplies keep failing, HUR said.

articles.title: Two re-arrested over alleged help to Iranian intelligence
articles.body:
Two men have been re-arrested in the investigation into activity close to RAF Fairford last month on suspicion of assisting a foreign intelligence service, with police confirming that the country the investigation relates to is Iran, according to a statement issued by Counter Terrorism Policing.
A 24-year-old United Kingdom national and a 25-year-old dual British and Iranian national, both from the London borough of Westminster, were re-arrested on Tuesday under Section 3 of the National Security Act 2023. The 24-year-old was first arrested on Sunday 27 September near the Gloucestershire base, and the 25-year-old was arrested in Westminster on Thursday 1 October.
Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of National Counter Terrorism Policing in the United Kingdom, said: “Since the events at RAF Fairford on Sunday 27 September, our specialist teams have been working tirelessly to interrogate the many lines of enquiry involved in this hugely complex investigation.
“So far seven men have been arrested in connection with our investigation.
“As a result of the ongoing efforts of our officers, earlier today two of those men were re-arrested for offences relating to Section 3 of the National Security Act, assisting a foreign intelligence service.
“This is very much a live investigation, and our evidence gathering continues, but at this time our position remains the same; we consider it highly likely that there is Iranian state involvement. Our investigators are continuing to examine what that level of involvement was and the ambition behind it.
“Due to their sensitive nature, national security investigations can take time to progress, and I’m grateful to everyone who has given my teams the time and space needed to pursue this work thoroughly and effectively.
“From the outset our priority has been to uphold the integrity of this investigation and hold those who wish to do our country harm, accountable.
“We know the public have unanswered questions. I want to be as transparent as possible and when we are in the position to share more, we will.”
The other five men arrested remain on police bail.
Moving the two men onto Section 3 of the National Security Act marks a shift in how the case is being pursued. Five men in their twenties were arrested near Fairford on 27 September, and the Westminster arrest on 1 October was made under Section 5 of the Terrorism Act 2006, which covers preparing terrorist acts, with police saying at the time that they were considering all possible angles including foreign state involvement. The offence now under investigation is one of working for another country’s intelligence service.
Section 3 was created by the National Security Act 2023, which replaced the Official Secrets Acts and built a modern framework around espionage, sabotage and foreign interference. The offence carries a maximum sentence of fourteen years and applies where a person engages in conduct intended to materially assist a foreign intelligence service, including inside the United Kingdom.
RAF Fairford is a standby base operated by the United States Air Force under British ownership, with a runway long enough for the heaviest American aircraft, and it has hosted B-2 Spirit and B-52 bomber deployments to Europe for decades. It has no permanently based flying units, which is precisely what makes it useful when American bombers are sent across the Atlantic at short notice.
Louise Sandher-Jones, the Minister for the Armed Forces, told Parliament this week that security had been strengthened following the events at Fairford and at RAF Molesworth, that the Defence Investment Plan provides an additional £470 million over four years for site protection, and that the department would not hesitate to use the full range of powers available including the National Security Act.
Iran has been the subject of repeated British counter terrorism and national security operations in recent years, with MI5 having said publicly that it has disrupted a large number of plots linked to the Iranian state on British soil since 2022. None of the seven men has been charged.

articles.title: Russia wants AI to help design its next aircraft
articles.body:
- Russia’s United Aircraft Corporation said it is evaluating new software, including artificial intelligence, to speed up the design of future aircraft and modifications.
- UAC is already running a pilot project with Sberbank’s GigaChat AI for generative design at the early stage of a new aircraft.
Russia’s United Aircraft Corporation is looking at artificial intelligence and other new software to speed up the design of future aircraft and cut the cost of developing new versions of existing ones, the state-owned planemaker said in a statement on its social media.
UAC, which builds nearly all of Russia’s military and civil aircraft, from Su-57 and Su-35 fighters to the MC-21 airliner, said its engineers are evaluating new software products, including AI technologies, as the company moves its design work onto digital models.
The company said digital models let its engineers analyze far larger volumes of data and test many more aircraft layouts before choosing the best one, which makes developing new modifications faster and cheaper over an aircraft’s life cycle. UAC added that it is taking a measured approach to AI and will only use the new tools where they make sense and help solve specific engineering problems.
“Digital technology makes it possible to take a larger sample and understand a problem more deeply. Over the life cycle, this will be faster and cheaper when creating the next modifications,” UAC specialists said.
The statement follows remarks by UAC general designer Sergey Korotkov, who said on Oct. 13 that there is no reason not to use AI in aircraft design as long as it helps with the task at hand and is applied thoughtfully. UAC has already been testing the idea, and in May its chief executive, Vadim Badekha, said the company was running a pilot project with Sberbank to use the bank’s GigaChat AI model for generative design of a new aircraft at the early design stage, with plans to extend it later to strength and aerodynamic calculations.
The shift to domestic digital tools has been driven largely by sanctions, since Western design software vendors such as Dassault Systèmes, Siemens and Autodesk pulled out of Russia after the 2022 invasion of Ukraine and left the country’s aerospace industry without the programs it had relied on for decades. UAC says it has since replaced software at its design bureaus with Russian products, equipping about 4,000 engineering workstations and swapping out nine key product lifecycle management modules, and on Oct. 16 it said digital design had cut some aircraft system calculations, such as cabin heat balance and hydraulic networks, from months to days.
Those efforts come as UAC struggles with delays on its most important civil programs, which have had to replace Western parts and systems with Russian-made equivalents. President Vladimir Putin said in June that the MC-21 had been set back by almost two years, partly because of problems with the wing, and First Deputy Prime Minister Denis Manturov said certification of the version built entirely with Russian components is now planned for the end of 2027.

articles.title: Russia waits for answers about work on bioweapons in Ukraine with Pentagon support — MFA
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 20. /TASS/. Russia is waiting for responses from the United States regarding issues related to the development of biological weapons in Ukraine with the support of the Pentagon, Kirill Vorontsov, deputy head of the Russian delegation and deputy director of the Department for Non-Proliferation and Arms Control at the Russian Foreign Ministry has said.
"Legitimate questions, officially raised by Russia, remain unanswered. These questions concern the uncovered facts regarding the implementation of a military-biological program in Ukraine - in violation of the Biological Weapons Convention - with the support of the US Department of Defense and its affiliated entities, including private companies," he said during a discussion on Other Weapons of Mass Destruction within the First Committee of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly. A transcript of his remarks has been published on the Russian Foreign Ministry’s website.
As Vorontsov noted, "an analysis of the projects carried out in Ukrainian laboratories leads to the conclusion that components of biological weapons were, or perhaps still are, being developed in the immediate vicinity of Russian territory." He emphasized that Russia views this as a direct threat to its national security.
"The admission - cited by Tulsi Gabbard - regarding Washington’s long-term funding of 'potentially risky' virus experiments in over 120 foreign biolaboratories - more than 40 of which are located in Ukraine - only confirms the validity of Russia’s concerns regarding American military-biological activity near our borders," Vorontsov pointed out. "We expect the United States, as one of the depositaries of the BTWC, to provide appropriate responses to the questions we have raised. This would help resolve this unsavory situation and ensure that Washington complies with the obligations stipulated by the Convention," he concluded.

articles.title: North Korea Sends 12,000 Workers to Russia to Build Shahed Drones
articles.body:

North Korea Sends 12,000 Workers to Russia to Build Shahed Drones
North Korea has reportedly sent 12,000 workers to Russia to help manufacture Shahed-type attack drones at the Alabuga Special Economic Zone in Tatarstan, expanding Pyongyang’s involvement in Russia’s military production supporting its war against Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to a joint report by the Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) and the George W. Bush Institute on October 14, North Korean workers receive approximately $2.50 per hour, while the North Korean government reportedly takes between 70% and 90% of their earnings.
The report identifies three main groups involved in drone manufacturing at Alabuga: Russian students and young workers, foreign recruits from other countries, and North Korean nationals. Researchers raised concerns about coercive labor practices affecting all three groups, particularly the systematic withholding of wages from North Korean workers.
Russian students are recruited through Alabuga’s educational programs, which combine technical training with industrial work. Some reportedly work shifts lasting up to 12 hours, with their pay tied to strict production targets.
Workers have also reportedly faced threats of financial penalties for disclosing details about the facility’s operations, including to family members.
The Alabuga industrial complex is a major Russian production site for Geran-2 drones, based on the Iranian-designed Shahed-136, which Russia regularly uses in attacks against Ukrainian cities and infrastructure.
Satellite imagery published in September showed additional production buildings and warehouses under construction at the site, indicating continued expansion of its manufacturing infrastructure.
North Korea’s involvement in Russian drone production comes amid growing military cooperation between Moscow and Pyongyang. Beyond providing personnel, North Korea has reportedly sought to incorporate lessons from Russia’s use of drones in Ukraine into its own military development programs.
Analysts have also indicated that Pyongyang is working to expand domestic production of Shahed-type drones and smaller unmanned aircraft, potentially benefiting from Russian technical expertise.
Earlier, Bloomberg reported on September 17 that approximately 25,000 North Korean nationals were working at Russian drone manufacturing facilities, including Alabuga. Many reportedly entered Russia on student visas to circumvent international sanctions, while North Korean authorities confiscated most of their earnings.

articles.title: India & United States to boost defence, energy ties, Marco Rubio says trade deal close
articles.body:
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and US ambassador to India Sergio Gor stand for the national anthem, as they attend a Freedom 250 reception at the Jio World Convention Centre in Mumbai.
External affairs minister S Jaishankar met his US counterpart Marco Rubio in Mumbai, agreeing to further expand cooperation in energy, defence and technology ties and committing to an early conclusion of the trade deal still under discussion.While Rubio emphasised the role that the US can play in the diversification of India's energy and defence supplies, Jaishankar said in a post on X that they also discussed people-to-people ties, alluding to India's concerns over immigration and H-1B governance issues.
Speaking at the US anniversary celebrations later, Jaishankar said in Rubio’s presence that Indian talent and skills have helped shape the tech era in the US.The ministers met ahead of a likely meeting between PM Narendra Modi and President Donald Trump next month in Manila on the margins of the ASEAN summit, and also before Modi's visit to the US in December for the G20. Both sides are also working to schedule a Quad leaders’ summit in Manila.A State Department readout said Jaishankar and Rubio discussed regional and global issues, including developments in West Asia. Rubio reiterated that increased energy trade with the US can play a transformative role in diversifying India’s supply chains while meeting its sizable consumer demand.
Rubio’s second visit to India is taking place against the backdrop of US’ Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act meant to penalise countries purchasing Russian oil and Trump’s subsequent suspension temporarily of related tariffs. India maintains that its oil procurement is essential not just for its own energy security but also stability of the global markets. Rubio lauded “substantial progress” made by India in diversifying its energy portfolio.Rubio focused on reducing India's reliance on Russia also in defence as he stressed deepening of defence interoperability, framing enhanced technology purchases by India as a win-win situation for both nations.According to the US readout, Rubio also commended recent progress in bilateral defense and civil nuclear cooperation, and advocated increased purchase of US technologies and systems, which can enhance the security and prosperity of both countries.Rubio said in a post on X that he and Jaishankar reaffirmed the importance of advancing the US-India strategic partnership. The ministers will meet again on the sidelines of the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting in Atlanta later this month. Both will also join their counterparts from Japan and Australia for a meeting of the Quad foreign ministers in Atlanta.According to the MEA, Jaishankar and Rubio welcomed the progress made in negotiations on the India–US Bilateral Trade Agreement (BTA) and reaffirmed their commitment to working towards its early conclusion. Rubio said both sides were “as close as you can be without having an executed agreement”.“I think there's a small number of items left to wrap up. So, I think that will happen shortly...and hopefully have some good news to announce fairly soon, and perhaps the leaders can sign it thereafter,” said Rubio, addressing the US travelling media.
Shortly after his arrival, Rubio laid a wreath at Mumbai’s Taj Mahal Palace Hotel to honor the 26/11 terrorist attacks victims 166 victims, strongly condemning the attacks and reaffirming the US “unwavering solidarity” with the people of India.“Secretary Rubio underscored the Trump Administration’s commitment to dismantling terrorist networks and ensuring that those responsible for acts of terrorism are brought to justice, including individuals facing charges for their roles in planning the 2008 Mumbai attacks,” said the State Department, without naming Pakistan.According to the Indian readout, the visit reflected the sustained momentum of high-level exchanges between the two countries, underscoring the importance both sides attach to further advancing the India-US COMPACT for the 21st century. Modi and Trump had launched the COMPACT (Catalyzing Opportunities for Military Partnership, Accelerated Commerce & Technology) initiative last year to drive transformative change across key pillars of bilateral cooperation.

articles.title: Death toll from Houthi strike on Yemen govt camp rises to 73
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Death toll from Houthi strike on Yemen govt camp rises to 73
Local Yemeni authorities on Tuesday raised the death toll from a Houthi strike a day earlier on a military camp belonging to government forces to 73, as fighting between the foes escalates.
It marked the deadliest attack in weeks as fighting between the Iran-backed Houthis and Yemen's internationally recognised, Saudi-supported government rages after the collapse of a years-long truce.
The death toll from Monday's strike on the camp in the energy-rich Shabwa province "increased to 73 martyrs, while search and follow-up efforts are ongoing to discover the fate of 14 missing people", provincial authorities said in a statement.
Local authorities had put the death toll at 53 on Monday, adding that more than 200 others were injured, all new members of the internal security forces who were undergoing training.
Majed al-Nuzaili, spokesperson for the Yemeni armed forces, stated Monday on X that the Houthis targeted Shabwa with three ballistic missiles, and that the attack "struck a training center for personnel of security and police agencies."
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree later confirmed that the group was responsible for the attack, saying it targeted "Saudi enemy gatherings in Al-Alam camp, which is run by a Saudi officer from the eastern regions".
Shabwa contains major oil and gas fields and is home to the Balhaf liquefied natural gas terminal, the country's largest energy facility and a key economic asset.
A government military source in the province on Monday said the army feared the strikes could pave the way for a ground offensive "similar to what happened in Mokha", the strategic Red Sea port city seized by the Houthis last month.
(AFP)

articles.title: Lebanon judge to question Hezbollah officials over explosives
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Lebanon judge to question Hezbollah officials over explosives shipment
A Lebanese judge on Tuesday ordered two Hezbollah officials to appear for questioning over their alleged involvement in a delivery of explosives seized by authorities this month, a judicial official told AFP.
Lebanese authorities had been carrying out investigations after arresting two suspected Hezbollah members accused of transporting half a tonne of explosives, which the Iran-backed group subsequently said were part of its "capabilities" to be used against Israel.
They were caught on October 8 at a security checkpoint in Dahr al-Baidar in Lebanon's east in a vehicle headed towards Beirut, with a source telling AFP that one was the son of a Hezbollah official and the other was also a group member.
The judicial official, requesting anonymity, told AFP that the judge on Tuesday ordered two Hezbollah officials to appear for questioning "after initial investigations... established their identities".
Security agencies are working to locate them and take them into custody, the official added.
Last week, Hezbollah lawmaker Hassan Fadlallah said the explosives belonged to the militant group, demanding the shipment be returned and calling for those arrested to be released, in a rare admission by the group.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio subsequently urged Lebanon not to return the explosives.
Lebanese authorities have announced the seizure of three large shipments of explosives this month alone.
Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam has vowed that authorities "will deal with weapons outside the legal framework with the required firmness".
President Joseph Aoun on Saturday said the army and security forces were "implementing the government's decisions on extending the state's authority... and confiscating weapons and ammunition".
"Violators are referred to the judiciary, which carries out its duties fully in applying the law and the political authorities' decisions," he added.
Lebanese authorities last year committed to disarming Hezbollah after months of cross-border hostilities culminated in a 2024 war between the group and Israel.
But Hezbollah drew Lebanon into the Middle East war this year by attacking Israel, which responded with heavy strikes and a ground invasion.
In June, Lebanese and Israeli authorities signed a framework agreement which involves the disarmament of Hezbollah, a gradual Israeli withdrawal from territories it occupies, and the deployment of the Lebanese army to the area.
Hezbollah, the only militant group that refused to disarm after Lebanon's 1975-1990 civil war, has rejected surrendering its weapons and the direct negotiations with Israel.
(AFP)

Russia attacks Ukraine with Iskander-K missiles and 186 drones, air defences down 150 UAVs
Russia attacked Ukraine with Iskander-K cruise missiles and 186 drones on the night of 20-21 October. Air defence forces have destroyed or jammed 150 UAVs, while another 10 remain airborne.
Source: Ukraine's Air Force
Details: The attack began at 18:00 on 20 October. Russian forces launched Iskander-K cruise missiles from the airspace over Rostov Oblast. The number of missiles launched and how many were intercepted have not been reported.
Russia also attacked Ukraine with 186 Shahed loitering munitions (88 jet-powered), Gerbera attack drones, S-8000 Banderol/Dan-T drone- and air-launched cruise missiles and Parodiya decoy UAVs.
The drones were launched from the Russian cities of Oryol, Kursk and Primorsko-Akhtarsk as well as from temporarily occupied Donetsk, Chauda and Hvardiiske (Crimea).
Aircraft, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare assets, unmanned systems units and mobile fire groups from Ukraine's defence forces have been involved in repelling the attack.
Quote: "As of 08:30, [Ukrainian] air defence forces had destroyed or jammed 150 Shaheds (63 of which were jet-powered), S8000 Banderol/Dan-Ts, Gerberas and drones of other types. Another 10 attack drones remain airborne, combat work is ongoing!
Hits by aerial assets have been recorded at 27 locations and the fall of downed aerial assets (debris) at 13 locations."

articles.title: Drone alert issued ahead of Putin-Witkoff talks
articles.body:
Drone alert greets US envoy’s arrival for Putin talks
A drone threat has been announced south of St. Petersburg shortly after US President Donald Trump’s special envoy, Steve Witkoff, arrived in the city for talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin on the Ukraine conflict. The warning comes just days after a massive Ukrainian drone barrage on the city and outskirts killed one person and injured 15 others.
Witkoff arrived at Pulkovo Airport on Wednesday morning. His motorcade headed for Constantine Palace, around 20 km southeast of St. Petersburg.
Shortly after arriving, Leningrad Region Governor Alexander Drozdenko announced a UAV threat in the airspace over Luga District, around 125 km south of the venue for the talks. The governor warned that mobile internet speeds could be reduced but did not specify the number, exact location, and direction of the drones, and did not report any interceptions.
Russia’s air regulator also imposed temporary airspace restrictions around Pulkovo Airport, citing flight safety. The facility earlier received Witkoff’s aircraft from Oslo, where he met with Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky and European officials on Tuesday.
The alert follows Sunday’s unprecedented Ukrainian drone attack on St. Petersburg and the surrounding Leningrad Region. According to the Russian authorities, the strikes killed one person and injured 15, damaged residential buildings, and sparked fires at an oil terminal, oil depot, and industrial facilities.
Commenting on the raid at the time, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov described it as “final manifestations of agony” of Ukraine. “The Kiev regime is fighting back [but] it cannot alter the course of history.”
Kremlin foreign policy aide Yury Ushakov said the Putin-Witkoff talks will center on the Ukraine conflict. This comes after the Oslo talks where the US, Ukraine, and Kiev’s Western backers discussed security guarantees, a postwar economic plan, and a broader European security architecture, according to Reuters.

articles.title: Germany’s most popular party targeted by unknown hackers
articles.body:
Hackers target Germany’s most popular party
Germany’s most popular party, Alternative for Germany (AfD), has suffered a massive cyberattack, with unknown hackers reportedly stealing and publishing hundreds of thousands of internal emails, while the country’s political establishment seeks grounds to outlaw the opposition party.
The breach, which was first reported by Bild on Tuesday, reportedly exposed 421,179 emails totaling 281 gigabytes, including correspondence involving AfD co-chair Alice Weidel, honorary chairman Alexander Gauland, and other senior party figures.
The leaked material reportedly includes photographs of identity documents, bank statements, invoices, membership applications, and internal party lists. Bild said it examined a small sample of the files, including an identity card belonging to Markus Frohnmaier, the deputy leader of the AfD parliamentary group in the Bundestag.
The identities and motives of the hackers are unknown, and the authenticity of the published material has not been independently established.
The AfD confirmed that a hosting provider working with the party was hacked in September, but disputed suggestions that its current communications systems was compromised.
“Only a few email inboxes were unlawfully copied, most of which had not been used for years,” a party spokesman told Bild, adding that current federal party email accounts were unaffected.
The AfD condemned the breach as an “attack on the German party system and therefore on democracy” and said it reported the cyberattack to the security authorities.
No statement from investigators or condemnation of the breach by senior government officials has emerged as of early Wednesday.
The leaked correspondence has already drawn scrutiny from activists seeking to outlaw the party. Valentina Chiofalo, a representative of the German civil liberties organization Gesellschaft fuer Freiheitsrechte, told taz that the stolen emails could help strengthen the case for banning the AfD, while their publication and journalistic scrutiny could also shape public opinion against the party.
The attack comes amid an escalating campaign by Germany’s established political parties to isolate and potentially ban the AfD. The Euroskeptic party, which advocates stricter immigration controls and opposes Berlin’s military support for Ukraine and sanctions on Russia, has surged to 30% support in the latest INSA poll for Bild, opening a 12-point lead over Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s CDU/CSU bloc, which has slumped to 18%.
Earlier this month, the AfD secured the presidency of Saxony-Anhalt’s state parliament for the first time, breaking through the political ‘firewall’ maintained by establishment parties. Its rise prompted Social Democratic parliamentary leaders to demand the creation of a federal-state working group to examine a possible ban, accusing the AfD of threatening democracy from within and promoting extremism.
Germany’s domestic intelligence agency has also sought to classify the party as a confirmed right-wing extremist organization, but a Cologne court blocked the designation in February pending further legal proceedings.
The AfD has rejected the accusations, portraying the proposed ban as an attempt to overturn the will of millions of voters and eliminate political competition.

articles.title: Israel seeks to cast Lebanon army as 'failing' ahead of US talks
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Israel seeks to portray Lebanese army as failing to curb Hezbollah ahead of talks
Hours before Lebanon and Israel were due to resume negotiations in the United States, the Israeli military on Tuesday accused the Lebanese army of failing to curb Hezbollah’s activities in southern Lebanon, in what a retired Lebanese brigadier general described to The New Arab as an attempt to heighten tensions ahead of the talks and put Lebanon on the defensive.
The Israeli military accused elements within the Lebanese army of allegedly coordinating with Hezbollah to obstruct the enforcement of security arrangements, reportedly allowing the group to anticipate operations and move weapons out of targeted areas. It said the Lebanese army had also failed to dismantle a Hezbollah military site in the south, despite announcing that it had taken the necessary measures there.
The Israeli military said that the Lebanese army was responsible for ensuring the full implementation of the security arrangements, saying it expected it to take more decisive and effective measures to prevent Hezbollah from maintaining weapons and military infrastructure in southern Lebanon.
The Lebanese army later rejected the claims, describing them as false and accusing Israel of seeking to undermine its credibility and cast doubt on its ability to carry out its responsibilities in southern Lebanon.
Lebanon and Israel are due to hold technical military talks in Tampa, Florida, on Tuesday, resuming discussions after the last round of talks in Rome in early August. An eighth round planned for September in the Italian capital did not take place.
The Lebanese delegation is expected to reiterate its demands for a full Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon, which continues to come under daily Israeli attack despite a framework agreement signed in June.
Pressure on the Lebanese army
Retired Lebanese Brig. Gen. Bassam Yassin described the Israeli accusations as an attempt to undermine the talks and put the Lebanese army on the defensive.
"The intention is certainly to create tension around the negotiations and put the army in a position where it has to defend itself," Yassin told The New Arab.
He said the Lebanese delegation was expected to focus on technical issues, including the work of the ceasefire monitoring committee, locally known as the mechanism, and demands for an Israeli withdrawal.
The mechanism was established following the November 2024 ceasefire agreement between Israel and Hezbollah.
"All this talk about the army’s failure does not reflect the major successes it achieved south of the Litani River in 2024 and 2025," Yassin said, questioning why the alleged violations had not been raised with the mechanism at the time.
In a statement on Tuesday, the Israeli military said it expected the Lebanese army to take "more decisive and effective action" to prevent Hezbollah from maintaining weapons and military infrastructure in the south.
It alleged that, despite the Lebanese army announcing in December 2025 that it had dealt with a Hezbollah facility in the southern town of Kafra, footage showed members of the group continuing to operate there and attempting to remove weapons from the site months later.
The Israeli military said its forces had subsequently struck and destroyed a truck carrying the weapons. It also accused members of the Lebanese army of coordinating with Hezbollah over enforcement operations, allowing the group to anticipate military activity and move weapons out of targeted areas.
Yassin rejected the suggestion that the Lebanese army was failing to carry out its responsibilities. While the Lebanese government has made dismantling Hezbollah’s military infrastructure and disbanding its armed wing in the south a stated objective, he argued that the army could not be expected to forcibly disarm the group while Israeli forces continued to occupy Lebanese territory and carry out attacks.
"Of course, the army is not going to dismantle Hezbollah’s weapons and infrastructure in the south right now. There is an occupation and aggression on your land. Can the army confront civilians and tell them: ‘I want to dismantle your defences’? That is impossible," he said.
Yassin maintained that the army had taken control of every Hezbollah site it had entered following the November 2024 ceasefire, and said Hezbollah had helped it access many of its former positions.
Some sites were empty when the army arrived, while others were discovered by chance or with the help of local residents, he said. Some of the people responsible for those sites had been killed during the 2024 war, he added, meaning information about their locations was no longer available.
Yassin said the Israeli military's publication of footage now was intended to undermine confidence in the Lebanese army and portray it as weak.
"If there is something old [still there], that does not mean the Israelis can release videos now. The intention is to confuse the Lebanese army and portray it as being in a weak position, when that is not the case," he said.
Lebanese army rejects allegations
In a statement shared with footage on X, the army said its units had begun work on a military facility in the southern town of Kafra in December 2025. They continued working there until 16 March 2026, when they suspended operations and evacuated the area at the request of the mechanism, following Israeli threats to strike the site.
The army said it had informed the committee that the operation was incomplete and that military equipment and ammunition remained inside the facility, which was subsequently targeted by an Israeli strike. It added that repeated requests to secure permission to resume work and remove the remaining equipment had been rejected by Israel.
According to the statement, the army resumed its operation on 15 August 2026 in coordination with the mechanism, eventually completing the work and closing the facility on 16 October.
The Lebanese army also disputed the Israeli military's account of the footage showing a truck carrying weapons being struck. It said the video dated back to 3 July 2026 and was filmed in the village of Seddiqin rather than at the Kafra facility.
The army said all the events and measures it described had been documented with the mechanism, adding that Israel's repeated allegations and disinformation campaigns were aimed at damaging the military institution's credibility locally and internationally, particularly amid the ongoing negotiations.
It reiterated its commitment to carrying out its responsibilities and assigned tasks, while accusing Israel of continuing to violate existing understandings.
No progress on pilot zones
The talks are due to take place under US auspices against a backdrop of continued Israeli strikes and demolitions in southern Lebanon and growing concerns in Beirut about the consequences of a possible wider confrontation involving the United States, Israel and Iran.
A US official, in remarks carried by the US embassy in Beirut, said the meeting would be limited to working-level teams and focus exclusively on security issues within the tripartite framework signed by Lebanon and Israel in Washington on 26 June 2026.
Little progress has been made on the initial pilot areas announced under the arrangements this summer. Lebanese military sources told The New Arab that continued Israeli attacks were obstructing the army’s work in the areas and making the return of residents difficult and dangerous.
Beirut also rejects any direct coordination between the Lebanese and Israeli armies, despite pressure from Washington and Tel Aviv. Lebanon continues to pursue the diplomatic track, viewing it as the only viable option to end the conflict.
Fears of a more devastating war
Lebanese official sources told The New Arab that President Joseph Aoun was monitoring developments in the region and feared the consequences of any escalation for Lebanon. They said these concerns had also been raised by international officials and diplomats visiting Beirut, including Arab League Secretary-General Nabil Fahmy, who met Aoun on Monday.
The sources also expressed concern about Hezbollah’s increasingly confrontational position, warning that it could draw Lebanon into another war.
They said Lebanese officials were holding internal consultations through their advisers to convey their concerns and urged all sides to put Lebanon’s interests above external agendas.
The sources added that officials had received warnings that another war could have even more serious consequences than the previous rounds of fighting in October 2023 and March 2026.
Hezbollah and Israel began exchanging fire in October 2023, with the conflict escalating into a full-scale war in September 2024. Fighting resumed on 2 March 2026 following the start of the US-Israel war on Iran.
Although fighting largely subsided in June following the signing of the tripartite framework, Israel has continued attacks and demolitions in its so-called buffer zone in southern Lebanon, occupying strategic sites and destroying Hezbollah tunnels.
Israeli attacks over the past three years have killed 8,596 people and wounded more than 30,660 others, many of them civilians.

articles.title: Israel’s Katz vows to strike Beirut’s southern suburbs over any rocket and drone fire

articles.title: ‘He Just Doesn’t Like Him’: Trump’s Personal Animosity Toward Zelensky May Be Shaping US Policy on Ukraine
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump’s personal animosity toward Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky may be influencing Washington’s approach to Russia’s war against Ukraine.
This was reported by Politico, citing European officials and diplomats.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Trump recently said that Russia had “been fine on Ukraine” and “not been doing that much,” despite intensifying Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities. His remarks reinforced concerns among European allies that Washington is putting more pressure on Kyiv than Moscow.
“I do think it’s a personal thing,” David Lidington, a former British Cabinet minister and distinguished fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, told Politico.
He cited Trump’s “personal predilections for dictators and autocrats” and “his desire to give opportunities to US businesses” as important factors behind the president’s approach.
EU officials privately share that assessment.
“Trump doesn’t like [Ukrainian President Volodymyr] Zelensky. He just doesn’t like him,” one government official who has observed both leaders closely told Politico.
“That makes it harder to get the US to help on peace. Everything is a rational business deal with Trump, until it’s not,” the official added.
A diplomat from an EU country said Trump had repeatedly criticized Ukraine, the EU and NATO while rarely making comparable criticisms of Russian President Vladimir Putin.
EU Seeks More Ukraine Aid From Canada, UK as Kyiv Faces €70 Billion Funding Gap
“He seems to be supportive of the Russians,” the diplomat said, adding that Europe must contend with “an administration that seems to be more pro-Russian than anything else.”
As per the report, Trump’s animosity toward Zelensky may date back to 2019, when he pressed the Ukrainian leader to help investigate Joe Biden, who later defeated him in the 2020 election.
Lidington also pointed to the February 2025 Oval Office confrontation between Trump and Zelensky, saying he believed the encounter had a strong personal dimension.
“It was clear that in the infamous meeting in the White House that Trump and [Vice President JD] Vance had planned that public beating-up of Zelensky,” Lidington said.
He added that Trump appeared particularly drawn to authoritarian leaders.
Recalling a 2018 dinner with world leaders in Paris, Lidington said Trump seemed impatient with French President Emmanuel Macron and then-German Chancellor Angela Merkel, while showing greater interest in leaders such as Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan.
Pressure on Kyiv, doubts about Moscow
Trump’s repeated criticism of Zelensky has alarmed European officials, who believe Russian President Vladimir Putin has shown little genuine interest in ending the war.
“American negotiators have been trying to push Ukraine into surrender for already almost 2 years, 1.5 years now,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas told the European Parliament on Tuesday.
She said Ukraine had resisted surrendering on Putin’s terms largely because of Europe’s support.
“There is a clear consensus across Europe that Putin does not want peace,” a second EU diplomat told Politico. “He will need to be forced into peace.“
Instead, Trump has accused Zelensky of not wanting to end the war and suggested that Ukraine should replace its leader or change its negotiating representative. He has also argued that Zelensky could have reached a deal with Moscow earlier.
“Ukraine’s leader is feeling the strain, as he told his EU counterparts in private meetings in Brussels last week, according to the first diplomat,“ Politico’s report said.
A senior European official told the outlet that Trump’s approach reflects a mix of political calculations, business interests and personal preferences.
“They are currently in an election cycle and need someone to blame for rising prices,” the official said.
EU diplomats have also expressed frustration at being excluded from US-Russia discussions.
“There is probably much more dialogue between the Americans and the Russians than we might know,” one diplomat said.

articles.title: South Sudan accuses neighbor of deadly drone strike
articles.body:
South Sudan accuses neighbor of deadly drone strike
South Sudan has accused neighboring Sudan of carrying out a drone strike on a market in the disputed Abyei region which reportedly killed 73 people and injured 19 others.
The South Sudanese Foreign Ministry said on Monday that it had summoned Sudanese Ambassador Essam Mohamed Karrar to express its strong objection to the attack on Amiet Market, located north of Abyei town.
“The Government of the Republic of South Sudan has learned with grave concern of the drone attack carried out by the Sudanese Armed Forces against Amiet Market, situated north of Abyei Town,” the ministry said. However, officials in Juba and Abyei did not provide direct evidence pinning the strike on the Sudanese Army. The Sudanese government has not publicly commented on the allegations.
Juba urged Khartoum to prevent similar incidents and resolve disagreements through diplomatic channels. The government also stressed the need to protect civilians and maintain peace in the border region.
The attack took place on Monday morning, hitting several sections of the market, including its northern entrance. At least 73 people were killed and 19 injured in the attack, Abyei’s information minister, Yohana Akol Ngor, told Radio Tamazuj.
An anonymous diplomatic source and an aid worker told Reuters that the strike hit a fuel depot at the market. The facility had previously been used to supply Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), the source added.
Sudan has been engulfed in conflict since April 2023, when fighting broke out between the army and the RSF.
Sudan descended into chaos in April 2023 when fighting erupted between the national army, the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). The conflict followed months of tension between their commanders, Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as Hemedti, over a planned transition to civilian rule. What began in the capital, Khartoum, as a power struggle has devastated the country, killing tens of thousands, displacing millions, and pushing parts of Sudan into famine.
Regional and international peace efforts, including African Union mediation and Saudi-US talks in Jeddah, have repeatedly stalled. In September 2025, the Quad group – the US, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, and the United Arab Emirates – proposed a three-month humanitarian truce leading to a permanent ceasefire and a civilian-led political transition. Burhan rejected a subsequent US-led proposal that November, arguing it would dismantle state security institutions while leaving the RSF in place. The paramilitaries said they accepted the truce.
The UAE’s involvement has deepened mistrust of mediation. Sudan’s army-backed government severed diplomatic ties with Abu Dhabi in May 2025, accusing it of supporting the RSF. The UAE denies supplying weapons to the paramilitaries. Relations with Washington deteriorated further in September 2026 after the US questioned both factions’ legitimacy. Sudan rejected the remarks and called for peace efforts free from foreign dictates.
Meanwhile, rival administrations have entrenched Sudan’s divisions. Burhan’s government returned to Khartoum in January 2026 after the army recaptured the capital, having operated from Port Sudan during the fighting. In July 2025, the RSF-aligned TASIS coalition announced a rival government based in Nyala, Darfur, with Dagalo heading its governing council. The UN Security Council and African Union rejected the move.
Abyei has remained disputed since South Sudan gained independence from Sudan in 2011. The UN maintains a peacekeeping mission in the area, known as UNISFA, to help prevent violence.
South Sudan has been plagued by political instability and armed conflict since gaining independence in 2011. A five-year civil war erupted in 2013 over a feud between President Salva Kiir Mayardit and former First Vice President Riek Machar, rooted in power struggles within the ruling Sudan People’s Liberation Movement (SPLM – the party was founded in Sudan in 1983 and still keeps the same name). The 2018 peace agreement formally ended the civil war, but clashes continue across the country, driven by local militias and resource disputes.
The situation has been further complicated by political upheaval, including the arrest of Machar in March 2025. Machar’s party, the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement‑in‑Opposition (SPLM‑IO), has warned that his detention effectively nullifies the 2018 peace agreement. Machar has been accused of supporting the White Army, a militia composed largely of Nuer fighters, which reportedly participated in clashes in Upper Nile state.
Ongoing insecurity has displaced hundreds of thousands, worsening the humanitarian crisis. According to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), by the end of 2025, South Sudan had over 2.7 million internally displaced persons, and more than 9 million people in total are in need of humanitarian assistance.
In May, Russia’s deputy permanent representative to the UN, Anna Evstigneeva, warned that armed groups were obstructing efforts to settle Abyei’s status. Addressing the UN Security Council, she said RSF activity and continued fighting in neighboring areas were worsening security conditions. “It is the actions of elements opposing Khartoum that are the main obstacle to the start of a comprehensive settlement process,” Evstigneeva said.

Details: In 2024, the suspect was an authorised representative of Vladimir Putin in the presidential election, the Prosecutor General's Office reported.
The Book of Executioners, a Ukrainian project documenting Russian war criminals and those who betrayed Ukraine, says the suspect is Artem Sharlai, a native of Zaporizhzhia who has actively supported Russia since the beginning of the war in Ukraine's east.
Investigators say the suspect worked with Russian troops and officers of Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB) to persecute clergy with pro-Ukrainian views.
Quote: "He demanded that services in Ukrainian be stopped, that Ukrainian military personnel no longer be mentioned in prayers, that ties with religious organisations in Ukraine be severed and that congregations be re-registered under Russian law.
He also collected information about pro-Ukrainian priests and passed it on to FSB officers for further persecution."
Details: In December 2022, Sharlai personally took part in a search of a Greek Catholic parish and directed the search for religious literature deemed "extremist". This material was subsequently used as grounds for detention.
The investigators believe the suspect's actions facilitated the unlawful expulsion of Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church clergy, who are protected under international humanitarian law. He is accused of violating the laws and customs of war under Article 438.1 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine.

articles.title: NATO to send planes and drones to Black Sea after attacks on shipping
articles.body:
NATO to send ‘additional assets’ to Black Sea after drone attacks off Bulgaria, Romania
- NATO will send “additional assets” to the Black Sea, including surveillance, reconnaissance and forensics, after drone strikes near Romania and Bulgaria.
- Bulgaria said a US P-8 Poseidon has started patrols, and Sofia expects “further assistance” after the attacks on ships and missing sailors.
- EU diplomat Kaja Kallas called “six attacks in 10 days” a “dangerous and unacceptable escalation”, warning of risks to grain exports and global food supplies.
AI generated
BRUSSELS - NATO said on Oct 20 it will deploy “additional assets” to the Black Sea after a string of drone strikes off Romania and Bulgaria in the latest spillover from Russia’s war on Ukraine.
“NATO will be sending additional assets to the region, including support for surveillance, reconnaissance, and forensics,” NATO spokeswoman Allison Hart posted online, after a meeting of alliance ambassadors in Brussels.
“We will continue to stand united and ensure that we are ready and able to address any threat and to keep our one billion people safe,” she added.
The announcement from NATO came after Bulgaria’s Prime Minister Rumen Radev said that a US military plane had started to patrol the Black Sea following a plea for help after recent drone attacks.
“An American P-8 Poseidon... has begun patrolling the Black Sea to conduct reconnaissance missions and detect any activity that could pose a risk,” said Radev.
He said some NATO countries were quick to answer his call for help after the attacks and that Sofia expects “further assistance”.
The spate of strikes on ships in the waters off NATO and EU members Bulgaria and Romania have left more than a score of sailors missing and stirred condemnation in Europe.
The European Union’s top diplomat Kaja Kallas on Oct 20 said that “six attacks in 10 days by suspected Russian drones marks a dangerous and unacceptable escalation”.
Kallas accused the Kremlin of once again stepping up efforts to hit exports of Ukrainian grain via the Black Sea in a bid to starve Kyiv of revenues.
She warned that the latest strikes were adding to a “perfect storm” facing global food supplies already being battered by droughts in multiple regions and the war in the Middle East.
The attacks have also compounded worries at NATO over what is seen as increasingly reckless actions by Moscow at a time when its forces are bogged down in Ukraine.
NATO and the EU are grappling with what they say is a “hybrid” campaign of sabotage and interference by the Kremlin aimed at undercutting Western support for Kyiv.
NATO has sought to signal to Russia to tamp down its actions after high-profile incidents over the summer, including the discovery of an explosive-laden drone at a German airport. AFP

articles.title: Anti-corruption agents target Ukrainian central bank chief – media
articles.body:
Anti-corruption agents target Ukrainian central bank chief – media
Anti-corruption investigators are reportedly targeting the head of Ukraine’s central bank, Andrey Pyshny, in a series of searches.
The National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) confirmed on Wednesday that its detectives were searching the National Bank of Ukraine (NBU) and the residence of one of its employees. The agency, seen as a Western-backed beach-head for tackling rampant corruption in Ukraine, neither confirmed nor denied media reports that Pyshny was involved.
Pyshny was identified by several opposition MPs and law enforcement sources cited by Ukrainskaya Pravda and the US-funded Ukrainian branch of RFE/RL. Both outlets have a track record of obtaining insider information from NABU.
The central bank chief was previously mentioned in the Ukrainian press as a possible person of interest in the so-called Forest Gump case, a NABU investigation into the alleged laundering of money intended to cover bail for former Energy Minister German Galushchenko.
The anti-corruption agency accused Irina Mudraya, then-deputy head of Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky’s office, of improperly influencing state-owned Sense Bank to conceal the origins of millions of dollars in cash. She was subsequently dismissed.
Vadim Vesyoly, a former adviser to the bank’s supervisory board, has been described by Ukrainian media as an informal overseer influencing its decisions on behalf of Zelensky’s inner circle. Pyshny has denied allegations that he arranged Vesyoly’s appointment in 2023, shortly after the bank was nationalized. Vesyoly’s formal advisory role ended last year, although some Ukrainian outlets claim he continued to wield influence.
Vesyoly’s name surfaced in surveillance recordings linked to Timur Mindich, a longtime associate of Zelensky. Last November, Mindich was accused of masterminding a $100 million kickback scheme involving the state-owned nuclear power company Energoatom.
After Mindich fled Ukraine, Sense Bank and Vesyoly reportedly began dealing directly with Zelensky’s office, allegedly enabling Mudraya to carry out the money-laundering operation. Galushchenko, the former minister whose bail was allegedly financed with dirty money, is also a suspect in the Mindich case.
In surveillance recordings leaked to Ukrainskaya Pravda, Vesyoly and one of Mindich’s alleged accomplices can be heard discussing appointments to Sense Bank’s supervisory board and a potential takeover of Karpatneftekhim, a major petrochemical complex in western Ukraine.
MP Yaroslav Zheleznyak, one of the lawmakers who first publicized Wednesday’s searches, claimed NABU detectives were pursuing leads concerning Vesyoly’s involvement with Sense Bank and Karpatneftekhim at the central bank.

articles.title: Emily Feng on the Uyghur fighters who helped topple Assad
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Our Hearts Burned For Home: Emily Feng on the Uyghur fighters who fought Assad for a homeland of their own
How did a few thousand Uyghur hairdressers and farmers, shoe salesmen and writers, become part of an elite fighting troop, a pivotal force in overthrowing Syria's brutal dictator Bashar al-Assad?
That is the question at the centre of this remarkable, rarely-told story. Journalist Emily Feng had gone to cover the Israel-Lebanon ceasefire in December 2024, but instead made her way to Syria as Assad fell.
In 2025, she found Central Asian fighters everywhere she went. With the help of exiled Uyghur writer Abduweli Ayup, essential when the new regime banned her from interviewing them directly, they tracked down some five dozen fighters and families from a 20,000-strong Uyghur community that had made Syria home.
About 4,000 of them took up arms. But why would stateless people endure hardship and martyrdom for a country that was not their own?
The answer is that Syria was never the point. The history of this rebel movement is not straightforward. Feng's candid interviews shed light on their complicated, fractured story. Our Hearts Burned For Home: Uyghur militants in Syria’s Civil War is the result.
A revolution within a revolution
Their presence in Syria was almost accidental; a mix of China's crackdown after the 1990s protests and 2009 Ürümqi riots, geographical chance, and revenge.
Unwilling to live in what they called the prison of Xinjiang, they made their way, some via Afghanistan to Syria, not to save Syrians but to learn how to fight for Hotan and Kashgar.
With no Arabic and no war experience, they typically got three months of training and were sent straight to the front.
In Jisr al-Shughur, in houses emptied by war, they built a state within a state: schools, businesses, their own security, raising children for the next war.
"We are raising our own army," one commander tells Feng. They decorated classrooms with cardboard tanks and anti-aircraft rockets to "acclimatise" children to war.
Never losing sight of that goal, they avoided joining other rebel groups and insisted on fighting as Uyghurs. But ideologically, things got complicated and fractured.
From 2014, ISIS/ISIS-K tried to recruit Uyghurs for a global caliphate. Most Turkestan Independence Party (TIP) Uyghurs rejected it; they wanted a Uyghur state, not a caliphate. Those who joined ISIS were arrested and became enemies.
When East Turkestan Islamic Movement (ETIM) leader Abdul Haq in Afghanistan pressed them toward al-Qaeda and the Taliban, they split from the Afghan Uyghurs in 2018, swapped the black Islamist flag for the blue flag of East Turkestan, and recast themselves as nationalists.
As far as the new regime-in-waiting was concerned, it made them rather unreliable allies. In 2016-17 they refused to formally merge into Ahmed al-Sharaa’s Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS). Their goal was Xinjiang, not Syria, and joining HTS meant mission creep.
And yet they fought against the regime. Ferociously.
From neutral newcomers, they were dragged into the rebel independence fray in 2015, earning a fearsome reputation for holding the northern front against Russian bombardment for a decade.
They lived off savings brought from Xinjiang and weapons captured from regime forces. Forced to learn fast, they fashioned shoulder-launched rockets from scrap canisters and mixed their own explosives.
"War became free training," one says, for the future war with China.
Feng is compelling on the brutal reality of that training. The rebel regime was punishing and relentless as it hammered the motley band of volunteers into disciplined soldiers versed in intelligence, strategy and logistics.
Bilal, a former hairdresser, says, "Sometimes, I was so sad I cried.” Revenge pulled him through.
The book's heart is how they fought. After ten gruelling years of fighting hand-to-mouth, the book builds to its climax: Operation Deterrence of Aggression in November 2024.
Triggered by a regime strike that killed children in Ariha, the Uyghurs used a disused tunnel at Dadikh to penetrate Assad's stronghold.
Tragically, digging 500 metres short of their target, they pushed on regardless to break the line to Aleppo. Half their team was stuck with a jammed motorcycle in the tunnel, and one of their tanks was lost to a minefield.
But by November 30, thanks to a rebel-negotiated ceasefire with Russia, Aleppo finally fell. Days later, rebel troops stormed Damascus, and Uyghur fighters waving blue East Turkestan flags rolled into town, earning the respect of the new regime and a place in Syria’s independence struggle.
A new Syria, an uncertain future
It should have been triumphant. But it was hollow.
Feng captures the mood perfectly. They had fought tooth and nail for ten years, losing hundreds of kin. But this was not their war. They wept — not for Syria, but for home. They preferred to save their tears for Hotan or Kashgar one day.
What comes next is the book's most painful part. Where do 20,000 stateless Uyghurs fit in a new Syria when their loyalty lies 4,500 km away?
There are almost as many answers as there are Uyghurs.
Some Uyghur children feel no affinity with East Turkestan and want to become Syrian.
Others, with their long black beards and children who call Alawites and Christians "infidels," frighten locals and want to remain a state within a state independent of Syrian state institutions.
Neutrality, however, might have made them good wartime partners, but how could political independence work in the new Syria?
For many others, comfortable inertia has set in, and the debate over whether to settle or keep fighting for a liberated East Turkestan now dominates.
The new Syria is moving forward anyway, with or without the Uyghurs, and it has big decisions to make.
The TIP has been disbanded into the Syrian Army’s 84th Brigade, and Uyghur commanders have been given posts in the Defence Ministry.
Many hope for citizenship and schooling. But as one interviewee tells Feng: "I hope this exile does not last very long, because they will become more and more Syrian. I hope at the end, when we have our own land back, maybe they at least will still want to visit me in East Turkestan."
Debates about their future rumble on both inside Syria and among the exiled faithful marooned in Turkey.
Many of those in Turkey are de facto stateless after Ankara refused passports over their East Turkestan independence activism.
Living under a cloud of frequent threats of repatriation to China, Syria looks like the perfect place to raise children free to study the Quran and practise their faith.
Squeezed from all sides, the Uyghurs are threatened not only by Turkey but also by Beijing, determined to drag them back to the homeland.
Radicalised Syrian Uyghur fighters have been in China's sights for years, and the fear they might stir trouble in Xinjiang is never far from the surface.
One way for Beijing to solve that problem is to use them as a bargaining chip in Syria's desperate need for reconstruction. Rumours of such a deal abound, but Damascus has denied them for now.
What comes after victory?
Feng and Ayup have done something extraordinary in Our Hearts Burned For Home. This is not just a war story, but one of exile, ideology and what happens when a displaced people borrows another people’s revolution to train for their own.
Their story is not without controversy.
Some Uyghurs fear their militancy is justified, while others find it distasteful. They fear being tarred with the terrorist brush and thereby vindicating Beijing in its crackdown in the Uyghur region.
Feng was drawn to the sheer improbability of Assad's overthrow: some 30,000 rebels in fractious bands up against the Goliaths of Iran, Turkey and Russia. And winning.
In her conclusion, she hints their story might not be over: "What several thousand highly motivated, highly experienced Uyghur fighters can do may end up surprising us all. They have already surprised me."
The author is writing under a pseudonym to protect her identity

articles.title: Russia Releases Imprisoned American Man as Trump Envoy Meets With Putin
articles.body:
Russia has released a retired American teacher who had been imprisoned for more than four years on charges of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine. Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff confirmed the release Wednesday, during a meeting in St. Petersburg.
Witkoff referred to Putin as a "humanitarian" as he thanked him on behalf of U.S. President Donald Trump. "You talk so much about my President, President Trump, being a humanitarian—you are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that," he said.
Stephen Hubbard, 74, was sentenced to nearly seven years in a penal colony in 2024, after being detained in April 2022. Russian authorities accused the Michigan man of signing a contract with Ukraine’s military in the eastern Ukrainian city of Izyum after Russia’s full-scale invasion of the country in February 2022. The U.S. State Department under the Biden Administration declared that Hubbard, who was sentenced in a closed trial, had been wrongfully detained.
Trump said the release was secured at his request, "made directly" to Putin in a telephone conversation last week and was not part of a swap.
"Stephen is on his way back home and will soon be with his family," Trump said, noting that the U.S. "was not required to give anything in return."
Trump had hinted to reporters in the Oval Office on Tuesday that Hubbard’s release was pending. "Just stick with me," he replied, when asked about the American man’s case. "I don't want to talk about it, but everybody has been after Hubbard for a long time, long before I got here. And just remember that question for a couple of days from now, okay? Because I do things that nobody else can do."
The release of Hubbard comes in the wake of Trump waiving sanctions on Russia in a bid to progress the controversial diesel deal he made with Putin as he attempts to lower fuel prices, which have soared in the wake of his war with Iran.
The deal has earned bipartisan condemnation, with several Republican lawmakers joining calls for Trump to reverse course, insisting the action will only serve to bolster Putin’s war efforts as Ukraine braces for a fifth winter under attack.
Read More: Lawmakers Argue Trump's Russia Diesel Deal 'Violates' the Law. Here's What Legal Experts Say
Meanwhile, relations between Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky have deteriorated, with the latter voicing grave concern over the U.S.-Russia diesel deal. Trump announced an “energy cease-fire” between Russia and Ukraine on Oct. 11, calling on the two countries to stop targeting each other’s assets.
Zelensky accused Moscow of breaking the apparent agreement and, in turn, resumed strikes against Russian oil facilities, defying pressure from Washington. Trump called Ukraine's fresh wave of strikes a "disgrace" and said Zelensky is “more difficult to deal with than Putin.”
